Rubio took time out of his diplomatic schedule in a bid to to soothe jitters back home, where thousands of Americans saw their flights grounded, along with outages in banking and communications.
Earlier Tuesday a top-secret network that the National Security Agency uses for internal communications went down, the agency acknowledged.
The NSA said it had experienced "temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance," but that its capabilities remained operational and "our ability to defend national security continues."

The Trump administration has insisted Americans and their various systems remain secure, with Homeland Security secretary Markwayne Mullin insisting that the wave of recent outages does not stem from cyber criminals.
"I can tell you with complete certainty that we are not under attack," Mullin told CNBC. "There's no cyber threat that's taking place. The homeland is very secure."

313b86d738e03280: TOKYO: Bank of Japan Governor Kazuo Ueda said on Wednesday the central bank should continue raising interest rates while stressing the need to anchor underlying inflation around its 2.0 per cent target.
Speaking in parliament, Ueda said it was important to see underlying inflation anchored around 2.0 per cent over time and conduct monetary policy appropriately to ensure that this could be achieved.

"Given that financial conditions are still accommodative, it would be appropriate to continue raising the policy rate and adjust the degree of monetary easing in line with developments in the economy, prices and financial conditions," Ueda said.

The BOJ kept interest rates steady at 1.25 per cent at its October 30 meeting but declared victory in its 14-year battle to hit its price target and stressed its policy had entered a new phase focused on avoiding an inflation overshoot, reinforcing its hawkish bias.

Ueda said the planned consumption tax cut on food would likely support economic growth by boosting households' real purchasing power, though the size of the impact would depend on factors such as companies' pricing behaviour and consumer sentiment.
Once the details of the measure are finalised, the central bank will assess its impact on underlying inflation and reflect that analysis in future policy decisions, he added.

Asked about the possibility of emergency bond-buying operations, Ueda said the BOJ would make a comprehensive assessment based on conditions at the time, including whether serious disruptions to market functioning had emerged and required a policy response.

He also cautioned against using such operations to contain long-term yields, saying the move could prove counterproductive if markets perceive the BOJ as helping finance government spending. "In that case, long-term interest rates could become even more volatile," he said.

4510621dd9db4cda: At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.
The Zoom.com homepage loading the malicious JavaScript file from Optimizely. Image: blog.report-uri.com. Click to enlarge.

According to a blog post from the security firm Report URI, on November 16 malicious JavaScript code was served to visitors of 178 organizations through Optimizely’s platform. Report URI researcher Scott Helme wrote that the payload delivered by the malicious Javascript was rebuilt 26 times during the day, dropping a multi-purpose malware kit that could steal payment card data, cookies and screenshots, and swap any cryptocurrency payment addresses for the attacker’s.

Helme noted the affected websites also served exploit code custom made to attack known vulnerabilities in older Apple iPhone and iPad devices. Known by such names as “DarkSword” and “Coruna,” these are zero-click exploit kits that chain together a half-dozen security holes to seize complete control over outdated devices and extract data.

“The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy,” Helme wrote. “A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.”

Contacted for comment, Optimizely said that on November 16, 2026 it “identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in the Optimizely Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.”

“We acted swiftly to contain the incident and have fully remediated the identified vulnerability,” reads a written statement shared by Optimizely. “These measures included blocking access to the vulnerable path, deploying a fix, removing the injected code from affected projects, ending active sessions, revoking tokens, and resetting access for affected user accounts. We have also implemented additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered in Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation.”

Many top web properties no longer fully display content unless visitors agree to let often dozens of third parties serve JavaScript, a powerful web scripting language that enables interactive content. JavaScript code is run on the user’s device, and it can read information displayed in the user’s browser and even modify a website’s appearance or content.

One reason JavaScript is so heavily used is that it enables fairly precise browser fingerprinting and other ways of tracking visitors and clicks. According to the 2025 Web Almanac by HTTP Archive, the median homepage loads at least 22 JavaScript files. But as the incident with Optimizely shows, a compromise at a third-party vendor’s website can quickly snowball into a supply chain attack against downstream websites that end up serving visitors tampered and malicious JavaScript files.

Zach Edwards is a researcher at Infoblox and the co-founder of the ad-tracking service DecryptAds. Edwards said Optimizely is a vendor which often collects data outside of consent flows, with their JavaScript snippets being embedded as close to the top of the page as possible to ensure that it’s one of the first things to render, which is important since the product is primarily built for A/B testing.

“So to make the product work as expected, this code is setup to fire immediately on-page load, and not restrict rendering behind a consent dialog box,” he said. “This means that this supply chain attack didn’t require any clicking or consent to trigger — most of the impacted clients would immediately serve up the payload as soon as someone loaded the page, further increasing risks from this type of JavaScript snippet being compromised.”

Websites can minimize the chances that a breach at a third-party content provider spirals into a supply chain attack by taking full advantage of “Content Security Policies” or CSPs, which specify the domain names that are allowed to serve third-party content. But Edwards said most websites — apart from perhaps the largest e-commerce, social media and financial platforms — don’t even bother with CSPs, or else tend to leave them overly permissive for marketing reasons.

“With literally all websites which embed 3rd party JavaScript resources, if you don’t have a content security policy then if any of those partners get compromised, new domains can be injected into your website via JavaScript which won’t be stopped,” he said. “We’re in the age of JavaScript supply chain attacks and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators, even though it’s not always simple to get it initially deployed.”

How broadly deployed were CSPs at the websites impacted by the Optimizely attack? According to Report URI, 68 of the sites had no CSP at all, while 50 of them had a CSP that still allowed the malware payload and the data theft. The company found only 24 of the affected sites (15 percent) had CSPs that fully blocked the malicious payload.

The overall deployment of CSPs across the Web’s busiest sites is somewhat lower — about 10 percent — according to Helme’s site crawler.ninja, which scans the top million websites daily for security issues. Helme said he hopes this incident will encourage more sites to adopt effective CSPs, noting that it could have been far worse: By Report URI’s estimates, the purveyors of this malware attack managed to steal only around $7,500 worth of virtual currency from affected users, as well as an unknown number of payment card records.
Helme said he often compares the current widespread lack of CSPs to the Wild West.

“Organizations are running all this code, but they don’t know what it’s doing,” Helme said in an interview with KrebsOnSecurity. “This is why we keep seeing such large scale breaches in places [where] there are no checks and rules in place on the code we’re running, so this was kind of inevitable. Once an attacker gets to the point of running code on your site, the question is what do they want to do with that and can they write the script to do it. Now with AI that’s not a problem anymore.”

Internet users can control the JavaScript elements allowed to run on webpages by using simple script-blocking plugins like NoScript. But these tools have always only been effective for diehard security and privacy nerds who are willing to put up with sifting through dozens of JavaScript requests on each new website.

Happily, modern ad blocking software can handily block most third-party JavaScript requests. Ten years ago, the standard security advice for end users was to install antivirus and enable a firewall. These days, your ad/script blocker is your firewall. We explored several options and approaches to blocking ads in our August 2026 story, Who’s Tracking You?
178822b42825844f: MUAR: The death of their second child from a high fever became a turning point for a rubber tapper couple, inspiring them to encourage their other children to pursue careers in medicine.
The dream of the late Loo Siew Chin and her husband, Lim Tang Too, grew into a remarkable family legacy, with eight of their 11 children becoming doctors.
Today, 46 doctors across four generations carry on that legacy, alongside 15 spouses, bringing the extended family total to 61.
Their eldest son, Datuk Dr Lim Boon Sho, 81, said 34 of them are specialists serving in Malaysia and abroad, including in the United Kingdom, Australia, Ireland and Scotland.
Recalling their journey, Boon Sho said his parents were particularly proud when he secured a scholarship at 17 to study medicine in India, followed by seven of his younger siblings.

"My late parents always encouraged us to pursue careers in medicine not just for our own benefit, but more importantly, to serve the community so that the loss of family members due to a lack of proper medical treatment would not happen again," said the former Sungai Bakap state assemblyman.
The family's story came to light following Loo's death at the age of 104 on Nov 12. She was laid to rest at the Trinity Church Muar Cemetery on Monday.

Also sharing their experiences were six of Boon Sho's siblings: Dr Lim Boon Sin, 77; Dr Lim Boon Ben, 75; Dr Lim Boon Seng, 73; Dr Lim Boon Hock, 68; Dr Lim Boon Han, 64; and Karin Lim Ai Ching, 66, a lawyer.

The couple's fourth child, Boon Seng, said one of his most unforgettable memories was fleeing their home in Serom with his parents following an attack by communist insurgents, before being taken in by a Malay woman they fondly called Aunty.
"At the time, we stayed in a hut she owned, and Jalan Serkam became the place where we grew up. It was there that our parents began running a small business.

"Although our family was quite poor, to the extent that even a loaf of bread or a packet of fried noodles had to be shared, our mother was always kind to others. Anyone who came to our home would never leave empty-handed," he said.
He added that his parents also had four adopted children, two of whom became doctors.
The couple's seventh child, Boon Han, said they were taught from a young age to always do good, help those in need and refrain from hurting others.

"One of our mother's pieces of advice that we will remember for the rest of our lives was to be generous, never look down on others and never cheat. These are the values we have held on to throughout our lives and have contributed to our success. She also reminded us that whether in good times or bad, our family must always remain united and help one another.
"Our mother was everything to us, and among the things we will remember following her passing is her favourite meal of rice porridge served with pickled vegetables and homemade salted eggs," he said.

b17ffa7e6c38b2e0: ‘…stability, where it exists, is only ever twelve months deep’
Originally published on Global Voices

Activists hold a candlelight vigil to commemorate those who lost their lives in post-election violence in Tanzania in Nairobi, Kenya, on November 20, 2025. Image by Anadolu Lucas-Mukasa courtesy of FORUS.
By Clarisse Sih, Bibbi Abruzzini, and Jake Wieczorek
“Every one of our grants is annual and project-tied. We have no reserves and no core funding, which means that stability, where it exists, is only ever twelve months deep.”

That is how one civil society organization in Algeria described its finances to us in a recent survey. It is a sentence many donors would recognize from their own grant files, and it captures a reality familiar to many organizations: years of navigating short-term grants, restricted budgets and uncertain renewals, with little room to plan beyond the next funding cycle.

For years, civil society organizations have been encouraged to diversify their income, develop new partnerships and build financial and capacity resilience. But the latest — and many would argue the chronic — funding crisis is exposing the systemic retreat in development funding. Alternative sources are scarce, civic space is under pressure, and the political environment is becoming increasingly hostile.
A shock on top of a squeeze

Official development assistance fell by more than 23 percent in 2025, the largest annual drop ever recorded, and is projected to fall even more in 2026. Twenty-six of the 34 members of the OECD’s Development Assistance Committee cut their aid, and the US aid freeze that flooded headlines turned out to be just one part of a wider retreat.

To understand what this means in practice, the European Union System for an Enabling Environment for civil society (EU SEE) consortium partners — Hivos, Forus, Democracy Reporting International, European Partnership for Democracy, Transparency International and Civicus surveyed organizations in their networks between August and September, receiving 195 responses from over 68 countries.

The findings reveal the scale of the disruption: three-quarters of respondents say their funding is lower than at any point in the past decade. A third say more than half of their budget has been affected since January 2025, and 86 percent report harder terms, such as grants not being renewed, being reduced or cancelled or even more complicated compliance terms.

“The results show a perfect storm for civil society. Funding is disappearing at the very moment many organizations are facing greater political pressure. What’s being lost is not just programs and jobs, but the independent voices to defend rights, give voice to vulnerable communities, and hold power to account,” explains David Kode, program director of EU SEE.

The hardest hit were mid-sized, locally rooted organizations, despite having the most diversified funding. Among them, 90 percent reported funding cuts, 77 percent lost staff or reduced programs, two-thirds scaled back advocacy and community outreach, and 59 percent became less vocal publicly.
These are organizations connecting communities with services, donors and local governments.

Responses to question 11 in the survey: From January 2025 until today, what percentage of YOUR organization's budget has been impacted by donor budget cuts? Budget impact differs across organizational profiles. Screenshot from the survey. Fair use.
“We have had to sacrifice even our own salaries from other private sources to keep the NGO open and those who received a monthly salary are now working ad honorem,” said a respondent from Honduras.
In Indonesia, some organizations put staff on unpaid leave, while others could pay only half of their employees’ salaries.
What is lost beyond jobs

Yet the damage is not only monetary: almost half of respondents report reduced capacity for advocacy and about 40 percent say they have become less vocal or reduced their reach. A third of the respondents report having less control over their own priorities, and some have moved away from contested areas of work to keep their funding.

At the same time, almost two-thirds say civil society work has become less safe since early 2025, with more than half reporting more scrutiny, harassment or legal and administrative restrictions and half pointing to narratives portraying civil society as foreign-influenced.

This reflects a wider deterioration in the environment in which civil society operates. As one respondent from Zimbabwe put it: “The current funding crisis should not be viewed only as a financial challenge; it is fundamentally a civic space and democratic governance challenge.”

“An enabling environment is not simply the existence of a supportive policy. It is being able to register without unnecessary obstacles, access resources without compromising independence, speak and organise safely and meaningfully, influence decisions that affect communities — and knowing that when risks emerge, there are institutions and partners willing and able to respond,” says Marie L’Hostis, program and advocacy director at Forus.

These narratives do not stay rhetorical for long. The relationship between funding and civic space is particularly visible where governments are introducing or enforcing restrictions on organizations receiving resources from abroad.

In El Salvador, President Nayib Bukele accused journalists and civil society organizations of misusing USAID funds as part of a global money laundering operation, just as the US aid freeze hit. A few months later, the Legislative Assembly approved a Foreign Agents Law requiring anyone receiving funds from abroad to register and pay a 30 percent tax on those contributions.

By September 2025, long-standing organizations had begun to close: FESPAD, founded in 1988, and FUDECSO, after 33 years of work, both announced their dissolution, citing legal uncertainty and an unsustainable financial burden.

In Uganda, the proposed Protection of Sovereignty Bill 2026 would require any individual or organisation receiving money from outside the country, even from Ugandans living abroad, to register as a “foreign agent” and seek ministerial approval. In a country where most NGOs depend on foreign funding, that turns the loss of donor money into a question of legal survival. Foreign agents laws are spreading, stigmatizing civil society and choking the funding that remains.
The bigger picture

The consequences extend beyond the loss of individual projects. David Kode warned that the current crisis also involves “an erosion of relationships” and a breakdown of trust between donors and civil society.

A separate Forus report, “Strengthening the Enabling Environment for Civil Society: Evidence and Priorities for Action,” reaches a similar conclusion: abrupt funding shocks are not simply financial setbacks but structural threats to civil society’s independence and ability to act.
As report researcher Nicole Walshe put it during the launch, “without the resourcing, there is no civil society.”

The report points out that “these shocks transfer risk to local actors and weaken institutional capacity.” How long funding lasts, how restrictive its conditions are and who decides priorities all shape whether civil society can advocate, organize collectively and hold decision-makers to account.
So, what would make a difference?

Donors should protect continuity before disruption becomes irreversible: bridge funding, early warning of cuts and responsible exits. They should make compliance proportionate to context and risk, and fund legal, physical, and digital protection. The respondents call on national governments to protect access to domestic and foreign funding and the freedom to speak.

Governments can deepen the crisis or soften it. In Botswana, as international donors including USAID withdrew, the government reduced its own funding to civil society, including cutting all funding to the Botswana Council of Non-Governmental Organizations (BOCONGO), the national umbrella body. Organizations that support some of the country’s most vulnerable communities were left with neither international nor domestic support at the very moment both were needed most.

For Chris Nkwatsibwe of Uganda’s National NGO Forum (UNNGOF), civil society needs predictable, multi-institutional financing, alongside reserves that allow organizations to withstand political pressure and financial shocks. Domestic resources and alternative forms of ownership are equally important to reduce dependence on foreign funding and accusations of foreign influence.
“What kind of financing can now enable civil society to really genuinely remain independent, but also continue thriving in conditions of civic restrictions?” Nkwatsibwe asks.
The opportunity is to move from funding civil society to sharing power with it: in decisions, resources and defining success.
As Forus Co-Chair Moses Isooba told the Aid Matters 2026 conference in Vienna, “Power moves when three things change: who decides, who holds the resources and who defines success.”

In Morocco, Latifa Soufiani of Espace Associatif called on international donors and financial institutions to make respect for freedom of association central to their cooperation with governments. “We must be present to make our voices heard,” in international cooperation, she argued.

Luisa Rodríguez Táriba of Venezuela’s Sinergia highlighted how shrinking international support is undermining organizations’ ability to maintain teams and sustain both humanitarian and civic space work. As she observed, “The reduction of civic space doesn't happen overnight. It is multifactorial and happens over time.”

Despite the pressures, she offered a reminder that should remain at the centre of funding decisions: “The most important thing is people” and the communities they are part of must come before institutions, priorities and funding agendas.

a5fc2eaeb0734af0: LOS ANGELES: Mauricio Pochettino's reign as United States coach ended with a simple 2-0 win over Haiti on Tuesday, sent off in style by a Christian Pulisic bicycle kick as he heads to his new role at Manchester United.

Alex Freeman, the 22-year-old defender given his debut by Pochettino who has become a stalwart at right-back, did superbly to intercept a clear-cut chance for Josue Casimir.
Hall's header in the final few minutes bounced off the crossbar.

e7e02a671eb04136: SHAH ALAM: Property developers cannot escape liability for construction defects even after the defect liability period (DLP) has expired, the High Court has ruled.

Judge Sumathi Murugiah made the ruling after finding that Astana Modal (M) Sdn Bhd had failed to effectively rectify recurring water leaks and related damage in luxury homes at D'Island Residence in Puchong.
She said developers remained responsible for poor workmanship despite having carried out repairs, particularly when defects persisted or recurred.
"Astana's earlier rectification works and the expiry of the DLP do not provide a complete defence where the water leakage remained or recurred because the repairs were ineffective.

"I therefore find that the plaintiffs have proven that Astana breached its obligation to construct and deliver the affected properties in a good and workmanlike manner," she said in her grounds of judgment delivered yesterday.
The ruling followed two lawsuits against Astana involving 69 purchasers of 41 semi-detached and super-linked houses, as well as two other purchasers of a double-storey house in the same development.
The purchasers claimed that their properties had numerous defects, including cracks, water leaks, staining, uneven finishes and alleged structural deficiencies.
Although Astana had carried out repairs on several occasions, some defects persisted or recurred, prompting the purchasers to take legal action.
Sumathi said the recurring defects were concerning, given that the properties had been marketed as luxury homes and sold at high prices.
"Given that the properties were marketed as luxury homes and sold for high prices, it is impossible to ignore the recurring occurrence of defects.
"Defects may ordinarily arise during the DLP and be remedied by the developer.
"However, the defects in the present case were not isolated complaints confined to the DLP.
"Some of them recurred despite Astana's previous attempts to rectify them and continued to appear even after the DLP had expired," she said.
She said Astana's own structural expert had also accepted that damage to plaster ceilings caused by water leaks was uncommon in a five-year-old building.
Sumathi said developers could not rely on an "as is where is" clause in a sale and purchase agreement to avoid liability for hidden defects or poor workmanship.
However, she dismissed the purchasers' claims that their homes were structurally unsafe or unfit for occupation.
She said they had failed to provide sufficiently reliable technical evidence to prove that the concrete used in the properties did not meet the required Grade C25 specification.
Grade C25 refers to concrete designed to withstand a compressive strength of 25 megapascals (MPa), a specification commonly used for structural components such as beams, columns and floor slabs.
Sumathi also dismissed their claims seeking to invalidate the Certificates of Completion and Compliance (CCCs) issued for the properties.
The court ordered Astana to pay the reasonable costs of rectifying recurring water leaks and the resulting damage to the affected properties.
The amount is to be calculated based on rectification quotations submitted during the trial, before the court order is filed.
The court also awarded the purchasers RM35,000 in legal costs.
Other claims, including refunds of the property purchase prices, expert fees, separate negligence damages, general damages for distress, aggravated damages and exemplary damages, were dismissed.

b3b92e37dd213603: From Mazli Noor

China’s industrial growth and capabilities have been a lesson in economic singlemindedness unmatched in recent history. Much as we might admire it, however, we must recognise that China’s industrial overcapacity has direct – and not necessarily all positive – implications for Malaysia’s own.

While lower-priced inputs bring significant short-term gains to consumers and producers alike, the consistent and prolonged import pressures they create can also pose long-term structural challenges for Malaysian industries, businesses and the broader Malaysian macroeconomy.

Overcapacity cannot be measured by any one given statistic, nor can undue trade or pricing practices be construed as a deliberate act of dumping simply based on volume or import trends. They are as contentious as they are opaque, as precedents brought to the World Trade Organisation have shown.

A significant portion of the trade deficit stems from an increasingly integrated supply chain, where raw components are assembled or finished in Malaysia for onward export to third-party markets. Regardless, the investment, trade and industry ministry (Miti) has been sufficiently concerned to initiate a detailed product audit that aims to differentiate between legitimate industrial inputs and imports that effectively constitute dumping, which might threaten the operational viability of local factories.

Goods from China now account for an estimated 26% to 27% of Malaysia’s total imports. The last full year figures from 2025 put Malaysia’s trade deficit with China at between RM146 billion and RM163.4 billion. This has widened markedly in 2026, with the first-nine-month deficit at RM191.5 billion, or 70% more than in the same period a year earlier.

By contrast, Malaysia recorded a 2025 trade surplus with the US of RM100 billion to RM101.5 billion. The comparison becomes even more vivid when we consider that Malaysia’s total trade surplus grew by 115.7% year-on-year to RM232.4 billion in the first nine months of 2026.

A deficit does not mean that all imports are harmful. The figures do, however, make it crucial that we keep a close eye on local producers, and how the country’s future investment and production capabilities are affected.

The widening influx of lower-cost manufacturing inputs from China has seen local firms simply unable to compete. Domestic factories in the iron, steel, plastics, chemicals and textile sectors have been compelled to scale back production. The dwindling orders mean machinery and labor operating at well below optimal levels, pushing up marginal costs and placing downward pressure on overall productivity.

The steel industry provides a clear example. The Malaysian Iron and Steel Industry Federation reports domestic crude steel capacity utilisation of just 39.1%, compared with a global average of 75%. A Miti anti-dumping investigation found utilisation in galvanised steel at 65% – well below the 80% considered sustainable.

Similarly, SMEs are facing inordinate pressures: local SMEs struggle to compete with not just the more competitive prices but a broader and deeper catalogue of products from China, which benefit from scale, integrated supply chains and, in many cases, wide-ranging subsidies and state support. Sectors such as retail, food and beverage, construction, mechanical workshops and steel have registered the hardest hits.

The influx of well-capitalised foreign businesses has also driven up commercial property rents significantly, crowding out local merchants and vendors already dealing with regulatory and compliance expenses. Nor does the increased commercial activity benefit domestic job markets – many Chinese operators utilise "enclave supply chains" where they bring in their own capital, raw materials and workforce directly from home, limiting whatever spillover effects might have been factored in before.

With negligible to no uptake on local procurement, skills development, technology transfer or jobs creation, the domino effect this creates reverberates across Malaysia’s industrial landscape, posing a very real threat of premature deindustrialisation, i.e. the erosion of manufacturing just as we look to build a more resilient base of higher-productivity activities. The priority should be to deepen local capabilities, not increase dependence on imported products and components.

The last few years have also seen Malaysia grow increasingly exposed to China’s own trade disputes. The US, in particular, and Western markets in general, have been trading tariffs and punitive measures with Beijing across a host of industries, from farming to electronics to rare earths and semiconductors. Ironically, Malaysia’s place in China’s supply chain means it now faces the same scrutiny, but without a place at the table, placing its own access to other export goods and markets at risk with little recourse.

Lower prices are not, by themselves, evidence of unfair competition. Cheaper goods and services have given households much more affordable choices, with Chinese e-commerce platforms, retailers and brands expanding the range of products available to consumers. The concern is whether the competition is sustainable and fair, and whether consumers’ immediate savings come at the expense of local production, investment and reliable supply chains.

Malaysia should respond firmly and on the basis of evidence while honouring its trade commitments. The aim is to deal with unfair practices, secure greater benefits from foreign investment and help viable Malaysian businesses improve productivity. It should not be to insulate local firms from competition.

Miti should first make trade remedies faster and more effective. Reform of the Countervailing and Anti-Dumping Duties Act 1993 should allow investigations to proceed efficiently and duties to be imposed when evidence establishes dumping, subsidisation and injury under the relevant rules. Decisions must be timely and transparent, and ordinary price competition should not be a reason to qualify for protection.

Foreign investors should be mandated to build stronger links with Malaysian businesses. Local content and procurement expectations, designed in line with international obligations, can encourage the use of local suppliers, skills development and technology transfer. Supplier development programmes can help Malaysian firms meet the quality, scale and reliability standards major investors require.

Product standards and customs checks also need to keep pace with cross-border trade. Sirim and the customs department should strengthen risk-based inspections, including of goods sold through cross-border e-commerce. Imported products must meet safety and quality requirements, while origin declarations and product classifications must be accurate. The same standards should apply to local goods.

Support for SMEs should be directed strictly towards investment that raises productivity. Under the New Industrial Master Plan 2030, grants and financing can help smaller firms adopt automation, artificial intelligence and digital systems, strengthen quality control and develop new products. Tie support specifically to explicit improvements in operational or technical capabilities.

Malaysia also needs to move away from business models built on abundant, low-cost foreign labour. Reducing reliance on foreign workers will take a credible productivity strategy built around strategic input from employers, rather than ad hoc restrictions that leave firms unable to operate. Predictable labour policies, investment in automation, technical training and better management can raise output per worker. Workers, in turn, need opportunities to develop the skills required for higher-value jobs.

No single measure will be enough. Trade remedies cannot make firms more productive – investment incentives are worthwhile only if they help build local capabilities, and automation will not deliver much without finance, skills and reliable infrastructure.

Malaysia needs to turn today’s trade and investment flows into stronger domestic productive capacity across all sectors. That means monitoring imports accurately, enforcing trade rules, securing meaningful local participation in investment projects and helping firms move into higher-productivity – and higher wages – activities.
This is the only way that Malaysia can hold its own in a world dominated by China’s industrial might.
Mazli Noor serves on the boards of several public and private companies and is an FMT reader.

9aad3d1429562dda: Pakatan Harapan can blame racial politics, a polarised electorate, and the growing strength of its political rivals all it wants, but after another bruising defeat in Melaka, perhaps it's time the coalition look in the mirror.
Saturday's results saw Barisan Nasional win 21 seats, and its ally, Perikatan Nasional, three. PH's share was reduced to just four, one fewer than it secured in the 2021 polls.
It was another electoral setback following its poor showing in Johor and Negeri Sembilan.

Yet, if past experience is anything to go by, the coalition's post-mortem could once again revolve around familiar explanations: racial politics, the Malay vote, and its inability to penetrate the rural constituencies.
There is no denying that race and religion influence voters here, but these factors cannot forever serve as convenient explanations for PH's electoral shortcomings.
At what point does the coalition stop asking why voters are supposedly influenced by racial politics and start asking why those same voters are no longer convinced that PH deserves their support?
A coalition that has forgotten its promises
One of PH's biggest problems is its reluctance to confront the gap between what it promised before entering government and what it has delivered.
The coalition came to power in 2018 promising institutional reforms, greater accountability, transparency, and a cleaner political culture. But eight years later, how much of that enthusiasm remains?
PH cannot expect support simply because it once represented an alternative to BN.
It has been in government since November 2022, with Anwar Ibrahim as prime minister and its components holding important ministerial positions. It has had the opportunity to deliver on its promises.
Instead, voters are often given explanations about why reforms cannot be implemented or why political compromises are necessary.

Where are the apologies for promises that have been abandoned or watered down? Where is the sustained effort to reconnect with communities that feel neglected, not just when elections approach but throughout the term?
Perhaps the biggest contradiction is how PH has moved away from the principles it once championed.

The coalition previously fought for fairer parliamentary allocations, arguing that public funds should not be used as a political weapon against opposition MPs. Now, it withdraws the allocations for errant MPs.

Whatever the political justification, the irony is difficult to ignore. A coalition that once criticised the previous government for practising political discrimination now finds itself defending similar questions about the distribution of public resources.
Voters did not support PH merely to see a change in who exercises political power. They wanted a change in how that power was exercised.
The influencer experiment is backfiring
Another questionable aspect of PH's political strategy is its reliance on social media influencers and content creators.

There's nothing wrong with embracing digital campaigning, particularly to reach the younger voters. But there's a difference between using social media effectively and assuming trendy videos, scripted skits and supposedly relatable content will translate into political support.
During GE15, PH's campaign focused heavily on policy discussions, institutional reform, and fighting corruption. Today, some of its social media campaigning appears to have lost that seriousness.
PH has increasingly been associated with content that feels forced, cringey and disconnected from the supporters it's trying to engage. Even some PH supporters have criticised these efforts online.

Politicians aren't entertainers. A young voter struggling with stagnant wages, rising living costs and housing affordability is unlikely to be persuaded simply because a politician can perform a trending dance or deliver a rehearsed punchline.
PH appears to be mistaking social media engagement for genuine political engagement.
Parliament is not a ‘mamak' stall
The conduct of some PH MPs has also become increasingly difficult to defend.

Parliament should be where MPs debate policies, scrutinise legislation and raise the concerns of their constituents. While the opposition has MPs who rely on provocative rhetoric and attempts to bait government representatives, PH MPs should know better than to fall into the same trap.

The behaviour of certain representatives, including RSN Rayer (Jelutong) and Sany Hamzan (Hulu Langat), raises questions about whether they understand the difference between robust parliamentary debate and simply creating a commotion.
There's nothing wrong with being vocal or combative, but there must be substance behind the noise.

Voters want to hear what their MPs are doing about public transport, unemployment, housing and healthcare. They don't elect representatives to turn parliamentary proceedings into something resembling a heated argument at a mamak stall.
Candidate selection isn't a social media experiment
The Melaka election also exposed weaknesses in PH's candidate selection.

Giving younger candidates an opportunity is commendable, but youth alone should never be the qualification for public office. Candidates must be properly vetted and demonstrate an understanding of the communities they intend to represent.

One candidate who attracted attention for the wrong reasons was Mukhlisul Mubin Julasapiyah (Kuala Linggi), better known as Mukhlis Mubin. His campaign leaned heavily into a Gen Z identity, complete with the tagline, "This is how Gen Z works".
A campaign video attracted mixed reactions after he claimed to have secured a waiver of a penalty exceeding RM70,000 imposed on the Melaka Barat Area Fishermen's Association within a day.
Mukhlis said he approached Anwar's political secretary, who brought the matter to Anwar in his capacity as finance minister, who subsequently approved the waiver.
While helping an association representing 278 fishermen was commendable, the episode raised questions about the use of political connections to secure preferential treatment.
Critics questioned whether this was cronyism rather than the institutional reforms PH had promised.
There were also questions about his candidacy, given that his father had contested Kuala Linggi five times without winning.

PH must ask whether it selected candidates based on their ability to win public confidence or simply because they fitted a particular campaign narrative. An assemblyman needs considerably more than attractive online content to represent an entire constituency.
The electorate doesn't owe PH another chance
Another longstanding weakness is PH's grassroots machinery. The coalition cannot expect to build relationships through occasional visits and staged community engagements.
BN and PAS spent decades building networks through local leaders, party branches and community organisations. That machinery does not suddenly appear two weeks before polling day.

PH must understand that political loyalty is built through consistency, not campaign-season appearances. Perhaps the most uncomfortable truth the coalition needs to accept is that voters don't owe it their loyalty.
Those who supported PH in 2018 did so because they believed it could deliver a better Malaysia. They weren't signing a lifetime commitment to a party.
Some voters may not have rejected its reform agenda. They may simply have become disillusioned with the people entrusted to implement it.

Melaka should be more than another electoral setback followed by post-mortem meetings and familiar explanations. PH needs to take a hard look at its leadership, candidates, grassroots machinery, parliamentary conduct and, most importantly, its record in government.

Race and religion will remain part of Malaysian politics. But blaming racial politics every time voters turn away is not political analysis. It is an admission that the coalition has run out of answers.
PH once asked Malaysians to believe that a different kind of politics was possible. Now it must prove that that vision still deserves belief.
The question is no longer why voters are abandoning PH but why PH keeps giving them reasons to do so.
The writer is a journalist at FMT’s English Desk.
This article represents the writer’s opinion and does not necessarily reflect FMT’s position.

9b405e9e9b182487: WASHINGTON: Nvidia board chairman Harvey Jones opened a conference call with investors on Tuesday by saying the AI chip company would not rehire co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO and would not take questions on the matter.
Jones' start to a call about quarterly results was a forceful response to a movement to bring back Huang, who stepped down last week.

With Huang gone, investors are eager for clues about Nvidia's future and strategy, from its commitments of billions of dollars to cloud providers, suppliers and AI startups to who will ultimately lead the world's most valuable chipmaker.
Shares of the company rose 2% in extended trading, after Nvidia forecast sales ahead of Wall Street targets.
"It's no surprise that they're doing very well, and there'll be people who will breathe a sigh of relief about it," said Rick Meckler, partner at Cherry Lane Investments.
"But the story here is very complicated, and it's hard not to factor that in as an additional risk for people buying stock," Meckler said.
Jones said the board had hired executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles to help find a new CEO.

Interim CEO Colette Kress, who is also finance chief, kept her focus on financials and products in the statement accompanying results. "Our momentum is real," she said, without addressing the leadership issue. "Vera Rubin is off to an explosive start, our roadmap is on track," she added, referring to the company's latest flagship AI chip.
Huang, the AI boom's most prolific salesman, resigned on Thursday after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang and two with Nvidia employees.

US intelligence agencies are trying to determine the extent of Alice Huang's ties to China's state security ministry and what information she may have passed to Beijing, according to two people familiar with the matter.
Jensen Huang's exit ended three decades of founder-led control over Nvidia's chip roadmap, customer deals and Washington ties, making execution a bigger risk than near-term AI demand, analysts say.
Q4 outlook tops targets

The company expects fourth-quarter (Q4) revenue of US$130 billion, plus or minus 3%, above analysts' average estimate of US$125.25 billion, according to LSEG data. Nvidia said the outlook assumes no data-centre chip sales to China.
Adjusted gross margin is expected at 71% to 72%, compared with analysts' estimate of 71.7%.
Anshel Sag, principal analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy, said Nvidia's outlook was "quite positive, albeit not as ambitious as in previous quarters, which many have already anticipated".

"I don't think anything near-term will be affected by Jensen's departure. His executive leadership team is capable and has followed his leadership and executed effectively for years, reaching this point," he added.
The board is considering internal and external candidates for CEO, with Kress seen offering steady leadership during the selection process.
However, a growing "Stand With Jensen" campaign has complicated the search, and Huang said on Tuesday he would be "honored" to return if the board deemed it best.
National security scrutiny intensifies

Earlier on Tuesday, Nvidia's board created a committee on national security and export controls, its first major governance move since Huang's departure, as scrutiny grows over the chipmaker's national security role.

Washington has also tightened licensing rules for chip shipments to Southeast Asia and overseas data centres serving Chinese firms, while lawmakers prepare to question Huang, who had pushed for greater chip exports to China.
Investors were already uneasy about AI spending after the Democrats' sweep of the US midterm elections fueled fears of tougher scrutiny and slower data-centre expansion.
They also want to know whether Nvidia's next CEO will continue financing customers, a practice critics call circular.
Tuesday's results offer a first read on Vera Rubin, Nvidia's newest generation of AI processors and successor to Grace Blackwell.
Nvidia said in August that Vera Rubin would account for about a fifth of data-centre revenue in the October quarter and forecast 70% revenue growth in the next fiscal year.
Nvidia's third-quarter revenue more than doubled to US$115.84 billion, beating analysts' estimate of US$109.11 billion.
The company has topped Wall Street's revenue expectations for 17 straight quarters.
Adjusted gross margin rose to 74.9% from 73.5% a year earlier, also beating analysts' estimate of 74.1%, despite soaring memory prices and production ramps.
b96ca28a538fdb15: Kata beberapa penganalisis politik dan penyelidik termasuk daripada Ilham Centre, Barisan Nasional (BN) khususnya Umno, tetap boleh menang PRN Melaka tempoh hari walaupun bertanding solo. Begitu jugalah keadaannya di Johor dan Negeri Sembilan sebelum ini, kata mereka.
Ya, saya tahu ini membuat pemimpin, ahli dan penyokong PN terutama PAS marah. Apa lagi ketika pemimpin BN dan PN cukup yakin gandingan mereka boleh membawa kejayaan merampas Putrajaya.

Memang ada benar pandangan beliau. Namun pada PRN Melaka yang baru berlalu, PAS hanya bertanding dua kerusi. Maka tidak banyak 'peluang' untuk pengundi teras Umno beri 'sumbangan' kepada parti itu. Atau membuktikan semangat 'kesetiakawanan'.
Namun PAS menang jua di dua-dua kerusi. Wawasan, rakan PAS dalam PN juga menang, tapi satu kerusi sahajalah. Satu lagi komponen – Gerakan – seperti dijangka, tak menang apa-apa.

Apa pun mesti diakui, Melaka dan Johor memang kubu BN. Jadi betullah apa yang dikata penganalisis bahawa BN/Umno boleh menang on its own di kedua-dua negeri itu. I’m not sure about Negeri Sembilan. Dalam konteks kerjasama BN-PN, persoalan yang sering timbul untuk sekian lama adalah siapa tolong siapa lebih. Kerjasama lebih menguntungkan Umno-BN atau PAS-PN?
Kerap ditanya juga ialah soal transferability undi, yakni mana lebih banyak? Undi asal Umno pergi ke PAS atau undi asal PAS pergi ke Umno?

Tentu kita ingat Presiden PAS Hadi Awang beberapa kali menyeru ahli dan penyokong partinya mengundi BN di kawasan PAS tidak bertanding. Seruan beliau dibuat terbuka dengan lantang. Malah beliau turut meminta ahli dan penyokong PAS mengundi MCA dan MIC kerana 'mereka BN'.
Pernahkah pemimpin tertinggi Umno buat saranan ala Hadi? Iaitu meminta ahli dan penyokongnya undi PAS pada ketika Umno-BN tidak letak calon.
Setahu saya tidak. Adakah saya terlepas pandang dan terlepas dengar? Wallahua'lam.
Tetapi pada PRN Johor, Negeri Sembilan dan Melaka, bilangan calon Umno-BN melebihi calon PAS-PN. Di Johor, PAS-PN bertanding di 11 kerusi sahaja daripada jumlah 56 DUN.
Di Negeri Sembilan, PAS-PN tanding lima kerusi out of 36 seats in the state assembly. Manakala di Melaka, ada 28 kerusi DUN, PAS-PN tanding lima kerusi.

Saya beberapa kali menyatakan kerjasama Umno-BN dengan PAS-PN berjaya terjalin kerana PAS yang banyak mengalah. Parti itu tidak buat tuntutan (setakat ini), rela beri laluan kepada Umno-BN, tunduk akur meskipun dapat pittance. Needless to say, ahli parti tidak suka akan arrangement sebegitu. Ini diakui Hadi. Tetapi diteruskan juga 'demi Islam memerintah'.
Namun, saya sering juga tanya sampai bila PAS akan mengalah? Pada hemat saya, akan tiba masa PAS akan buat demand when the right time comes. By that I meant, pilihan PRU mendatang.
Bercakap mengenai PRU akan datang, lebih tepat PRU16, saya amat tertarik dengan kenyataan pengerusi BN yang juga Presiden Umno Zahid Hamidi yang disiar Malaysiakini tiga hari lalu.

Zahid dilaporkan berkata, BN belum merancang membentuk kerjasama atau persefahaman politik dengan PN bagi menghadapi PRU16. Ini bukanlah memeranjatkan kerana mungkin terlalu awal untuk bercakap mengenai PRU at this time.

92da6fb1944da7be: I watched the Bollywood film Ramayana last week and it was well worth the money. I went for a late morning show to avoid the crowd but was surprised to find only six families and a couple.
What was even more surprising—and pleasantly so—was the racial mixture of this small audience: three Indian families, a Chinese family, two Malay families, and an older Malay couple.

Why not? I thought. After all, the Ramayana didn’t just visit the Malay world; for centuries, it lived here. It was woven into the fabric of village life, shaped the language of court chronicles, and danced across white screens of buffalo skin in flickering torchlight.
Then again, I noted that only a very small number of Malays had ventured to watch the movie which had received rave reviews.

That made me think more deeply and I realised that the Ramayana in Malaysia today is a ghost story of culture—how an epic of foreign origin was lovingly adopted by the Malays, only to be quietly pushed to the margins by modern politics and shifting religious boundaries.
How did an epic composed in ancient India find its way into the hearts of Malay villagers and sultans?

Its journey happened in two distinct waves. Long before written books were common, the first wave arrived during the first millennium CE through maritime trade. Traders and travellers brought Indian culture, statecraft, and stories to early coastal trading centres such as Kedah Tua, Gangga Negara and Langkasuka, embedding foundational ideas into local life.

Centuries later came the second wave: the vernacular transformation. As scholar Alexander Zieseniss pointed out in his 1963 study, what reached the Malay world wasn't the classical Sanskrit text, but popular, post-epic oral versions carried by word of mouth from India.

You can still hear that journey in the names preserved in early Malay adaptations: Baradan, Wibisana, Maharaja Rawana, and Kumbakarna point directly to Tamil roots, proving the tales travelled through South Indian oral channels before anyone here ever wrote them down.

The result was the Hikayat Seri Rama, written in Jawi script. In a wonderful twist of global history, the oldest surviving illuminated manuscript of this text—dating back to around 1600 from the Aceh Sultanate—was brought to England by a trading sea-captain and eventually found its way to Archbishop William Laud, who donated it to Oxford’s Bodleian Library between 1635 and 1641.

While British colonial scholars like Richard Winstedt once framed this through the lens of Muslim courts simply "tolerating" old Hindu tales, modern historians see it as dynamic syncretisation. Local scribes and courts didn't feel conflicted; they indigenised the story, folding its heroes and moral dilemmas right into the Malay worldview.
In traditional literature, the Ramayana – which scholar C Hooykaas said “belongs to all ages and all creeds”- was a vital structural pillar.
Literary historians agree that these epics provided the foundational narrative DNA for classic court chronicles like the Sejarah Melayu and the Hikayat Hang Tuah.

Linguistically, the epic helped carry valuable Sanskrit vocabulary into the Malay language. While laksamana (traditionally derived from Rama’s loyal brother Lakshmana and historically used for admirals) is the most famous surviving direct borrowing, a whole vocabulary of statecraft, ethics, and storytelling entered everyday speech through this deep cultural exchange.
If court literature was where the epic found its intellect, the agrarian villages of northeastern Malaya were where it found its heartbeat.

For generations, wayang kulit Kelantan (traditional shadow puppetry) was not a museum piece or high art; it was community life. Imagine an all-night village performance under the stars. A single master dalang (puppet master) would sit behind a backlit cloth, single-handedly voicing dozens of characters while blending the grand plots of the Ramayana with local folklore, village humour, and Thai-Kelantanese aesthetics.

As traditional arts expert Ghulam-Sarwar Yousof noted, these epics provided the bulk of the raw material for the region's traditional theatre. In the villages of Kelantan, the Ramayana wasn't a foreign import. It was “our story”, performed collectively, without any modern anxieties about theological purity.

The fading of this vibrant tradition wasn't a natural accident of time. Shifting religious definitions in the latter half of the 20th century, especially from the 1980s, began to recast traditional folk arts through a narrower ideological lens.
The numbers tell a stark story. In 1969, Kelantan boasted around 300 active dalang. By the 1999 census, that number had plummeted to just 11 troupes.

While informal pressures accumulated soon after the Islamist party PAS came to power in Kelantan in 1990, the heavy blow landed legally with the 1998 Entertainment Enactment, which officially banned wayang kulit performances for containing "un-Islamic" elements - such as animist healing invocations and Hindu mythological roots.

Though the state government formally lifted the ban in 2019, it came with heavy strings attached: performances were only permitted under strict Shariah-compliant conditions, creating ongoing bureaucratic hurdles for traditional masters.

Today, only a tiny handful of senior dalang remain active in Kota Bharu, while Malaysia's national bid for UNESCO intangible cultural heritage status for the Kelantanese shadow play sits patiently pending.
Today too, active daily engagement with the Ramayana among the majority Malay population is practically zero. The living village tradition has faded under decades of regulatory constraints.
Yet the story hasn’t entirely vanished; it lingers in the background of modern life through regional identity, digital preservation, and occasional pop-culture references.

This is what I saw in the theatre that day. The Malays in the audience simply watched the spectacle as large-format entertainment—nothing more, nothing less, yet the myth's invisible threads ran right through the room. For I overheard the gentleman next to me telling his wife that Jatayu would come to the abducted Sita’s aid even before Jatayu’s appearance on screen.

Which reassured me that although it is not vibrantly alive in the way it once was, the Ramayana in Malaysia is not completely dead. It stands as a quiet, beautiful ghost story of culture—a reminder of a pluralistic past that still echoes softly in the dark of a cinema.

e76baf1a121aac1f: Hundreds of websites using the Optimizely website personalization platform served unsuspecting visitors a potent malware cocktail that targeted cryptocurrency wallets, stole payment card data, cookies, and screenshots, and delivered exploit kits for infecting iPhones and iPads, researchers said Tuesday.

ReportURI said it identified 178 websites—including CNN, Zoom, the BBC, and Salesforce—that were affected. JavaScript digitally signed by Optimizely and then loaded into customer pages had been modified to include malicious components that attempted to infect visitor devices with multiple payloads. When wares were installed successfully, they swapped user cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attackers. Other components skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and, on iPhones and iPads, delivered iOS exploit kits known as Coruna and DarkSword.

Optimizely serves JavaScript “snippets” that include both company code and code that is provided by each customer. The JavaScript, which can be served directly from Optimizely or from a customer endpoint, runs on every page the customer serves. Somehow, the attackers wrote their own code into a portion of each affected customer’s JavaScript and then delivered it from cdn.optimizely.com. A valid certificate for that domain signed the JavaScript.

<!--kg-card-end: html--> A few hours ago, I went to rent a Lime bike to ride the ten minutes to my therapy appointment. I opened Lime, scanned the QR code, and double clicked my iPhone’s side button to authorize Apple Pay. The app hung for a few moments, then closed. I tried several more times and the same thing happened. In the back of my mind, I wondered what was going on — was the Lime bike broken? Was my cell phone service out? Was it something else? I opened the Uber app and, similarly, wasn’t able to pay. I opened DownDetector and realized that the entirety of Apple Pay, a thing I thought existed only on my phone and not the cloud, was down. I texted my therapist, put my phone in my pocket, and started jogging.

Not being able to rent a Lime Bike for several minutes is an extremely minor inconvenience barely worth mentioning. And yet the mental gymnastics my brain did in those few minutes — what’s broken, why is it broken, how is it broken — is something that everyone I know have been repeatedly doing for the last few weeks as seemingly every service and system crashes down around us. Over the weekend, people who I do not normally talk to about my job asked me: What is going on with the airplanes? Why is my bank down? What about Microsoft?

The default assumption that many people are making is that these are either being caused by cyberattacks and/or “AI” broadly defined, whether that’s AI gone haywire, “rogue” AI agents, or something else, which is indicative of just how fearful people are of AI. What I have been telling people is, basically, that shit is broken and things are going to keep breaking. For lots of different reasons. It’s often not a hack and it’s often not explicitly AI-related, but everything now sort of looks like that XKCD comic of the dependency domino tower.

While not exactly true that AI and cyberattacks are causing these outages, it’s also not entirely wrong, either. What we’re seeing is — I think — a series of infrastructure failures (and some cyberattacks) that are not directly connected but are broadly a symptom of the same general trends and systemic problems we’ve seen across society, the government, and the tech sector over the last several years. (WIRED has a nice piece on how you can assess any given outage.)

First, it’s worth mentioning that anytime there’s a string of outages, there’s a tendency to tie them altogether. And outages or hacks that previously wouldn’t have been noted at all suddenly get more attention and become part of the narrative. Take, for example, the fact that the International Ice Hockey Federation has been targeted by a cyberattack; you probably would not normally hear about this but it has suddenly become part of the broader story.
The simplest explanation I can come up with for the broader disastrous trend we’ve seen is that since the pandemic we have seen:
mass layoffs of tech workers and software developers
mass deployment of AI-assisted and vibe coded products, software updates, and patches
mass layoffs in the government sector and outright destruction of government expertise and oversight
the loss of institutional knowledge associated with those layoffs and funding cuts
a failure to invest in upgrading infrastructure/redundancy
government contracts handed out to the President’s friends and political allies
AI and LLM-assisted/iterative exploit discovery, coding, and deployment
companies responding to the AI hacking threat with AI-coded and rushed patches

When Elon Musk took over Twitter and named it X, there were many people who thought his layoffs and the associated loss of expertise would result in the site failing basically because of an infrastructural failure. Twitter would basically “go down” because someone would break something and no one would know how to fix it. We haven’t really seen that happen to X, but that same philosophy of firing the experts and YOLOing AI into everything while hoping shit doesn’t break is now the explicit strategy of our entire economy and our entire government.

What we are seeing, then, is a mix of tightly clustered attacks, outages, and fuckups that you would expect to see when people and companies are careless, don’t know what they’re doing, or are working very fast to respond or duct-tape something together in the face of new threats.
"We are Ship of Theseus-ing our entire economy and infrastructure"

We know that this is happening to some extent because, in the aftermath of the PHP2Shell exploit, which was discovered with the assistance of LLMs, we saw various websites go down as they attempted to push updates faster than they normally would have to, because the time between a vulnerability being discovered and it being exploited is faster than ever. (As I was writing this, Calif, one of the companies that used LLMs to find PHP2Shell, announced that it had used LLMs to find apparently serious vulnerabilities in Java.)

Companies and agencies are pushing updates (including to, for example, our air traffic control system) on live systems, in part because of the threat of AI, and things are breaking. The National Security Agency, for example, said earlier Tuesday that some internal systems went down because of “temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance.”

Nick Andersen, the acting director of the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, said Tuesday that we need to build more resilience into our infrastructure, but building resilience and redundancies into software requires people who understand how systems can possibly fail, planning for it, and mitigating against it.

“Ultimately being able to prevail by being able to demonstrate resilience against disruptions, whether they occur because of things like an IT outage or a bad patch, or a modernization update gone awry, or because of a malicious malicious cyber incident — we want to make sure we’re engineering in the resilience that is going to be able to anticipate for and ultimately overcome those outages and those impacts,” Andersen said at an event called FedTalks.

We may eventually get to a place where expertise and understanding highly complex systems is once again a priority, but the last few years have been full of companies and governments moving incredibly fast to reduce reliance on humans and offload it to AI systems and AI-generated code in order to ostensibly save money on labor costs and/or carry out an antihumanist political project.

I thought this piece, called “Software is breaking down at a systemic level,” written by a software developer named Jimmy Breck-McKye, was quite good. He points at Kristen Maevyn’s The Decoherence Trap, which argues that AI-written code is causing a situation where people and companies do not understand their products.

“Most software engineers now are unable to tackle engineering problems without some form of AI assistance. That’s not because they’re incompetent — they just can’t keep on top of the complexity,” Breck-McKye writes. “Even if they could once, they now face a tsunami of AI generated code. This is affecting everyone, at all levels — we are all fighting the tide of small, incoherent changes that look rational in isolation but slowly lose sense as a whole.”

People increasingly don’t understand or have any idea how their code works, people are moving very fast, and bad things are happening. Any individual outage or breakdown is likely, to some extent, a coincidence. Many of the outages we are seeing have nothing to do with AI at all, but do have something to do with the broader lack of investment in infrastructure, redundancy, and expertise. We are Ship of Theseus-ing our entire economy and infrastructure and so, I guess, we must simply continue to expect bad things to happen.

80db653bfbebf32e: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella's Ignite conference keynote on Tuesday was all about trust. He opened by promising to earn back trust after last week's massive M365 outage and went on to focus on the need for organizations to trust their AI models.

"So last week in some sense was really a reminder of how critical digital infrastructure is as the dial tone for the world," said Nadella. "We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. And in that context, I know we have work to do to provide that resilience that you can count on, the world can count on, and we are committed to ensuring that we learn and we continuously improve."

Speaking at San Francisco's Moscone Center, Nadella described three areas of focus for the company as it works to build what he referred to as a frontier ecosystem: "Keeping the human at the center of it all, ensuring that you have ownership over your organization's intelligence and learning, and trust."

Anthrocentrism is a tough sell just weeks after offering buyouts to 60,000 employees. Describing the shift from hand-written code to agent-written code, Nadella suggested developers have moved from building software artifacts to building software factories that build those artifacts.
"The important thing here though is to remember still that that human intent, that judgment, that experience, skills, expertise all very much matter," he said.
People may judge development work, but ask them whether they have the same sense of ownership as when they wrote every line.

As to ensuring that organizations have ownership over their intelligence, that borders on heresy for a company with massive cloud computing commitments specifically to run AI workloads. If everyone really owned their machine learning models and ran them in their own data centers and on employee computers, Azure would be in trouble.
Yet Nadella emphasized ownership – which isn't at all obvious given the legal ambiguity of who owns AI generated code and whether it can be copyrighted.

"In the age of AI, the key question is how do individual firms continually build and own their learning and tacit knowledge?" he said. "For an economy to remain an economy where many firms exist and thrive, intelligence by definition needs to be broadly distributed versus just collapsed into a couple of models."

Suffice to say that Nadella is promoting client control over AI data that's processed mostly on equipment rented from Microsoft, with some allowance for customer-controlled infrastructure. But that still ought to concern frontier AI labs like Anthropic and OpenAI that favor a white-glove, black-box service model where they are the arbiters of access.
As for the third pillar of Nadella's vision, that's trust, which remains missing in action.

"How can you even trust all this powerful technology?" Nadella asked. "And the reality is, by definition, you can't. In other words, it becomes an architectural imperative to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it. And so our goal is to build a stack that addresses these three architectural imperatives."
Microsoft's original stack was built on ownership of the operating system. But the company's commitment to AI is such that it now describes Copilot in the terms once reserved for Windows.
"Copilot is the new operating system for work," said Nadella.
AI is eating software, and Microsoft is here for it
Fifteen years ago, venture capitalist Marc Andreessen famously observed that software is eating the world. Now AI, including Copilot, is eating software.
"Apps are just plugins to Copilot," Nadella mused. "That's why we in fact have brought all of Office, all of its richness, right built into Copilot."

Copilot is eating other companies too. Nadella said Microsoft is extending Copilot to take on specific roles by providing skills, connectors, and plugins for industry-specific tasks. Toward that end, "Copilot is the new front door to Dynamics 365," which now offers CRM plugins. And Nadella announced a partnership with Salesforce called Copilotforce that brings Salesforce context into Copilot, Teams, and Fabric.
He also talked up Microsoft IQ, the company's new enterprise context management platform.

"The idea behind IQ is to help every organization build, retain, and continuously improve your own intelligence across the organization," said Nadella, describing it as an externalization of the context system underlying Copilot.

Nadella went on to announce a new model family for GitHub Copilot Fusion, its code hosting subsidiary's model orchestration and routing play. He noted that Copilot Fusion today is ranked above Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 at less than half the cost on Terminal Bench, a measurement of how well AI agents complete tasks using a terminal.

Then there's Copilot Workspaces, which Nadella described as a multiplayer version of Copilot. Instead of a chat window where one person interacts with a model, it's an interface for team collaboration that shares context with a model.
Microsoft's decision model, intended to challenge TypeSafe AI's Jev, debuted about a month ago and now Decisions 1.1 is generally available.
"We have improved performance, making decisions more accurate and responses faster," said Nadella. "Already over 4,000 customers have used it."

He then said that Microsoft Foundry would offer OpenAI's GPT-6.2, which may have caused some confusion because at that point, OpenAI had no such model. A short time later, OpenAI announced GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol.
Microsoft also rolled out new coding models, in the form of Code 2, Code 2 Flash, and Cyber 2 Flash, and said its next-gen Cobalt 200 VMs are generally available.
It's a question of trust
After rattling off the various products and services Microsoft has prepared to help organizations with intelligence ownership, Nadella returned to the question of trust.

"Today we can see almost everything that models touch, but you cannot see what happens inside a model," he said. "And really what's worse is that we know that what a model tells us about itself is not even independent evidence and therefore cannot be trusted.
"And one model monitoring another model has the same issue. So you essentially have these unacceptable nested sets of black boxes, which we now need to make transparent and verifiable."

Microsoft's bid to bridge the trust gap is the Microsoft Transparency Initiative. The company says this will involve engagement with the National Institute of Standards and Technology's "SI Agent Standards Initiative."

Whether Microsoft AI will be compatible with NIST SI remains to be seen. That initiative also calls for collaboration with other organizations to develop accountable, verifiable, vendor-neutral AI transparency standards, and for Microsoft to incorporate this work into Microsoft AI, Foundry, and Copilot. Check in next year to see whether transparency is achieved. ®
