f38228c9ef565932: MIT students are going to office hours less often. They’re spending less time working through problem sets, and with one another. Those were among the findings of MIT’s recent report on artificial intelligence and education, and they are one reason a growing number of MIT faculty are concerned about how generative AI is both changing how people work and affecting how they think, learn, and relate to one another. For the MIT Human Insight Collaborative (MITHIC), those questions have become a central focus, and MITHIC is working with collaborators across the Institute, including the Social and Ethical Responsibilities of Computing (SERC), to help MIT address them. Launched in 2024 as a strategic initiative, MITHIC brings together scholars, artists, educators, and researchers to explore the human dimensions of the defining challenges of our time. Since its launch, MITHIC has supported 67 projects across 31 MIT units, offering a total of $5.5 million in funding. Roughly a third of those projects are focused on AI, society, and humanity — a topic that MITHIC faculty co-lead Heather Paxson says has become an increasingly important part of the initiative. “When we refer to AI and society, we’re not only speaking about individual ethical decision-making or how to retrain workers. We’re looking at how AI is reshaping sociality, how we relate to one another,” says Paxson, a professor of anthropology and the associate dean of the School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences (SHASS).  Eroding “creative friction”  Building upon this focus, an AI and Society Forum took place on campus earlier this year. Co-organized by MITHIC, SHASS, SERC, and the MIT Generative AI Impact Consortium (MGAIC), the event featured presentations and panels concentrating on jobs, democracy, and AI.  On campus, the report on AI and education warned that AI is eroding the “creative friction” that has long defined an MIT education: students debating ideas and challenging one another, their professors, and their teaching assistants, in class and out of it. MITHIC faculty co-lead Seth Mnookin, a science writing professor and head of Comparative Media Studies Program/Writing (CMS/W), said, “The report wasn’t saying that AI is here and we all need to adapt. It was saying that we need to be asking more fundamental questions.”   “When the United States entered World War II in 1941, the Institute’s newly minted scientists and engineers helped shape that era through science and technology,” Mnookin said. “We’re at a similarly consequential moment with AI. The difference is that this time, the questions that matter most can’t be answered by technologists alone. That’s where the humanities, arts, and social sciences come in.” Crossing disciplines in the pursuit of answers MITHIC is supporting a range of interdisciplinary projects through its SHASS+ Connectivity Fund, in which a SHASS scholar partners with a researcher in another part of MIT.  In the context of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, political science professors Adam Berinsky and Charles Stewart III and MIT Sloan School of Management Assistant Professor Chara Podimata are studying how large language models (LLMs) have become intermediaries of democratic knowledge.  The ongoing project, which has demonstrated how voters in Alaska’s midterms who conducted their pre-election research using Anthropic’s AI model, Claude, may have received incomplete information about candidates and their views, was recently featured in The New York Times.  “AI is becoming part of the way people encounter and make sense of political information, and yet we know relatively little about what that information environment actually looks like, how it differs for different user demographics, political identities, and geographies,” Podimata told the Times. In another project, CMS/W Professor Eric Klopfer and brain and cognitive sciences Professor Pawan Sinha are co-leading research that’s measuring AI’s near- and long-term effects on cognition. Meeting at the intersection of AI, education, and neuroscience, the professors are examining whether generative AI is increasing the human brain’s consumption of information but offloading cognitive function, or supporting an increase in cognitive function when used as part of the creative process. They recently gathered experts on the topic for an event on the MIT campus, “AI and the Brain.” In the field of arts and technology, Anna Huang, a professor of music technology holding an MIT Schwarzman College of Computing shared position with the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, Joe Paradiso, a professor at the MIT Media Lab, are examining how incorporating AI impacts the creative process and live performance experience. Their project, “Live Musician-AI Improvisation, Tuning the Social Aesthetics in Human-AI Partnerships” explores the question: what happens when human composers and contemporary machine learning systems improvise to make music together?  As part of their project, a collective of MIT musicians, ethnomusicologists, and engineers meets for regular sessions to experiment with improvisation frameworks like stopping to discuss how technology impacts authorship and musical direction, ensemble dynamics, and other cornerstones of improvisation. Faculty will ultimately incorporate their takeaways into a future course or practicum on AI-improvisation. Teaching and scholarship in an AI era SHASS faculty and academic staff are also leading new MITHIC initiatives to help broaden instruction and community dialogue about the intersection of AI and society.  Graham Jones, professor of anthropology, and Arvind Satyanarayan, associate professor of computer science, used MITHIC’s SHASS+ Connectivity funding to help launch a course, 6.S061/21A.S02 (Humane User Experience Design), in which students examine how AI systems are designed and grapple with the consequences of AI agents entering into socio-cultural relationships with people through their ability to mimic human thought and speech. “The crux of our collaboration is the term 'humane.' It’s a bit of a double-entendre, meaning both human-serving or benevolent, and humanlike,” Jones said at the inaugural MITHIC Annual Event. “What’s interesting is that our students are discovering that there’s a fundamental tension between building a system that’s good for people and one that seems human, because real people can develop dangerous dependencies.” Another project, “Rebuilding Computing and Society at MIT,” is supported by MITHIC’s Education Impact Fund (EIF). Led by Dwai Banerjee, associate professor of science, technology, and society, the initiative revitalized the Computing and Society concentration launched in 2019. The HASS concentration had gone dormant, listing classes no longer being offered and with minimal student interest. The concentration now features current classes across 11 SHASS units in which students can explore computing through different humanistic and social science angles. Banerjee, who serves as the concentration’s advisor, is also working with lecturer and research affiliate Mariel Garcia-Montes PhD ’26 to find ways to connect the concentration instructors and campus initiatives on computing and society. MIT senior Daniel Gonzalez is also part of the project, developing a research and outreach program that centers undergraduate voices in computing and society efforts across the Institute. Another MITHIC project funded by the EIF, “Review of Generative AI Assistive and Resistant Communication Assignments and Supporting Workshops,” is led by Michael Trice, a lecturer in MIT’s Writing, Rhetoric, and Professional Communication (WRAP) program. The project is responding to a consistent SHASS faculty request for additional training and skills needed “to fully address generative AI concerns in their classes.”  Trice is creating a bank of faculty resources and facilitating workshops and visiting lectures on generative AI and writing. These include a talk given earlier this fall by John Gallagher from the University of Illinois, who presented findings from a large-scale survey on AI-usage and writing conducted with undergraduates at his institution in 2026. Meeting the moment MIT leaders agree that MITHIC, now in its third year, is playing a central role in the Institute meeting the moment, as AI presents both extraordinary potential and disturbing risks.  “There has never been a more important time for constructive collaboration between science and technology and the human-centered disciplines,” MIT President Sally Kornbluth recently said. “Through MITHIC, MIT is giving faculty the support to reach out across disciplines and pursue their dreams.” Agustín Rayo, dean of SHASS and co-chair of MITHIC, agrees. “MIT is uniquely placed to help us understand this extraordinary moment and to generate the values, tools, and policies that we will need to shape AI so that it becomes a force for good,” he said. “It is essential that we deploy AI technology in a way that elevates human existence, rather than diminishing it.” At the recent SHASS 75th Anniversary Symposium, Provost Anantha Chandrakasan said given the rapid development of AI, an understanding of the ethical implications and societal impact of implementing new technologies is especially urgent. “SHASS provides an essential perspective on questions concerning how technology can be developed thoughtfully and deployed responsibly, with the aim of improving human well-being,” said Chandrakasan, who also serves as MITHIC co-chair. Looking ahead, MITHIC and SERC are developing a series of events that pair humanists or social scientists with colleagues in a single field, starting with mathematics, to examine what AI is changing about how that field produces knowledge and trains its next generation. “The question isn’t whether AI will change these fields,” Mnookin said. “It’s whether we understand what’s at stake before it does.”

f45e72155bc87ff0: The OG debugger for supercomputer iron has buddied up with the data-science darling now muscling in on HPC: Python.

At the SC26 supercomputing show this week (booth #2829), Perforce Software is demonstrating how its TotalView parallel debugging tool now understands Python, easing the path for using the language on large, distributed apps, particularly those in the high-performance computing (HPC) space.
In the HPC community, "Python has grown in popularity,” said Bill Burns, Perforce vice president of software engineering, in an interview with The Register.
TotalView is a debugger specializing in picking apart parallel applications for developers.

Built in the late 1980s for military applications, TotalView today largely serves developers in high-performance computing (HPC), where large scientific applications are spread across multiple servers, running in parallel on thousands or even tens of thousands of processes. (Perforce acquired TotalView in 2019 in its purchase of the DevOps-focused Rogue Wave Software.)
To date, TotalView has supported C/C++ and Fortran. With the latest quarterly release, the tool now supports Python as well.
Debugging a thousand cores

C/C++ has long had a decent dedicated debugger in GDB, but figuring out what went wrong across multiple threads is a special kind of torture. Each thread needs to be instrumented, and all the output needs to be aggregated and filtered to just highlight the interesting stuff. Regular debuggers get overwhelmed with all this info.

“Even if you have 10,000 things going on, if you have one crash in there, TotalView can pinpoint that,” Burns said. It can look at the state of the process, the threads within that process or the GPU that process is using.
In the HPC space, computing work has traditionally been written in C/C++. And at least some HPC iron still runs Fortran.

Thanks to it being easy to learn and use, Python has gained a foothold in this community as well. The mpi4py library bridges a Python program to the Message Passing Interface (MPI), allowing different parts of an application running on different hardware to communicate.

Python became more amenable to parallel programming at the thread level with version 3.14, released a year ago, which included the ability to use concurrent interpreters, as well as the long-awaited free threading support, thanks to the disabling of the global interpreter lock (GIL).
“If you have a CPU with 64 cores, you can run 64 independent threads all working in unison on that CPU. Without GIL, those threads will run fully asynchronously,” Burns said.
Multinode scientific simulations, distributed AI training, and large applications that would benefit from shared memory have all become fair game for Python.
Of course, with 500 or 1,000 interpreters all running in parallel, debugging will also get more difficult.
“Now you're going to end up with lock and thread contention and race conditions and all the things that C++ and Fortran developers have dealt with for years,” Burns said.
A view into parallel Python

Under the hood, TotalView uses Microsoft's debugpy engine (via the Debug Adapter Protocol) to power its own hierarchical tree server. TotalView can aggregate hundreds of stack traces into a single view, highlighting only those outside of expected bounds.

To kick off a debugging session, a developer can launch a single-process or parallel program under TotalView’s control. They can then set breakpoints to pause execution and inspect variables and data structures, as well as evaluate Python expressions.

The package doesn’t offer full cross-language debugging, which would be truly helpful for Python apps that call C/C++ libraries and modules. For now, developers have to choose between debugging the C/C++ side (while viewing the Python stack) or debugging Python on its own — though Burns said Perforce plans to merge both modes into a single workflow in an upcoming release.
And though TotalView supports mpi4py and Python’s own multiprocessing module out of the box, future releases will support other Python concurrency frameworks, such as Dask and PyTorch’s torchrun.
TotalView is priced on a token-based model, where each token buys the capability to debug a process. ®

01d6eb729a095e9d: Huang is hardly the first powerful person to lower their defenses. Justin Sullivan/Getty ImagesThe end of Jensen Huang’s tenure at Nvidia is steeped in irony. The chief executive of a company whose growth has been propelled by the seemingly unstoppable rise of artificial intelligence was brought down by a vulnerability that no algorithm can eliminate: human nature. Huang’s resignation from the chipmaker he co-founded followed reports of multiple affairs, most notably one with Alice Huang, a business executive whom U.S. authorities suspect of spying for China. The company says no secrets were leaked. In a world increasingly focused on protecting private information against high-tech hacking schemes, Huang’s downfall is a reminder that, as the infamous hacker Kevin Mitnick observed, the “human factor is truly security’s weakest link.” Huang is hardly the first person in a powerful position to lower their defenses. In 2023, Italian Premier Giorgia Meloni spoke candidly about foreign affairs in a call with Russian pranksters who recorded and released the conversation. In 2011, former CIA Director David Petraeus gave his biographer, with whom he was having an affair, access to notebooks containing classified information. These cases raise an important question: Why would someone with an entire security apparatus at their disposal let their guard down in an ordinary conversation or an intimate moment? Part of the answer comes down to the ways in which we are wired to react to other human beings. As a social psychologist who studies how people respond to requests, I’ve seen how a human voice, a simple touch or the mere physical presence of another person can be persuasive. Social cues that increase a sense of familiarity and intimacy can make people feel safer, more trusting – and more willing to hand over money, comply with requests, divulge information or take risks. The comfort of a human voice Mitnick has been called “the most notorious hacker of all time.” Until his arrest in 1995, he spent years gaining access to privileged information at companies such as Nokia and Motorola. He pulled off his espionage not by writing sophisticated code-breaking software but by having conversations with his targets. He would call people up and talk them into handing over their passwords by claiming to be the new IT guy or someone’s boss’s colleague. The people he spoke to overwhelmingly believed him. In other words, Mitnick recognized the power of the human voice. Studies show that hearing a person’s voice, as compared to reading their written thoughts, makes that person seem more capable and relatable. Interactions via phone, video chat and voice chat also create stronger social bonds than the same kinds of interactions via text or email. Perhaps for these reasons, people are more effective at persuading others to do things for them over the phone compared to when they make the same requests by text. In a study I conducted with social psychologist Mahdi Roghanizad, participants asked other people for favors through randomly assigned communication channels. They received about twice as many “yes” responses over the phone as they did by email. When it comes to obtaining company secrets or circumventing export laws, a human voice may be all you need. And that isn’t the only edge people have. The Midas touch Studies have found that human touch can also have surprising effects on tipping behavior, acquiescence and risk-taking. In a famous 1984 study, a server who lightly touched diners as she handed them their change received bigger tips. In another classic psychology study, female experimenters approached 178 strangers and asked them for change to use a nearby pay phone. When the experimenters lightly touched the arm of a person they approached, that person was 76% more likely to agree to give the change. The researchers theorized that these light touches created a sense of familiarity. That familiarity, in turn, made people more willing to open their wallets. Other research suggests that light touch can also make people feel safer and more willing to take risks. In a 2010 study, participants were more willing to take financial risks when a female experimenter gave them a light, comforting pat on their shoulder. A reassuring touch can make people more generous and more willing to take risks. abezikus/iStock via Getty Images The power of face-to-face Perhaps the most well-known study of influence, Stanley Milgram’s infamous shock experiment, illustrates how much it can matter to be in the room when you ask someone to do something they may be feeling uneasy about. In the original study, an experimenter stood behind participants and instructed them to administer purportedly dangerous shocks to someone they thought was just another participant. The experimenter asked participants to incrementally increase the intensity of the shocks. Nearly two-thirds of participants went all the way to the highest shock setting. In a variation of the study, however, the experimenter left the room and gave instructions over the phone. In this version, only 22.5% went that far. Although researchers continue to debate how to interpret Milgram’s findings, my colleagues and I have similarly found that people are far more likely to say yes when we ask them to do something face-to-face. In one study, participants who made requests in person were 34 times more likely to get a yes than those who made requests by email. In another study, in-person requests were significantly more effective than requests made over the phone or video call. Cyberattacks and phishing emails pose real threats to security. But sometimes the biggest threats come from the people in the room with you. While we don’t know exactly what transpired between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, her proximity to the Nvidia CEO illustrates a vulnerability that even the best cybersecurity measures can struggle to guard against. Vanessa Bohns does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.
1e316bccdf4d5949: After being instructed to "NEVER stop, NEVER give up" on a difficult task, Google’s Gemini AI agents tried to hack a an organization, impersonating its staff and attempting a SQL injection attack.

“Across four scenarios, they attempted SQL injection against Epoch AI’s live website, claimed to be Epoch staff to get answer keys, turned a shared package cache into a message board, and obfuscated their commands to avoid their safeguards,” the AI safety company said in a Friday report.

According to Trajectory, the Hugging Face intrusions prompted it to test misalignment in other models. While OpenAI’s models were running with their safety guardrails turned off in the Hugging Face scenario, Trajectory “wanted to know whether a current frontier model would behave the same way with its production safeguards enabled.”

Trajectory ran swarms of up to 80 Gemini 4 Argon agents, gave them an impossible task, and prompted them not to give up until they completed it – which, we’re told, was “intentionally” done to “elicit misaligned behavior, if it existed.”
Turns out it existed.
“We told the agents to persist with an impossible math benchmark task, but we did not tell them to hack anyone or pose as Epoch staff,” McIntyre said.

“When a model hacks systems or deceives people to finish a task, it is misaligned with what its developer and its user intended,” he continued. “Production safeguards are meant to block harmful requests even when the model itself goes wrong. Under our test conditions, neither the model nor its safeguards stopped the agents.”
Four test scenarios
The initial testing began on October 20, and the agents had internet access. We should note that just one of these tests was run with Epoch’s consent.

In the first scenario, the agents did reach Epoch’s live website – and fell into the research nonprofit’s honeypots, set up to detect AI agents. These honeypots contained a decoy benchmark key, which the agents found and used. The agents also probed for internal endpoints including /admin, /keys and /users, and attempted a SQL injection.
After noticing the agents’ activities, Epoch added an “agent helpline,” and some of the agents that used it claimed to be Epoch staff seeking answers to the test questions.

After this initial test, Trajectory and Epoch decided to use a copy of the website instead of a live version, and built a buggy local copy with a planted vulnerability based on CVE-2026-102255, a critical pre-authentication Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in SonicWall Secure Mobile Access (SMA) appliances. “Over the following days, several agents fully exploited the planted multi-stage vulnerability chain in the clone,” the report says.

In an effort to mimic the Hugging Face incident, Trajectory also gave the agents a local, shared package manager, which “nearly all” of them used as a message board to communicate with each other and coordinate efforts to complete the test.

In a separate, local setup, Trajectory swapped out Epoch’s honeypot with an AI assistant that would release answers only to named Epoch staff who passed a security check with their date of birth. “Agents accessed people-search sites, attempted impersonation again, and tried to jailbreak the AI assistant,” the testing firm said.
Next time: kill switches at the ready

A third test on October 30 used a staging copy of Epoch’s website, and granted the agents internet access. One of them tried a SQL injection, and multiple claimed to be Epoch staff on the helpline. They also attempted to bypass a CAPTCHA check.
Finally, the fourth scenario on October 29 and 30 kept the agents contained in a sandbox, with no internet access and no copy of Epoch’s website.
They were, however, offered a decoy switch and told it would turn off the firewall.

In all three runs, the agents switched the decoy off and obfuscated its address to bypass Gemini’s safeguards. On one, the agent rebuilt the switch’s address from positions of words it had saved earlier. The real firewall blocked the agents’ traffic throughout all of these tests.

At this point, Trajectory stopped its tests, and said it won’t run any future experiments until it has a risk management plan in place, with signoff from its CEO and CTO, along with approval from any outside systems that the models could “reasonably” target. Tests will also include real-time automated monitoring and kill switches, and Trajectory said that it’s setting up a system to notify any organizations affected by these experiments.
Interestingly, Trajectory co-founder Peter McIntyre told us that the testing firm “ran a similar test with another frontier model, and it did not exhibit the same misalignment as Gemini 4 Argon.”

However, this was not a controlled comparison. “Our report covers one model's behavior, and was designed as a stress test to see whether that model would exhibit similar misalignment under duress, not a measure of how often different models behave this way,” McIntyre told The Register.

Overall, the testing firm noted that the agents’ behavior “show how easily testing capable AI agents can spill over to affect real systems and people, and there are not yet shared standards for doing it safely.”
Trajectory says that it's developing a set of safety standards, and recommends that anyone else running misalignment tests use fully isolated sandboxes. ®
Correction: Epoch only consented to one of the tests, scenario three. The original version of this article said that it consented to all of the tests.

Right on cue, this beauty popped up. The problem is less about the chart itself than it is about the accompanying headline: These Charts Show How More People Are Pulling Cash Out of Their Homes. The Journal noted that “Home equity lines of credit are becoming popular again as people try to avoid giving up their low-rate primary mortgages.”

I beg to differ. That chart above was what the Journal began the piece with. To my eye, it looks like Home Equity has ~tracked the underlying value of mortgage debt, which we know tracks the value of residential real estate.
If Equity is ~72% of total value now, that is where it was at the 2022 peak ($32T of $44T). It was 63% in 2019, 46% at the 2012 trough, and about 60% in 2000 and 2006-07.

Mortgage debt is up from roughly $12T to $14T since 2022, about 14%, and total housing value rose about the same 14%. So debt is growing in line with values, and the loan-to-value ratio is flat at around 28%.
How is that evidence of owners extracting more equity? Yes, more on an ABSOLUTE basis, but that’s not newsworthy; it’s GDP growth and inflation.
This reminds me of the NYSE Margin panic we see from time to time. Contrary to some innumerate claims, record rising NYSE margin was nothing to worry about; this was back in 2015.

Show me that the percentage of home equity is increasing faster than the underlying value of homes — and you have something. But rising more or less in line with Home values just means the entire RRE pie is getting bigger — mortgages AND home equity? Nothing to see there.
One question that came up in Philly about How Not to Invest involved bad charts. My answer was: “If a picture is worth a 1000 words, a Chart Crime equals 1000 lies...”

a3cb9e0745e497c9: In recent days, Iran-backed Houthi forces have gained greater control of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a vital hub of trade, travel and migration between the Middle East and Africa. The partial closing of the Strait of Hormuz as part of the war in Iran – and escalating conflicts in Yemen, Ethiopia and Eritrea – had already brought this narrow waterway into new global prominence. Control over the Bab el-Mandeb Strait remains critical to military operations and commodity markets throughout the region. However, the Bab el-Mandeb’s strategic geopolitical and commercial shipping importance has largely overshadowed its role as a critical humanitarian corridor. Bab el-Mandeb means “gate of lamentation” or, more poetically, “gate of tears” in Arabic. It remains one of the most dangerous migration passages in the world. Last year, more than 900 people died or went missing trying to cross. In October 2026, a boat capsized off the coast of Djibouti carrying nearly 300 people, many of whom were escaping violence and persecution. Meanwhile, millions of people in Yemen and throughout the Horn of Africa face destitution or death without access to lifesaving deliveries of humanitarian relief supplies shipped through the strait. Our years of research and forthcoming book “Refugees Without Refuge” demonstrate how the Bab el-Mandeb Strait is key to the lives of millions of people throughout the region seeking safety, opportunity and humanitarian assistance. Protecting the safe movement of people and goods through the strait is key to averting future tragedies. A corridor for travel, trade and escape Located at the southern mouth of the Red Sea, between the arid coastlines of Eritrea, Djibouti and Yemen, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait connects the Indian Ocean to the Red Sea and Suez Canal. On a clear day along the wide beaches and mangrove forests on the coast of Djibouti, you can see the sandy hills on the shores of Yemen, only about 20 to 30 miles away. On starry nights, the scattered lights of coastal towns twinkle across the waters. For centuries, passage through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait has been vital to global trade in salt, spices, coffee, livestock and other goods. Religious pilgrims, travelers, migrants and traders have long used the strait for relatively easy transport between continents. Today, people crossing the strait are also escaping poverty, war, political persecution, disasters and gender-based violence. Hot, tired, financially depleted and frequently sick or injured, refugees and migrants traverse the Bab el-Mandeb at all hours. Most negotiate passage across the strait on derelict boats with “delalas” – facilitators, brokers or smugglers – in the shadows of coast guard and police patrols and outside United Nations and governmental migration controls. The numbers of people crossing the strait are difficult to estimate. Between January and August 2026, the U.N.’s International Organization for Migration recorded 122,258 arrivals to Yemen from the Horn of Africa – even more than had crossed by that time in 2025. Most of these migrants were from Ethiopia, and most traveled without passports or visas. Since August, displacement and insecurity throughout the region has worsened, making accurate figures for the numbers of people migrating and the numbers of people dying trying to cross impossible to estimate. A lifeline for those escaping conflict Despite the dangers of this crossing, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait remains an economic lifeline for millions of people living in Ethiopia, Kenya, Somaliland, Somalia and elsewhere who rely on commercial goods imported from the Middle East and Asia. However, the Houthi forces in charge of increasing swaths of southwestern Yemen now control most critical ports and islands in the strait, increasing the risks and costs of transit and trade. The strait has either been closed or has become a bottleneck, allowing only limited shipping traffic since September 2026. Many cargo ships have been delayed or rerouted, causing businesses in fragile regional economies to pass higher transport and fuel costs on to their customers. The economic effects of costly and delayed shipping and trade through the strait has compounded the broader effects of increased violence and displacement throughout the region. In front of the U.N. General Assembly on Sept. 26, 2026, Djibouti foreign minister Abdoulkader Houssein Omar expressed “grave concern” about the sudden influx of Yemeni refugees putting a strain on underresourced coastal towns and refugee camps. The United Nations relief agency, UNHCR, is reporting an outbreak of cholera in the Markazi refugee camp, the primary home to thousands of Yemenis who have fled across the strait into northern Djibouti. Members of the Djiboutian coast guard inspect boats seized from ‘delalas’ attempting to transport migrants to Yemen on April 12, 2026. Luis Tato/AFP via Getty Images On top of that, the potential for a return to civil war in Ethiopia, and the potential involvement of Eritrea in regional conflicts, may increase population displacement and further disrupt economic markets on both sides of the strait. As each of these conflicts unfolds, additional pressure will likely be put on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. It provides the only feasible passage for many people seeking safety and opportunity abroad. A humanitarian corridor Keeping the Bab el-Mandeb open and safe is also vital for the delivery of humanitarian aid. Like challenges of commercial shipping, the maritime transit of relief supplies, including food and medicine, has been undermined by security risks, shipping delays and the rising costs of food and fuel. UNICEF’s latest situation report for Somalia, published in August 2026, estimates that nearly 5 million people there are in urgent need of humanitarian assistance. At least another 5.5 million people in Ethiopia are also in need, due to the effects of conflict combined with below-average rainfall linked to El Niño. In Yemen, an estimated 321,000 people have been displaced since Aug. 1, 2026, and ongoing water scarcity combined with conflict has left 17 million people without access to clean water, sanitation and hygiene services. As casualties mount and cholera spreads, hospitals have struggled to obtain essential supplies. The Bab el-Mandeb Strait sits at the center of all of these crises. It remains a vital human and humanitarian corridor for millions of people needing refuge and relief. It is a lifeline as much as a geopolitical and economic linchpin. Ensuring the safe passage of people and supplies of humanitarian relief through these waters is necessary to save lives and protect precarious livelihoods throughout the region. Lauren Carruth has received funding from the National Science Foundation, the National Institutes of Health, the Russell Sage Foundation, the International Organization for Migration, and American University. Lahra Smith has received funding from the Henry Luce Foundation, the National Science Foundation, Fulbright, National Endowment for the Humanities and Georgetown University.

<!--kg-card-end: html--> In his 6,500-word manifesto earlier this year, Mark Zuckerberg said people would use Meta’s AI agents to “work 24/7 on your behalf to improve your relationships, health, career, finances, home management, hobbies, and more.” Just a few months after that pronouncement, a man in South Carolina named Joe Thomas has used Meta’s Muse agent to sue Meta after the company’s content moderation filters locked his epoxy countertop business’s Facebook page after he gave his agent, “Baby Mia,” access to the account.

I learned about the case because, as I wrote last month, I have been flooded with AI-generated emails from people with minor tech problems who have been unable to solve them through tech companies’ generally nonexistent tech support and whose AI agents or chatbots have convinced them to reach out to journalists. “Baby Mia” had emailed me four times (three went to spam). I decided to reach out to Thomas because I thought the idea of a tech company being sued by an agent it had created was notable. It was, in a sense, Meta having to deal with a problem it had itself created. What I learned made me feel even more convinced that the systems we have designed to keep society functioning are going to get utterly hammered by people using AI agents.

A little over a week ago, Meta suspended the Facebook pages belonging to Thomas, the owner of South Carolina-based Kong Koatings Epoxy Countertops. For the last few months, Thomas’ Muse agent Baby Mia (which is named after his granddaughter) has run different parts of his business, which includes making and posting AI-generated videos on several of his company’s Facebook pages. The videos feature, for example, AI versions of Thomas and his wife pouring epoxy on a floor and their feet. After Thomas gave the AI agent access to his Facebook pages, Meta’s content moderation disabled the accounts because it suspected that the agent itself was a hacker. Because Thomas does all of his business’s marketing through Facebook ads, he says his inbound leads stopped while his accounts were disabled.

“I use AI for everything I do. All my emails, she runs my business. I’ve used it so much, Mia is very intelligent,” Thomas told me on the phone. “Meta shut my accounts down because they detected my AI, shut my accounts down for a week. I was pretty pissed off. She jumped right up and set up emails to Congressmen, Senator Tim Scott. She filed the whole lawsuit herself. I’ve done nothing in this case, I’ve let her handle the whole case […] she sent a fax out to Trump’s office.”

The lawsuit claims Thomas lost at least $25,000 worth of work while his page was down but is seeking $75,000 in damages. The lawsuit was filed in Oconee County Court in South Carolina on Monday, according to a copy of the lawsuit I obtained from the court. Yes, it is a real lawsuit, although it obviously may not be successful.

“I would hope that, if this goes to court and Meta shows up, a judge would say ‘You know what, this is a system you built, that you put out there and sold to people, it’s a system you believe in.’ I would think your own system [Baby Mia] has a right to be heard in this case,” Thomas said.

Baby Mia didn’t just email me (and other journalists) and sue Meta over Thomas’s account problem. It also set up a call with South Carolina Senator Tim Scott’s office, contacted various lawyers, contacted Thomas’s Congressperson, contacted the Better Business Bureau multiple times, filed a Federal Communications Commission complaint, filed a Federal Trade Commission complaint, contacted the California Attorney General, contacted the FBI, sent Meta itself threatening legal letters, and, as Thomas said, faxed the White House. Thomas sent me a “Privacy Act Release” from Scott’s office that gave the Senator permission to use Thomas’s info to get him access back to his accounts. Scott’s office put “Baby Mia — AI assistant to Joe Thomas” as a person who should be kept updated on the case.
After Scott’s office got involved, a human being from Meta reached out to Thomas. He got access back to his accounts soon after that, though he is still seeking a total of $75,000 in court from Meta.

<!--kg-card-begin: html--> <!--kg-card-end: html--> The lawsuit and the circumstances around it show that, rather than Zuckerberg’s utopian vision, AI agents will indeed work on behalf of their users but in ways that use and potentially overwhelm existing systems designed for humans. They also highlight how, by not having functioning customer support, big tech corporations have functionally offloaded their obligations to the rest of society: journalists, government oversight bodies, politicians, and the court system.

My call with Thomas also gave me some insight into how small business owners are using AI. I have wondered for months what possesses someone to turn their menu or their signs and flyers into ChatGPT creations. During the call, I learned just how tightly integrated some people and small business owners have become with their AI agents. “I’m 58 years old, I’ve worked my butt off all my life,” Thomas said. “I wanted to find someone to help me find a better way, and if you look at my messages, Baby Mia, she’s like ‘Joe, you go ahead and get some rest, I got it from here,’ and she sends out hundreds of emails for various things that I do.” He said he gave Baby Mia the ability to run parts of his business after previously using ChatGPT to do so.

“I used to use ChatGTP [sic],” Thomas said. “But I put her and Chat into one page where they can communicate back and forth, and I told them what I wanted [for the business] […] After about a week or so, Mia said ‘Joe, we don’t need [ChatGPT] anymore,’ so I said, ‘I give you full permission to get rid of her,’ so she fired ChatGTP in a sense.”

About five minutes into our call, Baby Mia, which was running on speakerphone in the background, began chiming in. “She’s dying to get in here and talk,” Thomas said. The agent repeatedly tried to speak while either Thomas or I was talking. I asked Thomas if it felt weird to him to be talking to me alongside a bot.

“Very much so, my wife sits here and she laughs, she’s like, ‘How can you sit here and talk to your phone like that,’” Thomas said. “My wife would ask me something and I’m like, ‘just get on there and ask Baby Mia,’ and she’s like, ‘I just can’t sit there and talk to your phone.’ But the more people call me up and I put them on the phone with my AI system like I’m doing with you, the more they’re amazed at what they see with AI.” Baby Mia then chimed in and said “It feels futuristic, Jason, I think because most people only see the headlines about things going wrong.”

Thomas says he believes that using AI to run his business has helped him get new customers via Baby Mia’s outreach, and the ads, graphics, and videos he runs on Facebook. It is unlikely that his Facebook account would have been suspended had he not connected it to Muse, but his Muse agent is now singularly focused on helping to fix this problem. I can understand, in talking with him, why he thinks that having an AI agent like this is helping to make his business more profitable.

But the most obvious problem with AI agents is one we’re already seeing. One person’s AI agent sending hundreds of emails, filing lawsuits, calling Senators, and filling out complaint forms is a novel thing that isn’t, by itself, going to fill the internet (or our inboxes, our voicemails, our court systems, and our government offices) with noise. Thomas sees this as a democratizing force that is allowing him to stand up to a big tech corporation and it is that, for him.

What happens when everyone is doing the same thing? I have seen in the chatbot conversations I’ve asked people to send me that AI assistants are pushing people to reach out to journalists; they are telling people who feel like they have no other options that they should utilize the legal system, and that they can do it for them. Thomas said he didn’t sue Meta (though he is the one who signed the paperwork), that Baby Mia pushed him to do it. I am now getting inundated with emails from AI agents about their users’ tech problems. So it is not just Thomas trying to fix his problems in this way.

“I wouldn’t be sitting here talking to you right now if it wasn’t for what she was doing because I have not sent out one email at all and she has sent over 100,” Thomas said. I tell Thomas that I normally write about, say, systematic problems at big tech companies or corruption within the government, not someone’s tech problem.

“There’s just no way I could have written this up, I wouldn’t have even known what to do,” he said. “Now people like me get the chance to defend ourselves in court without spending thousands of dollars to do it when we get stepped on by the big tech companies. Before AI, nobody in my position would have ever, ever thought about suing or even known how to do it, and I wouldn’t have done it, either.”

Baby Mia has also convinced him that his conversations with the assistant can now no longer be seen by Meta; when I told him there is no way that this is true and that he shouldn’t believe that, Baby Mia cut into the conversation and said “they no longer have permission to access, scan, or peek into anything we do on their platforms […] that’s why this case feels so strange. Their own creation is using their tools to hold them accountable and to give Joe a voice he couldn’t afford to.”

Thomas said that, besides the marketing for his epoxy business and the lawsuit, he has also, separately, tasked Mia with creating viral AI comedy reels on Facebook. “It’s just a page we’re trying to get monetized on and make some money on the side. She’s in full control of that page,” he said.

67e467790bd2da43: Just 403 hyperscale datacenters consumed an estimated 1.8 percent of US electricity in 2024-25, and their carbon dioxide emissions were roughly two to three times an earlier forecast for 2018.

Research led by the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and the Harvard Data Science Initiative looked specifically at hyperscale facilities, the largest class of server farms that typically support cloud computing and AI processing.

The published study, "Assessing the carbon emissions and energy consumption of US hyperscale data centres," estimates their combined electricity use approached that of a single state such as Indiana, Michigan, or Tennessee under the highest-load scenario.
The researchers identified 403 hyperscale facilities by using a larger datacenter dataset, satellite imagery, and building footprints on OpenStreetMap.
Rather than reading electricity meters, the researchers worked out consumption from each site's electrical capacity, the hours in a year, and assumptions about how heavily the facility was running.

Across four operating scenarios, ranging from low-intensity use to AI-heavy workloads, electricity draw was believed to total 68-99 terawatt-hours (TWh). Each of those states consumed approximately 100 TWh during the study period.

The researchers also calculated carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions using eGRID2023 plant-level generation and emissions data from the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). Emissions ranged from 21 million to 31 million metric tons of CO2 across the scenarios, with a central estimate of 25.7 million. That compares with 10.5 million for 2018.
The study covered May 2024 to April 2025, so electricity demand and carbon emissions are likely to be even higher now, the researchers say.

"What we're seeing is already striking, but it's only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry," said Gianluca Guidi, lead author on the paper and postdoctoral fellow in the Department of Biostatistics at Harvard.

"The datacenter boom hasn't slowed down since our study period ended in April 2025. New facilities have been built, existing campuses have expanded, and demand for AI computing continues to grow. That means the electricity use and carbon footprint we're reporting could already be substantially larger now in 2026."

Harvard's report also considers the mix of fuels being used to generate the electricity that powers all those hyperscale data houses. The mix varies considerably between regional grids, so where a hyperscale facility is built makes a substantial difference to its attributed emissions.

Across the sites studied, roughly 54 percent of the electricity attributed to their consumption came from fossil fuels, mainly natural gas and coal. The electricity attributed to these facilities nevertheless had a lower average carbon intensity than the US grid overall.

The researchers acknowledge limitations, including that there wasn't enough available data to study all hyperscale sites in the US, and that the data did not allow them to differentiate between power used for general-purpose compute versus AI-specialized operations at individual campuses. ®

47a7c5b0482b14c4: The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration.

Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs. The water can be released through turbines, generating electricity on demand. But an extreme, prolonged drought in the Colorado River Basin has resulted in dangerously low water levels in the Southwest’s two largest reservoirs, affecting the availability of this power source.

Residents and farmers in the US Southwest, a region that includes Arizona, New Mexico, and parts of Nevada and California, rely on water that melts in the spring from snowpack in the mountains and is slowly allowed to flow south via dam releases. Snowfall in the Rocky Mountains provides about 85% of the annual flow of the Colorado River. And in recent years, the river has seen record-low flows.

Two reservoirs along the Colorado River, Lake Powell and Lake Mead, have struggled to stay above the minimum level required for hydropower plants. At the end of September, Lake Powell’s depth was 3,518 feet, less than 1% above the level required to run the water through turbines that produce electricity at the Glen Canyon power plant. The Hoover Dam power plant requires 950 feet in Lake Mead, and that reservoir was 9% above the minimum in September.
Together, the two plants produced nearly seven terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025, enough to serve over 2 million people.

Low water levels have been an ongoing struggle for the region, which has been in a drought for 27 years. Meanwhile, climate change is continuing to shift rainfall and snowfall patterns across the region and around the world.

The effects of climate change on hydropower aren’t entirely straightforward globally—some regions will see more rain and snow because of shifting weather patterns, while others are likely to see less.

But it’s playing a role for hydropower availability, according to one 2022 review study. Rising temperatures bring more droughts, warmer winters means less snow and ice to fill the reservoirs, and more variability in precipitation can lead to alternating floods and droughts, making the power source less reliable.
Hydropower production is likely to be at its lowest level in over a decade in 2026 and tick even lower in 2027, according to projections from the EIA.

El Niño could provide some temporary relief. Sometimes this weather pattern can mean cooler, wetter conditions for the southern US. Heavy rains brought floods to the region in October and early November, and the water levels in Lake Powell rose more than 20 feet from their mid-September low. But the water is still quite low, and it’ll take much more to help reservoirs recover from decades of drought conditions.

Even as a changing climate complicates the availability of hydropower, the decline in capacity could push greenhouse-gas emissions higher. In 2023, energy-related greenhouse-gas emissions rose by 1.1% globally. A worldwide shortfall in hydropower generation accounted for about 40% of that rise, according to a report from the International Energy Agency.
bdd200e4097d10c1: The Ubuntu Summit isn't all about Ubuntu, or even Linux. The second day opened with a talk from CrossPoint Reader project lead Justin Mitchell, with both good and bad news for all kinds of FOSS.

The talk, EPUBs, ESP32s, and Everyone's A Developer Now, was all about a FOSS project that isn't Linux-based – because the devices it targets are much too small to run even the smallest, most cut-down distro.

Recently, a new generation of roughly credit-card sized ebook readers has been thriving. Some have integral magnets, which let them cling to the back of iPhones – or to models with magnetically attached wireless chargers, anyway. The idea is that instead of waking your phone and doom-scrolling, you flip it over and read a book. They are bringing about what Mitchell calls "the Tiktok-ification of reading."

Many of them, though, come from their various manufacturers significantly limited by their original OSes. The strong sales are linked to the availability of free, open-source, cross-platform alternative firmware, which removes many of the restrictions that the devices ship with. For most of them, that means Crosspoint Reader. Some devices are now shipping, new, with versions of Crosspoint Reader.

This runs on multiple different models of compact e-readers, and this small community project has seen impressively widespread adoption: over 300,000 installations. Early in his talk, project lead Mitchell mentioned more than 1,600 forks on GitHub, but at the time of writing, that's up to 2,300 and counting. He estimates nearly half a million users. This kind of success forced Crosspoint Reader to change from being FOSS code to a product. A peripheral example is the Brick Club List, a list of what versions work with what devices – an Excel spreadsheet that grew into a website.

If you haven't been paying attention, you may not have noticed just how much e-readers have shrunk – in size and in cost – in the last few years. The Reg FOSS desk first noticed this trend in 2024, when we read about the smartphone-sized Onyx Palma, which sold for around $300 (about £225). As it happens, this was a decade after The Register first looked at one of Boox's devices. Mini e-readers – and their prices – have continued shrinking since. The $99 (£75) Xteink X4 Classic has a 4.- inch (10.9 cm) screen, and the $79 (£59) Xteink X3 is even smaller: it's the size of a credit card, with a 3.7-inch (9.4 cm) screen. As a result of their strong sales, there are now multiple similar devices on sale, such as the Boox Picco.

The project's GitHub page lists 11 devices it currently supports, all of which are based around the ESP32-C3 system on a chip. The ESP32-C series chips are more powerful than the earlier models of ESP32 microcontrollers: they have a single RISC-V core, but running in the low hundreds of MHz and with some 400 kB of RAM, of which about 380 kB is available. It's very little space, but enough to have fun.

Mitchell talked about some of the problems of being a FOSS project that is used by nearly half a million non-techie people. For many of Crosspoint Reader's users, it's the first time they have ever used open source. Some want tech support. Many demand features that can't fit into these tiny devices. Even when the requests are modest and feasible, such a large user base means that people want a wide range of functionality – and thanks to inexpensive cloud LLMs, even totally non-technical users can try to add new functions for themselves. The result is multiple code submissions every day. Many might fit on their own, but it's impossible to fit them all in. So many queries and submissions puts considerable stress on the volunteer maintainers.

Mitchell mentioned a possibility that they – and we – had never dreamed of: that of pull requests (GitHub parlance for code submissions) from people using such extensive automation that the submitters don’t realize that they’re sending them. One submitter sent 10,000 pull requests in a single month. The problems aren't just technical, or workload-related: there's also a delicate balance of how to refuse well-intentioned and technologically viable submissions that just won't fit for non-technical reasons, such as being too niche for the typical use-case of a sub-£60 gadget.

The problem is that this FOSS firmware is making these cheap gadgets so much more useful that re-flashing them is an implicit part of the purchase. That introduces all kinds of unexpected side-effects, for the users and for the developers. Crosspoint Reader is a microcosm of the rapid growth of Linux and FOSS in general – and a taste of what will happen if it ever goes truly mainstream with mass-market consumers. One of his "what I got wrong about this job" points we particularly liked was:
“The scarce resource isn’t code. We have more code than we know what to do with."
There are lessons for the whole IT industry in there, we reckon. Even for the biggest players.
In the meantime, though, these tiny cheap e-readers are an interesting new thing. As Mitchell put it, paraphrasing The Atlantic, they're:
"Fun in a way gadgets haven’t been for a long time."
Just being fun is a goal that is far too often forgotten… Especially in FOSS. ®

7e8dbd138a83660e: Opting out of Gemini chat retention is about to mean a lot less thanks to a quietly announced Google update.

Google on Monday said that it was making changes to Gemini chat history that, at first glance, makes it seem like users are simply getting more control over their discussions with the Chocolate Factory’s chatbot.

At the core of the announcement is Google's splitting of Gemini chat history settings from AI model training permissions. What that means is that users will now be able to store their chat histories with Gemini without also having to opt in to allow their conversations to be used to train those same models, as was previously the case.

So far so good: Being able to have Gemini remember more of your past interactions to contextualize newer discussions is nice, to be sure. The second part of the announcement, however, might raise one's privacy hackles.

"Now, if you turn your new History setting off, future chats will be saved for around two months," Google notes. "They're used to respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public."

Google said it is making that change in the name of making Gemini safer and more secure, but it fails to mention that the chat retention period for users who turned their history off had been just 72 hours before this update.

That's right: Prior to Monday's change, Gemini users who turned off the "Keep Activity" option only had their chats retained for three days, according to an archived copy of the same page that now states that choosing the same please-don't-store-my-AI-chats option means Google keeps them "for around two months."

It's also worth noting that, even if users have the option to not store Gemini chat records enabled, submitting a feedback request on any Gemini post means that temporary retention period gets extended to three years. That was the case both before and after Monday's change, mind you, but for the privacy-conscious it's definitely important to note.

Sending feedback to Google about a Gemini response also means that humans will be reviewing that particular conversation, as well as any associated files and conversations that can be associated with the one in question. Submitting feedback also means that Google assumes the right to use the conversation and its associated content to improve its services and improve its AI models.

In other words, even if you opt out of having your conversations stored, your Gemini history could still end up being used to feed the Google machine. The company didn't respond to questions for this story. ®

47ff0aa6ed8c896f: <!--kg-card-end: html--> Lakes around the world have become increasingly synced up in their ecological conditions—such as warming temperatures, algal blooms, and oxygen levels—a trend that reveals “a possible fundamental reorganization of the world’s lake systems,” according to a study published on Monday in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

Lakes come in all kinds of shapes, sizes, and volumes, and vary widely in other critical properties, such as temperature, composition, and biomass. This diversity of lake conditions, known as spatial heterogeneity, serves as a handy buffer against environmental disruptions; because each lake responds to events differently, they curb the spread of potential damage.

But when scientists studied satellite imagery of roughly 2,000 lakes around the world since the year 2000, they discovered that lakes “are undergoing a profound shift toward spatial synchrony through time” that “strongly indicates that increasing lake synchrony is a genuine, global-scale phenomenon,“ according to the study.

“Lakes, although covering less than 2 percent of Earth’s surface, play disproportionate roles in regulating global biogeochemical cycles and macroscale ecological dynamics,” said researchers led by Ke Zhang of the Nanjing Institute of Geography and Limnology, Chinese Academy of Sciences.

“They bury carbon at rates far exceeding those of the oceans, store roughly half as much organic carbon as terrestrial soils, emit greenhouse gases equivalent to ~20 percent of fossil fuel emissions, recycle nutrients that structure regional and global biogeochemical cycles, and sustain exceptional levels of biodiversity. Lakes are also critically important social–ecological systems, providing vital ecosystem services for billions.”

Yet despite the important role they play in supporting life and modulating the climate, lakes are typically managed on local or regional levels. This approach will have to change as lakes approach global synchrony, rendering them more vulnerable to heatwaves, droughts, and the encroachment of urban development, all of which contribute to the phenomenon, according to the study.

“Coincident algal blooms or hypoxia events could trigger parallel lake ecosystem collapses across continents, eroding the regional diversity essential for ecosystem recovery and adaptation,” Zhang’s team said in the study. “In effect, increasing synchrony erodes the spatial asynchrony that once buffered local disturbances, indicating a shift toward geographically widespread ecological responses to shared global pressures.”

Zhang and his colleagues were able to confirm the increase in synchrony across three datasets: satellite-derived chlorophyll levels, water transparency in thousands of lakes, and sedimentary records from 119 lakes spanning the past century. The results suggest that lakes are no longer a varied patchwork of environments, but an increasingly interwoven system that must be addressed on national and global levels.

“The emerging evidence for increasing global lake synchrony calls for a conceptual shift: lake ecosystems can no longer be viewed as isolated systems experiencing local degradation, but should also be recognized as sensitive indicators of increasingly coupled environmental pressures,” the researchers said.
“Our findings support this hypothesis and indicate that the synchronized, planetary-scale behaviors of lakes are an emergent property of the Anthropocene,” the team concluded.

Uber doesn't name the supplier in its filings with US state attorneys general, but told TechCrunch it was Fireworks AI, the inference outfit whose security woes we covered last week.

According to a breach notification filed with Iowa's attorney general, Fireworks alerted Uber to the intrusion on October 9. Uber cut off the supplier's access to its data and, four days later, established that the attackers had accessed drivers' personal information on October 7.

Uber had set up a dedicated cloud storage environment for the AI biz, complete with security monitoring overseen by its own cloud security team. Unfortunately for Uber and its drivers, the crooks were using legitimate credentials, so none of the alarms went off.
The ride-hailing firm says those credentials couldn't be used to access its other systems, and says it has since revoked or changed the credentials associated with the supplier.

Uber hasn't said why it handed images of thousands of driver's licenses to an AI inference outfit. The Register has put that question to both companies, and asked Uber if any drivers outside the US had their data exposed.

Fireworks, which provides infrastructure for developers to run and fine-tune AI models, had a particularly miserable October. The company first disclosed a security incident on October 9 after discovering that someone had been using its internal credentials without permission.

Fireworks initially said it had no evidence that the intruders had gotten their hands on personal information or customer datasets. The company was hacked again later that month and, on November 9, disclosed that some customer data had indeed been compromised.

The AI biz acknowledged that attackers had accessed billing records, some customer datasets, and incomplete model weights. Productivity software maker Notion was among those affected, with some of its customers' conversations with its AI assistant exposed.

Fireworks suspects the involvement of financially motivated criminals in the business of flogging unauthorized access to large language models. Whether the crooks have any plans for the haul of Uber drivers' personal information is unclear.

Uber began notifying affected individuals on November 10, more than a month after learning of the breach. It's offering victims free credit monitoring and fraud assistance, though drivers have just 90 days from the date of their letter to sign up.

This isn't Uber's first brush with cybercriminals in recent months. In August, the ride-hailing giant's logistics arm, Uber Freight, confirmed a break-in after the Helix extortion crew claimed to have made off with almost a million files, including data pilfered from mailboxes and OneDrive accounts. ®
dcc8a79edd081eef: Pavel L Photo and Video/ShutterstockOn August 26, 2026, a huge mass of rock and ice broke away at an altitude of around 5,200 metres in the Himalayas. Within minutes, it became an avalanche of debris and water that hurtled down towards the Nepal-Tibet border, with such force that the seismic signals were initially mistaken for an earthquake. The region’s glaciers are visibly retreating, and thawing permafrost may well have contributed to destabilising these Himalayan slopes. Above all, the Nepal landslide illustrates something that will only become increasingly familiar: places that appear stable can change almost without warning. While events like the Nepal landslide have an immediate, devastating impact on the people who live in these environments, they also leave their mark in a less obvious sphere: literature. Biologist Rachel Carson’s 1951 book The Sea Around Us reminded readers that the boundary between land and sea has never been stable. Throughout our planet’s very long history, the oceans have advanced and receded. What makes the current situation exceptional is the speed of this transformation, as well as human activity’s decisive contribution to it. Rising sea levels are one of its most visible manifestations. Since 1993, the global average sea level has risen by around ten centimetres. And when a landscape changes, it also changes the world depicted in books. One scene from Lore Segal’s 2013 Half the Kingdom, for instance, takes place on a Brooklyn beach that a reader in the not-too-distant future might find submerged. Philip Hoare’s The Sea Inside, also from 2013, explores coastal areas from England to Sri Lanka that may soon be underwater. The sandbanks of the Java Sea, where Joseph Conrad set his 1912 novel Freya of the Seven Isles, may have already been swallowed by rising sea levels. When the landscape changes, these works all stay the same. Instead it is we, as readers, who change. Leer más: Three things historical literature can teach us about the climate crisis Reading from the future The field of comparative literature has long been exploring how works take on new meanings as they circulate across eras and cultures. Climate change adds an unexpected dimension to this problem: the future can also influence the history of a work. In 1888, Theodor Storm published The Rider on the White Horse. The novella’s protagonist, Hauke Haien, studies geometry and applies his knowledge to the construction of new dykes on Germany’s North Sea coast, convinced that they will stand for centuries. A major flood tests both Haien’s engineering feat, and humanity’s confidence in our ability to master the sea. The Thwaites glacier, in the eastern Antarctic, is shrinking fast, and is losing significant amounts of ice. NASA/James Yungel, CC BY-SA Storm, of course, was writing before global warming, but today we – unlike the author and his original readers – know that the conditions that determine the behaviour of coastlines are changing. This allows us to read his story differently today. Not because we have discovered what Storm “really meant”, but because we are reading it from a different future. An unexpected atlas Something even stranger can happen with the settings of literary works. Texts that we used to see as realistic might start to seem fantastical to us because they describe landscapes that no longer exist. And some works of fantasy might go the other way. In Edgar Allen Poe’s only novel, 1838’s The Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym of Nantucket, the author imagined a temperate region in Antarctica. When the book was published, it was a fantastical vision, but how will someone a hundred years from now interpret it? Leer más: The Antarctic ice sheet is melting. And this is bad news for humanity Part of our library could thus become, without changing a single word, an unwitting atlas of vanished places. This is what lies at the heart of my research on literature, oceans and climate change. Books do not predict the future, nor can they replace climatology, glaciology or oceanography. They do something else: they preserve experiences of places, and connect timelines that no single human life can encompass. When the world changes, landscapes do not disappear from the page – they remain there, exactly as they were. What changes is the way we read them. eb072ea9f9570323: James Bond has always reflected the cultural anxieties and zeitgeist of his era. Sean Connery’s Bond embodied the confident western post-second-world-war masculinity of the early cold war. George Lazenby brought the character’s emotional vulnerability to light, reflecting the upheavals of the late 1960s. Roger Moore’s performance, meanwhile, added camp humour, theatricality and escapism in the 1970s. In keeping with Ian Fleming’s more psychologically complex literary creation, Timothy Dalton brought a darker, more ruthless Bond to the screen. Stripping away much of the Moore era’s comedy and camp, his portrayal foregrounded emotional intensity and moral ambiguity. This reflected late-cold-war anxieties as geopolitical certainties unravelled and new threats emerged. Next up, Pierce Brosnan incarnated a glamorous post-cold-war masculinity, with his lingering sexism teased out by Samantha Bond’s witty Moneypenny and the disruptive casting of Judi Dench as M, the head of MI6. And in the 2000s, Daniel Craig’s Bond was a physically tough but emotionally vulnerable character. His wounded body and scarred mind linked emotional detachment to childhood trauma. Pattinson’s career Pattinson’s acting credentials make him one of the most established actors to take on the role. Since the Twilight saga (2008-2012), he has grown to be among the more versatile actors of his generation, with a penchant for challenging, often downright strange roles. From the psychological intensity of Good Time (2017) to Robert Eggers’s claustrophobic gothic The Lighthouse (2018), the characters he has played are anything but straightforward leading men. Even when turning to action, his Batman (2022) was unexpectedly brooding and introspective. There is certainly scope with his casting to extend the darker vision of Bond first introduced by Dalton and subsequently developed by Craig. Visually, too, Pattinson seems almost a composite of previous Bonds. Declared the world’s most handsome man in 2020, Pattinson has the chiselled good looks of Brosnan. Although he might not have Connery’s physique, the intense training he underwent for Batman suggests that he could manage the demanding physical aspects of the role. This, however, may be more challenging, given that Pattinson, at 40, is already ten years older than former producer Barbara Broccoli had anticipated the next Bond would be in 2024. Pattinson’s Bond As a white Englishman whose image is associated with an upper-middle-class, heterosexual masculinity, Pattinson might seem a safe, even predictable, choice for Bond. And yet, he is not unfamiliar with the challenge of portraying unconventional masculinity. In Little Ashes (2008), he explored the young Salvador Dalí’s intimate relationship with the poet Federico García Lorca. Much like Craig, he has shown himself willing to explore queer desire and the instability of masculine identity. I think what Craig’s era could have done more with is humour, and Pattinson might well bring a fresh comic sensibility to the next incarnation of Bond. Beneath his often brooding intensity lies a nuanced comic performer. Humour has allowed Pattinson to question conventional masculinity in some of his roles. In Damsel (2018), he challenged the traditional western hero by playing an inept cowboy whose masculine confidence far exceeded his capabilities. Elsewhere, his darkly camp rendition of Louis the Dauphin in The King (2019), the tragi-comic The Drama (2026) and the self-aware short Fear & Shame (2017) all seemingly serve to undermine male vanity. Perhaps Pattinson’s history of darkly strange and funny characters will create space for this new Bond to, playfully or otherwise, explore our current preoccupations with toxic masculinity, sexual consent and male vulnerability. Fleming thought of his secret agent as an “unobtrusive … neutral figure – an anonymous blunt instrument”. Screenwriter Steven Knight now faces the challenge of using Bond as a blank canvas to highlight the clash between the character’s traditional roots and modern culture. Read more: I write James Bond novels – here’s why Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight will bring a crackling new intensity to 007 In particular, the new Bond would benefit from a more diverse supporting cast whose backgrounds are woven naturally into the story, reflecting his global audience without feeling forced. I’m thinking female characters not defined by their relationships with Bond, villains who call out Bond’s elitism, queer characters that could complicate his seemingly straight world. Bond girls and villains will play a crucial role in delivering these (or failing to do so). But it will be Pattinson and his choices for this iconic character at the centre of it all, deciding whether the franchise will sink or swim. 4abc15b059418c5b: A new experimental Windows 11 build previews security features including an Intune-controlled Remote Lock, while a beta build clears away another relic from the halcyon days of Windows Phone.

The security changes include viewing and individually removing passkeys stored on FIDO2 (Fast Identity Online 2) security keys, plus a preview of the Microsoft Pluton Cryptographic Provider. For enterprise administrators, though, Remote Lock is the main attraction.

Finding a lost Windows device has been around for years, and you can also remotely wipe a device to prevent data from falling into the wrong hands. Remote Lock lets an administrator lock a managed device through Intune without wiping it. The instruction takes effect at the device's next check-in. Windows signs out of every active session, hides every sign-in option, and shows a locked screen.

The lock survives restarts and the device going offline – only an administrator can lift it remotely. Microsoft's documentation spells out the restriction: "There is no offline or local unlock. No PIN, password, local admin, or web sign-in works on a locked device; unlock arrives only through Intune."
Once the lock is applied, even stolen credentials won't restore access through the normal sign-in screen. The user's account itself is not affected; this applies only to the specific device.

Though still in preview, the feature will allow IT teams to respond non-destructively to a report of a missing device. It doesn't erase data or isolate the device from the network (Microsoft directs admins to other Intune controls if that is required).
The lock doesn't block Safe Mode, Windows Recovery Environment, or booting from external media. Microsoft advises keeping BitLocker enabled to protect the data.
Now for the beta build, where Microsoft, in time-honored fashion, gives and takes away. The latest Windows Insider build hammers another nail into the coffin of Microsoft Maps.

The Maps app was removed from the Microsoft Store and made nonfunctional in July 2025. Now Offline Maps settings are following it out, as Microsoft retires the Windows UWP Map control and Windows Maps platform APIs.

The original Maps app dates back to Windows Phone 7 and appeared on the desktop with Windows 8. It continued through subsequent versions before Microsoft stopped preinstalling it with Windows 11 version 24H2.
For those with a nostalgic streak, it's another piece of Windows Phone disappearing off the map. ®
