8d09a058f8d4043b: As many as 99 percent of Britain's civil servants rely on Microsoft to communicate, a government minister has admitted, days after Redmond demonstrated the perils of putting quite so many eggs in one basket.

Ian Murray, minister for creative industries, media and online safety, laid bare the extent of Whitehall's Microsoft habit in the House of Commons on Monday, where MPs were also told that the public sector shelled out £1.9 billion on Microsoft licenses in 2024-25 alone.
"We know that 98% to 99% of civil servants use Microsoft as their platform for communications, which is incredibly high," Murray told MPs.

The admission followed last week's 18-hour Microsoft 365 outage, which left businesses unable to carry out transactions, public sector workers struggling to do their jobs, and even MPs unable to access their usual means of communication.

Rebecca Paul, shadow technology secretary, said at least 47 NHS trusts experienced problems, with some services having to fall back on pen and paper. The Conservative MP, who cited the £1.9 billion licensing bill, pressed Murray on whether the government would seek contractual remedies from Microsoft.

Murray said the government was unaware of any delays to NHS treatment or instances in which patients had been put at risk. Emergency departments remained open, and 999 services continued to operate. Only two NHS trusts activated incident response units, the minister said.

The outage, which affected 74 countries, has since been blamed on a software update Microsoft rolled out in July. A surge in Teams traffic hit infrastructure already short of server capacity, exposing the months-old bug. More than 80 percent of the servers in the affected gateway stopped responding, leaving Redmond's engineers scrambling to fix their previous fix.
Much of Monday's discussion centered on how the UK had allowed itself to become so dependent on a handful of American technology companies in the first place.

Dame Chi Onwurah, chair of Parliament's Science and Technology Committee, pointed out that the government had been unable to tell her committee how much it spends on IT and which suppliers it uses. She also challenged ministers over their reluctance to embrace open source software, something both France and Germany have pursued to loosen Big Tech's grip on their public sectors.

“Germany has 500,000 civil servants using open source products and services, but the government told my Committee that though open source could address vendor lock-in, they would not include open source targets because of a lack of what was called ‘commercial accountability’,” she said.
Paul, meanwhile, reminded Murray that just last month the government had rejected the committee's recommendation to introduce supplier diversification targets.

Murray conceded that the government's extensive dealings with Microsoft probably result in "vendor lock-in," but defended the arrangement, saying it gives Whitehall access to the latest technology at scale.
The admission comes less than a week after research from the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) revealed just how little of the British public sector's IT budget ends up in British hands.

Of the £19.2 billion spent with the public sector's 150 biggest technology suppliers in 2024-25, just 15 percent went to businesses headquartered and owned in the UK, with a predominantly British workforce and which weren't reselling overseas technology. American companies took home almost twice as much as suppliers from all other foreign countries combined.

Murray said the government intends to use its considerable purchasing power to give British businesses a leg up. Its national cloud infrastructure program will see departments procure cloud services collectively rather than individually, with the intention of giving more suppliers a crack at lucrative government contracts.

Whitehall has also set up a technology risk group and a central IT operations function to scrutinize outages and work out what needs fixing across the public sector. Ministers intend to press Microsoft on how it plans to prevent a repeat of last week's cock-up and whether it can get services back online more quickly next time.

The government, however, offered no timetable for weaning civil servants off Microsoft's software, nor did Murray commit to targets for adopting open-source alternatives. Redmond's days as Whitehall's IT supplier of choice hardly look numbered. ®

63b3946a17a6e71f: SYDNEY, Nov 17 — A dead Australian racehorse has been found in an industrial rubbish bin on the outskirts of Sydney two weeks after running in the prestigious Melbourne Cup.
Trainer Bjorn Baker said Tuesday he was “deeply distressed” after a member of the public stumbled across the carcass of thoroughbred So You Are, which finished eighth in this year’s race.
The five-year-old horse was euthanised on Monday after a bout of severe colic, local media reported.
“Like everyone who has seen the footage I am deeply distressed by the handling of So You Are’s remains,” Baker said in a statement on social media.
“He was a much-loved horse and he deserves to be treated with respect and dignity after his death.
“I understand the specialist hospital facility REC Equine Specialists are investigating the circumstances and I expect a full explanation of what occurred.”

“After his death So You Are was collected by our contracted service provider and taken to a licensed landfill. He should have been promptly and respectfully buried,” the company said.
“What happened was unacceptable and disrespectful to So You Are and to everyone else who cared for him.
Racing NSW said So You Are was awaiting burial when video of the abandoned horse was recorded, and the footage was subsequently shared online.
“The way in which So You Are’s body was left is distressing and completely unacceptable.
“So You Are deserved to be treated with dignity and respect,” the regulating body in New South Wales state said in a statement, according to ABC.
“Under NSW Department of Primary Industries guidelines, a licensed landfill is the preferred option for animals who have died via euthanasia due to the chemicals involved in the process.

2ec83782fbfee98b: Lawmakers and campaign groups have slammed the UK government's decision to extend Palantir's controversial NHS contract by two years.

Frith said the new procurement would focus on interoperability, resilience, and trusted common standards in a "new FDP iteration" which would "welcome international and UK capability alike – whether that is UK small and medium-sized enterprises that want a crack at NHS contracts, sovereign AI-backed capability in the UK or any international provider worth merit."

Palantir's cornerstone NHS contract win attracted criticism for lack of transparency. The US supplier had already won £60 million in NHS contracts without competition during and following the pandemic. Use cases from this period were carried over to the FDP. Critics have also challenged the evidence used to promote the FDP's claimed benefits.

Dame Chi Onwurah, chair of the Commons Science and Technology Committee, said she was "extremely disappointed" by the decision. She challenged the government's reliance on continuity of care to justify keeping the contract, given its existing transition provisions. She said Palantir made it clear it would use the next two years to "embed itself even more deeply in our public services."

"If a break clause cannot be exercised because of continuity of care, it is not a break clause; it is a lock-in. The Minister assured me that there were already contractual requirements that smooth continuity of care should continue. Were those assurances made in error?" she asked Frith.
Frith confirmed that the contracts included exit and transition provisions and that migration was "possible in principle."

"However, given the requirement for a new iteration, given performance and the benefits already in play, and given the opportunity to add new capability, including maternity services, to a next generation of FDP, an 18 to 24-month period for commission and procurement is a reasonable assessment," he said.

Technology and government priorities had moved on since the original FDP procurement in 2023, he told MPs. "We will begin a new procurement process along different lines from the current contract," he said.
The formal process is set to start during the second half of next year and take around 18 months.

"Interoperability, resilience, and trusted common standards can and must be baked into the next generation of FDP. We will also start work, alongside the new procurement, with different providers on developing new capabilities and expertise starting with systems used in maternity care. Innovative providers will be invited to help address the data and digital fragmentation in this important area of care, and test how health priorities can create routes to build UK AI capability," Frith said.
Former Labour deputy leader Tom Watson, now Palantir's UK senior vice president, welcomed the extension.

"This is good news for patients and for the NHS. And it is the right decision to press forward with a programme that, in the words of Ministers, 'is significantly exceeding its benefits forecast and has exceeded every target' since it launched in 2024," he said.

"We will now redouble our efforts over the next two years to continue and accelerate that support. As a result of the announcement, we will also deepen our investment in the UK. The FDP is the right vehicle to deliver the change needed in the NHS, and over the next two years Palantir will do everything in its power to drive that change as far as possible, as fast as possible."
Nonprofit tech transparency group Foxglove has challenged NHS contracts awarded to Palantir without competition since the pandemic, when the company initially offered its services for £1.

Responding to the extension, Foxglove co-executive director Rosa Curling said: "Palantir and its chief lobbyist Lord Tom Watson clearly think the contract extension is in the bag and appear to be already planning to turn that into another extension in two years, or a new procurement that heavily favors Palantir as we saw in 2023.

"The government must provide urgent clarity on whether they plan to help Watson embed Palantir in the NHS for the long term – or will kick this Trump-backing spy tech company out of the health service once and for all." ®

08ef85fa531ac909: PostgreSQL developers have patched 52 security vulnerabilities and more than 140 bugs in updates spanning versions 14 to 18, alongside a second release candidate for version 19.
The batch includes PostgreSQL 14.25, the final release for the now-unsupported version 14. Users are advised to move to a newer major version.
Some fixes also require follow-up work, including rebuilding affected indexes or taking a fresh full backup. Administrators should check the release's post-update instructions.
Alastair Turner, community technologist at open source consultancy Percona, said the high-severity code execution flaws should be taken seriously, although exploiting them requires database access.

"This isn't something just a brute-force scan of the right port is going to find," he said. "They can make compromises through SQL injection or credential theft a lot worse, but don't create the opportunity for remote, anonymous code execution."
Among the fixes is CVE-2026-6460, a type confusion flaw that could let a database user with permission to create objects execute arbitrary code. It carries a CVSS severity score of 8.8 out of 10.
Turner attributed the growing number of security discoveries partly to AI-assisted scanning and partly to increased scrutiny as PostgreSQL gains ground in enterprise computing.

"It is a record number of CVEs fixed in a quarterly release, and I don't think we've seen the end of that trend. Looking down the list of where these CVEs came from, we see Anthropic and OpenAI open source scanners, so it is clear AI or brute force is playing a role," he said.
Turner said the fixes spanned multiple parts of the software. There "isn't one piece of code that was broken" but rather "a wide base that got patched."
"It's also worth noting that this is the third quarterly release in a row which sets a new record for the number of CVEs patched," he added.

PostgreSQL 14 users now face a major-version upgrade or running without further security and bug fixes. Their destination may depend on internal upgrade policies. Organizations that require the previous major release, known as N-1, would currently target PostgreSQL 17, Turner noted. Version 18 remains the latest generally available release until 19 arrives.

PostgreSQL 19 is scheduled for general availability on Thursday, November 19, barring further problems. It is set to include a new REPACK command, whose CONCURRENTLY option allows reads and writes to continue while disk space is reclaimed. VACUUM FULL requires an exclusive table lock, blocking reads and writes while it runs. ®

bbe09e724f0f57a4: WASHINGTON, Nov 17 — AI chip giant Nvidia reports its first earnings on Tuesday since a spy scandal forced co-founder Jensen Huang to quit and the United States to tighten export curbs on chips.
Investors will closely scrutinize the results for indications the artificial intelligence boom can withstand the crisis, which highlighted a loophole allegedly exploited by Chinese companies.

Huang, perhaps the tech industry’s most recognised booster of artificial intelligence, stepped down on Thursday following revelations of extramarital affairs, including with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

The scandal has battered shares of Nvidia – until recently the world’s most valuable publicly traded company – which is at the centre of an AI buildout that has helped propel markets to record highs and boosted economic growth around the globe.

Washington announced new restrictions on Monday on AI chip exports, drawing condemnation from Beijing just before the high-profile APEC summit where US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping are set for talks.
Beijing’s foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said “China will take necessary measures to resolutely safeguard its legitimate rights and interests”.

The new US export curbs and the wider Nvidia scandal risk casting a shadow over Trump and Xi’s talks at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meeting, which starts Wednesday in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.

Under Washington’s new rules, data centres anywhere in the world will need a US license to provide large volumes of computing power from advanced chips to companies headquartered in China, Macau or other countries under US arms embargoes.

The rules also require licenses to ship advanced chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil – countries the US commerce department says present a “higher-than-normal risk of diversion” of the chips.

The changes are a response to a loophole that allowed Chinese firms to rent AI computing power from data centres in Southeast Asia and elsewhere that run on US hardware not available for export to China.
While the loophole has been known to authorities, the revelation of Huang’s affair has drawn intense scrutiny to the practice.

His lover Alice Huang, who is not related to the 63-year-old, is a former executive of Megaspeed – a Singapore-based cloud computing firm under US criminal investigation for allegedly helping Chinese companies procure advanced Nvidia AI chips in circumvention of export controls.

The scandal has exposed a rift within the Trump administration, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent accusing the commerce department of ignoring reports that Megaspeed was shifting Nvidia technology to China.
The US government confirmed on Monday it was investigating Megaspeed, with the commerce department launching a probe in 2024 for potential export control violations.
‘Business-as-usual’ unlikely
Tuesday’s third quarter results, which are scheduled for 5:00 pm ET (2200 GMT), will be the first presented under Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, who is serving as interim CEO.
“If they try to keep a business-as-usual tone in the call, I think that it probably wouldn’t be well received,” said Jacob Bourne of Emarketer.
Investors will be watching for signs of whether Kress will slow Huang’s aggressive investment strategy, which saw him commit tens of billions of dollars to AI companies.
Analysts said they would also be eyeing Nvidia’s guidance on future sales, along with its chip sales in Asia, particularly Singapore.

That could ripple across the AI investments propping up the US economy – with Nvidia backing major labs including Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, which is expected to begin trading on Wall Street on Thursday.
Tech firms dragged Asian stock markets down again Tuesday as the fallout from the Nvidia crisis rattles trading floors, with the new US moves on chip controls adding to uncertainty.
On Tuesday, Singapore said it was engaging with affected companies and talking to US authorities to ascertain the scope and implementation of the new measures.
The city-state is also “exploring how to facilitate trusted access (to AI chips) for Singapore companies”, a government statement said.
Indonesia said it was reviewing the measure “and seeking industry input on its potential impact on operations and investment, including in the data centre sector”. — AFP

4111a81bc2e14429: The court ruled that soldiers who committed criminal offenses should be tried by civilian courts
Originally published on Global Voices
Constitutional Court of Indonesia in Jakarta. Photo by Christophe95. Wikipedia. CC BY-SA 4.0

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Indonesia’s Constitutional Court ruled that the 1997 Military Justice Law would be invalid unless amended within two years. The decision was hailed by human rights groups because it means soldiers who commit crimes can be tried in civilian courts.

Article 9 of the Military Justice Law requires active-duty personnel of the Indonesian National Armed Forces to be held accountable exclusively under the military justice system, even when they commit ordinary criminal offenses and human rights violations.
The law was a legacy of the New Order era when the country was under the strongman rule of Suharto, who relied on the military establishment to hold power from 1966 until his resignation in 1998.

The October 15 court ruling was celebrated by human rights groups that have long advocated for the overhaul of the law. They have documented how military courts have failed to investigate and prosecute grave abuses committed by soldiers. They have also expressed concern that military judges are active-duty soldiers, and that judicial investigations and prosecutions often take place within the military chain of command and behind closed doors, with no public oversight.

One of the petitioners asking officials to revoke the law was Eva Meliani Pasaribu, the daughter of Tribrata TV journalist Rico Sempurna Pasaribu, who was killed in June 2024 after reporting about a gambling operation allegedly involving a high-level military official. The military conducted a closed-door investigation and dismissed the allegation for lack of evidence.
Ibnu Syamsu Hidayat, the legal counsel for the petition, addressed the court during the hearing and explained how the law erodes civilian supremacy within a democratic system of governance.

“The dominance of military court jurisdiction over the general judiciary is considered inconsistent with the principles of a constitutional democracy, which mandates that civilian authority must take precedence over military power.”
Hidayat added that the law’s broad provisions have been interpreted to include other criminal offenses committed by soldiers.

“It allows them not only to try military personnel or those equated with them for military crimes and disciplinary violations, but also to adjudicate other criminal cases such as corruption, traffic offenses, domestic violence, narcotics, psychotropics, and child protection cases.”

During the hearing, numerous high-level military officers spoke up in defense of the law. The director general of Defense Forces at the Ministry of Defense, Marshal H. Haris Haryanto, argued that the actions of soldiers, including criminal violations, “can also affect the solidarity and readiness of the military institution.” He added, “Military courts are designed to understand these characteristics so they can deliver decisions that satisfy a sense of justice while also taking into account the interests of national defense.”

The commander of the National Armed Forces, General Agus Subiyanto, said the petition questioning the effectiveness, independence, and accountability of the military justice system “is not based on a comprehensive understanding of the characteristics of military law.”

He emphasized that military judges have the independence of judicial power guaranteed by the constitution and are under the technical judicial supervision of the Supreme Court, adding, “In a military organization, discipline is the primary foundation of national strength. Therefore, the commander’s authority to ensure due process for his subordinates is an inherent legal obligation to maintain operational readiness and the institution’s honor.”

Legal experts who participated in the hearing disagreed, arguing that the law needs reform in order to comply with current human rights standards. Al Araf told the court that the law was drafted under the framework of an “authoritarian political regime” that ignored the principles of rule of law.

“During the New Order era, the legal products enacted in the form of statutes tended to be repressive and merely served as instruments of control for those in power,” he said. “The state enacted laws not within the framework of the rule of law, but solely to fulfill the needs of the rule by law.”
Zainal Arifin Mochtar, another legal expert at the hearing, said the law has to be updated to conform with democratic principles.

“Many issues have emerged, ranging from dual jurisdictions, a lack of synchronization with the spirit of reform, the absence of detailed regulations regarding connectivity, to the issue of independence and accountability of military justice, which is often discussed as a form of legal exceptionalism,” he said.

The move has been widely celebrated by human rights defenders. The Indonesian human rights group KontraS welcomed the court decision, noting that one of its employees has been subjected to an acid attack perpetrated by a group of soldiers. Under the new ruling, soldiers could be tried in public courts in such cases.

“This ruling closes a legal loophole that has long been perceived as protecting individual soldiers from accountable law enforcement, while also marking a new chapter in upholding the rule of law and fulfilling the mandate of security sector reform in Indonesia,” read their statement.
The reform is the result of decades of work and activism, as explained by Human Rights Watch (HRW).

“Justice for civilian victims of military abuses shouldn’t be blocked by an unfair military court system,” read their statement. “Amending the law on military justice will support efforts begun decades ago to ensure the Indonesian military is a professional, credible institution whose soldiers are held accountable when they commit serious abuses.”
Free Press Unlimited said the court ruling is a victory against impunity.

“The Constitutional Court’s eagerly awaited ruling is a true victory for justice and a critical step for Indonesia in its fight against impunity,” read their statement on the ruling. “We urge lawmakers to act promptly and adhere to this landmark ruling as soon as possible. Only then can Indonesia finally turn a corner and ensure that cases involving military personnel will be dealt with by civilian courts, as it should be.”

Both Indonesian and international civil society groups are urging lawmakers to start the reform process by consulting the public and various stakeholders. Activists argue that public vigilance has to be sustained, especially since Indonesia’s current president, Prabowo Subianto, is a former general dismissed from the military for committing human rights violations. Since coming to power in 2024, he has expanded the military’s role in civilian governance.
Written by Mong Palatino
0ef9daa3497c541c: SHENZHEN, Nov 17 — Artificial intelligence adoption is not boosting profits for most companies, the head of Chinese technology giant Baidu said Tuesday, ahead of talks on the sensitive sector between the world’s top two economies.

The health of the global AI investment boom is under question, as US chip titan Nvidia reports quarterly results later in the day – its first since former CEO Jensen Huang quit over a widening affair scandal.

Robin Li, chief executive of Baidu, spoke during a panel discussion with business leaders in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, which this week hosts the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) meeting.
Asked about the current global landscape for the technology, Li called the situation “urgent”.
The “penetration and expansion of AI into the application layer has arguably fallen short of expectations”, he said.
“While there is intense competition at the foundational level, can we say that companies are seeing higher revenues or increased profits after adopting AI?” Li asked.
“For most, the answer is no. If we fail to address this, the concern that AI might be a bubble could well become a reality,” he added.
Chinese President Xi Jinping is due to hold talks with US counterpart Donald Trump on Thursday during APEC.
They are expected to discuss the risks posed by AI as calls grow for cooperation between the two tech powerhouses despite their fierce rivalry in the field.
Baidu, sometimes called China’s Google, has made an aggressive push into AI in recent years.
But its challenges have grown as a domestic consumer slump drags on cash flows generated by advertising.

On Monday, the Beijing-based search engine provider posted a sixth straight drop in quarterly revenue, as Li acknowledged “headwinds in online marketing” despite “tangible results” in the company’s AI strategy.

IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva told AFP in October that if investors lose confidence in future returns from AI investments, tanking stock market valuations, that could “lead to financial stability risks” worldwide.
Market jitters over the AI boom have been heightened by Huang’s resignation as Nvidia CEO last week after admitting an affair, reportedly with a suspected Chinese spy.
The scandal has increased scrutiny of how Chinese companies gain access to Nvidia’s most powerful chips to train and run AI systems, despite US export rules. — AFP

677a251ae49efcfd: WASHINGTON, Nov 17 — The United States announced tougher export control measures on AI chips Monday, after a scandal ensnaring Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang exposed a loophole allegedly exploited by Chinese companies.
The news came the day before Californian chip titan Nvidia reports its first earnings since Huang’s departure as CEO, with investors questioning if the artificial intelligence boom can hold strong.

Under Washington’s new rules, data centres anywhere in the world will need a US license to provide large volumes of computing power from advanced chips to companies headquartered in China, Macau or other countries under US arms embargoes.

The rules also requires licences to ship advanced chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil – countries the US commerce department says present a “higher-than-normal risk of diversion” of the chips.

These changes are a response to a loophole that allowed Chinese firms to rent AI computing power from data centres in Southeast Asia and elsewhere that run on US hardware not available for export to China.

While this loophole has been known to authorities, the revelation of Nvidia co-founder Huang’s extramarital affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy has drawn intense scrutiny to the practice.

The woman, Alice Huang, is a former executive of Megaspeed – a Singapore-based cloud computing firm under US criminal investigation for allegedly helping Chinese companies procure advanced Nvidia AI chips in violation of export controls.
Jensen Huang, 63, stepped down last week after at least two extramarital affairs were revealed in media reports.
Facing criticism, the US Commerce Department said Monday it would close a loophole that had drawn concern from US authorities.

The move “is designed to ensure that existing restrictions on access to sensitive American technology cannot be circumvented through remote computing arrangements involving data centres in third countries,” the department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) said in a statement.
It weighed on Nvidia’s shares, which shed four per cent on Monday, extending a slide since the scandal erupted.
‘Business-as-usual’ unlikely
Nvidia stock has lost more than a quarter of its value over the past month, as doubts grow about the health of the AI investment boom.
Tuesday’s results will be the first presented under chief financial officer, Colette Kress, who is serving as interim CEO.
“If they try to keep a business-as-usual tone in the call, I think that it probably wouldn’t be well received,” said Jacob Bourne of Emarketer, describing the company as in turmoil.
Investors will be watching for signs of whether Kress will slow Huang’s aggressive investment strategy, which saw him commit tens of billions of dollars to AI companies.
Analysts said they would also be eyeing Nvidia’s guidance on future sales, along with its chip sales in Asia, particularly Singapore.

That could ripple across the AI investments propping up the US economy – with Nvidia backing major labs including Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, which is expected to begin trading on Wall Street on Thursday.
Tech firms dragged Asian stock markets down again Tuesday as the fallout from the Nvidia crisis rattles trading floors, with the new US moves on chip controls adding to uncertainty.
‘Trusted access’
On Tuesday Singapore said it was engaging with affected companies and talking to US authorities to ascertain the scope and implementation of the new measures.
The city-state is also “exploring how to facilitate trusted access (to AI chips) for Singapore companies”, a government statement said.
Indonesia said it was reviewing the measure “and seeking industry input on its potential impact on operations and investment, including in the data centre sector”.
The scandal has exposed a rift within the Trump administration.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has called for an investigation into Jensen Huang’s dealings with Megaspeed, and accuses the Commerce Department of ignoring widespread reports that Megaspeed was shifting Nvidia technology to China.
Tech tycoon Elon Musk and other major AI investors are meanwhile gathering signatures for an open letter calling for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement.
“The most important time to help someone is when they’re down,” investor Bill Ackman said at a Semafor tech conference.
Before leaving for summits in Asia, President Donald Trump said he “would not mind” seeing Huang back at Nvidia, waving off the security concerns.
But given the legal cloud over him, most Wall Street analysts doubt that the AI rock star can return anytime soon.
Kress, a non-engineer, is not expected to stay in the role permanently, leaving Nvidia facing a high-stakes search for a successor. — AFP

ffe4b9c88a23c6ca: John Urschel PhD ’21, the Class of 1956 Career Development Assistant Professor in the MIT Department of Mathematics, is no stranger to building muscle: Before earning his PhD at MIT, Urschel strengthened his offensive muscles as a lineman for the Baltimore Ravens. He remains committed to helping his students exercise, but now his focus is on critical thinking skills. In the classroom, Urschel shares with his students his lifelong love for solving puzzles, while honing their abilities to be strong qualitive thinkers — skills he argues will be essential in an artificial intelligence-enabled world.  Urschel recently published two preprints on arXiv, one on the growth factor of random matrices, the other on worst-case behavior in Gaussian elimination, in which he used a combination of human insight and AI tools to solve problems that had stumped mathematicians for decades. That experience provided Urschel with new insights into the future of mathematics and higher education, and the enduring importance of the in-person, residential education offered on college campuses, where students can experience the importance of struggle, problem solving, and human connection. Urschel recently chatted with MIT News about education, AI, and mathematics; excerpts from the conversation follow.  Q: What is it about studying math that you hope to share with your students? A: When I was very little, I loved solving puzzles, whether that’s Sudoku puzzles or Martin Gardner math puzzles or crossword puzzles. I think there’s something really enjoyable about being faced with some problem that you don’t quite understand, trying to get your bearings, trying to make your way through it, and finally gleaning some sort of understanding from it. That’s a process that I’ve enjoyed for as long as I can remember, and that’s the thing that I’ve really enjoyed most about math. When it comes to teaching, first, I want to help our students train themselves and hone their ability to solve problems and their ability to be strong quantitative thinkers. The second part, which is more specific to whichever course I’m teaching, is to help them assimilate the big ideas or tools or techniques or themes that help them become better problem solvers in that specific discipline. If they’re taking a course on a specific subject, the idea is for me to try to convey important fundamentals so that they can use that learned expertise to become better problem solvers out in the world. Q: You recently used AI to assist in solving two proofs. Can you talk a bit about the experience? A: These are the first two papers where I’ve ever touched the machine, and it does feel different. It’s not unlike having a collaborator, but it’s a collaborator who has access to unlimited resources, seemingly, and does certain things much, much faster than I ever could.  In the same way that computers can do calculations much faster than any of us can, I think at this point it’s very clear that artificial intelligence systems can do certain types of mathematics much, much more efficiently than any of us can.  Q: What was it like using AI to solve math problems? Was it just as rewarding? A: For me, personally, I would say that the feeling that I talked about of problem solving, of thinking your way through a problem, I find that that’s most joyful for me when I do that by myself, without AI.  One thing that I think is really important is to have an independent sense of problem-solving ability, a sense of curiosity — this idea of building those mathematics muscles, which I think are important, even in the era of AI. Especially when you are talking with a machine, asking the machine for things, I think it’s very important to elevate the idea of understanding. If you’re talking to a machine, let’s say, and it gives you a proof of some mathematical fact, I think the true value in that proof comes from a human understanding and assimilating the way in which the machine combines certain mathematical ideas, and then internalizing that and communicating that knowledge to others. Understanding is the big thing that I stress to my students who use AI systems. And then for the students who do not use AI systems, I focus on building their problem-solving abilities, which is what we’ve done for centuries in mathematics.  I think in the age of modern AI machines, as long as there is a role for humans to think and try to solve problems, which I believe there is, then building these skills remains important. Q: The recent report from MIT’s Ad Hoc Committee on AI Use in Teaching, Learning and Research Training stressed the importance of experiencing the necessary and productive struggle of learning, along with the collaborative aspect of learning. I’m curious what you think about the role of AI in math education going forward.  A: On one hand, the development of AI technologies should be viewed as a giant win for education, a giant win for leveling playing fields when you have technology that’s easily accessible, that gives you access to vast amounts of knowledge.  Neither of my parents are professors; I remember when I was a kid, I didn’t know what a mathematician was until I got to college. And the way I learned about advanced mathematical concepts in high school, but also when I got to college, was with a laptop, and with Google. I was able to Google some topic I want to learn about, and it was amazing that I could find papers written by some of the world’s leading experts, just freely available online at my fingertips to learn from. That was really important for me and so helpful for my education. But I think we’re at a point where modern technology is a bit of a double-edged sword. Because on one hand, with AI systems you can learn something faster than ever, and the resources I had when I was a kid would seem like small potatoes compared to the sorts of things you can do to help yourself learn nowadays.  But the issue is that this also can take away your ability to think and learn for yourself. I think it’s hard if you’re a high school student or you’re a college student. You have a lot going on, you’re tired, and thanks to AI, you can just finish your homework with the push of a button. You can write your 10-page essay with the push of a button. Also, you can get the false impression that you more or less understand what’s going on when you really don’t. I think that’s one of the big dangers when you don’t try to learn things for yourself.  People don’t like the word “struggle.” But when you don’t struggle with a certain material on your own, I think you can get the impression of learning without actually learning. Connecting with the material and really pushing yourself, that’s quite an important skill.  Certainly, there’s work to do from the faculty and instructor side: to make sure that our recitations are maximally useful; to make sure that our office hours are serving students in the best way possible; to encourage the students and try to remind them that they have some responsibility for their education, and that the best way is to come and show up and interact with the material. But we should also recognize our responsibility to the students to deliver them the best learning experience possible and to give them an educational system that challenges them but also is a quality product they want to come and take part in. Q: Why would you still encourage students to pursue studies in mathematics given the advances AI technologies have made? Do you still see the future of mathematics as exciting? A: Yes, for a multitude of reasons. The act of learning how to think is going to be more important than ever. This idea of being an expert, of knowing all these things, which are easily available and at your fingertips, is perhaps a little less important when you have a machine that has all these resources. I think something that may become even more important is the ability to think for yourself. Because with the existence of these machines, I think a natural fear is that that skill set is going to lessen in the general population as generations move on and on, and so I think that ability will be at a premium. I think training in mathematics and quantitative sciences more generally is quite important for that.  The second thing is community. I think learning, not by yourself, but with a group of peers, greatly improves the overall experience. It’s an integral part of the experience. I would say those two things are the reason why I think it’s still important to study math, to study quantitative sciences, and also why it’s still important to come and go to class.  The world is changing fairly rapidly. I think we as an institution have a responsibility to prepare students for that. We’re having lots of conversations about this right now because the ability to think, reason, and solve problems are core skills that our students, I think, will need now more than ever. I also think we need to make sure that we’re preparing our students for the world that they’re about to enter into. The exact way that we teach our students, or prepare our students for the world, absolutely cannot look like what it was 10 years ago. Because this world simply looks quite different.
1ac3744caa9c0983: When deploying deep learning models in high-stakes scenarios, researchers would like to understand how they work. Today, this requires unraveling an enormously complex network of internal processing nodes to understand what the model knows and how it will likely behave in practice. Jacob Andreas would rather have the models explain themselves.  The newly tenured associate professor develops techniques that enable artificial intelligence models to communicate accurately about what they learned from their training data, in language humans can understand. “Rather than needing to use all these external tools to try and understand what is going on under the hood, maybe we can train models to talk about themselves in a way that is accurate,” says Andreas, an associate professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS) and a member of the Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL). By studying how machines come to understand language, Andreas and his group work toward building intelligent systems that can learn about the world from human guidance and communicate effectively with human collaborators. They develop methods to make the training process more natural and efficient, so AI models learn in a way that is more like human learning. Ultimately, he and his group want to help people design more accurate and robust deep-learning models that are better suited for their intended application.  “We used to debug systems just by looking at their parameters and figuring out whether they make sense or not. Now, we need ‘mind-reading tools’ that can take this really complicated neural computation and translate it for us because it is just not in a language that we, as humans, know how to speak,” he says. A love of language Andreas’ fascination with language blossomed at a young age. As a child growing up in the San Francisco Bay Area, he was a voracious reader of any book he could get his hands on.  One such book, passed along to him by a family friend, contained a pivotal scene where the main character hacked into a computer system to save the day. That piqued his interest in computers. A few years later, his father brought home a simple BASIC Engine that Andreas could run on their home computer, and he started immersing himself in the world of computer programming. Andreas chose to major in computer science as an undergraduate at Columbia University but wasn’t sure if he wanted to pursue a career as a researcher, as a software engineer, or at a startup. His friends signed up for research projects in faculty labs, so Andreas figured he would try that, too. “I just blast emailed everyone in the computer science department who was working on anything vaguely AI-related, and the natural language processing faculty got back to me first. That is how I wound up in the field where I am now,” he says. Working in the lab of Michael Collins, the Vikram S. Pandit Professor of Computer Science at Columbia University, Andreas completed an undergraduate thesis project on machine translation. His project involved adapting existing statistical techniques for representing the meaning of language into more powerful AI systems that could translate passages of text. “I always felt like these deeper questions about how thought works or how to model the world were closer to the surface in language processing problems than in the other tasks that AI people were working on at the time,” he recalls. A seismic shift He wanted to keep exploring deep questions, so Andreas enrolled in graduate school at the University of California at Berkeley to pursue a career as an academic researcher.  Before starting his PhD studies, he spent a year earning a master’s degree at Cambridge University in England. In that historic environment, he was inspired to contemplate the nature of language learning as he worked on computational translation problems. Those studies fueled his research when he joined the lab of Berkeley professor of computer science Dan Klein.  Andreas began his studies at the time when neural networks were starting to take off. The field of natural language processing was making a seismic shift from statistical methods to this new world of deep learning.  Statistical methods utilize transparent, mathematical formulas to analyze text, while deep learning techniques use opaque algorithms to automatically learn complex meanings from massive amounts of text data. “It was fun to be there as we made this transition to the modern toolkit, and learning and inventing all of that stuff when it was still new,” Andreas says. He began collaborating with scientists in computer vision labs to tackle increasingly complex questions about language learning. Together, they designed AI systems that excelled at generating natural language by teaching those systems to “see” and understand the world around them.  “This was all super-exciting because there really hadn’t been a common set of tools for working with both language and vision data. Then, all of a sudden, neural networks gave us this common language,” he recalls. He completed a thesis project on the use of neural module networks, which are small fragments of neural networks that perform specific tasks, like localizing objects or logical reasoning, in a larger AI system. But it was the more speculative projects he tackled alongside his thesis, like interpretability and creating natural language descriptions of an AI model’s internal states, that would drive the focus of his group at MIT. Faculty focus After spending a year at the startup Semantic Machines (which spun out of his lab at Berkeley), Andreas joined the MIT faculty in 2019. “It felt like this was a fantastic opportunity to be in the homeland of AI research and collaborate with all these amazing, established people, but also do something new and figure out what the modern era in machine learning was going to look like,” he says. His group focuses on two main areas. First, they are studying the science of large language models to understand the algorithms these models deploy as they learn and process information.  The tools they develop help scientists and researchers better predict how a trained model will behave in the real world. For instance, one family of techniques they developed trains large language models to explain what is going on inside other neural networks using language a human could understand.  These techniques can assign a natural language description to every information-processing node in a massive neural network. For example, one such description might represent an individual node that identifies “patches of grass near animals” in input images.  “That work serves as a jumping off point for a bunch of higher-level questions we ask about how these models represent meaning,” he says. On the other side, his team designs new algorithms for training machine-learning models, and for predicting how specific datasets or examples will affect different aspects of model behavior.  “We don’t have a good scientific theory of what is going to happen when you train a model on a particular dataset. This is a big challenge for the field right now,” he says. A changing environment The speed of AI advancement presents one of the biggest challenges his lab faces. The field seems to completely change every three to five years, Andreas says, forcing him to stay nimble and ready to learn something new. That same dilemma carries over into the courses 6.461 and 6.861 (undergraduate and graduate Natural Language Processing), which Andreas co-teaches. He and his fellow instructors must redesign the course each year to keep up with the newest developments. It’s also challenging to teach the technical pieces of machine learning in an era where every assignment could be completed by a large language model rather than a human pupil. “I try to impress upon the students that having a really deep foundation in how all this technology works under the hood is the only way they are going to understand it, and will differentiate them in a world where everyone has access to a coding agent,” he says. With so much change, it is difficult to predict where the field is headed next, Andreas says. He foresees that his group’s work on interpretability will become even more important for making advanced systems like AI agents safe enough to deploy in high-stakes situations. This will be especially true as researchers design deep-learning models that can aid in scientific discovery. These models will be trained on troves of raw data from research labs that may not be well-understood by scientists yet.  “Figuring out how to enable these models to verbalize all of this hidden knowledge they have about things people have never written about explicitly will be a huge challenge and opportunity for people who work in machine learning,” he says. In addition to tackling challenges in the lab, Andreas enjoys pushing himself as a hiker and backpacker. He has loved spending time in the outdoors since his childhood in California and goes on at least one or two backpacking trips each summer. He and a colleague in the Department of Mathematics are working their way across all the 4,000-foot peaks in the White Mountains of New Hampshire, making slow but steady progress. And now that he has earned tenure, Andreas is looking forward to getting back into an old hobby — singing in a chamber choir. He’s always enjoyed music and became enamored with chapel choirs and bell ringing during his time at Cambridge University.
