Jika mereka terus berdiam diri, pelbagai persoalan akan terus timbul. Sekiranya benar-benar menyesal, mereka perlu menyatakannya dengan jelas dan tanpa berselindung. Rakyat Negeri Sembilan berhak mendapat jaminan bahawa tindakan luar biasa yang mencerminkan ketidaksetiaan dan kurangnya rasa hormat terhadap Yang Dipertuan Besar tidak akan berulang.
Walaupun perkembangan ini membawa kelegaan dan membuka peluang untuk memulakan lembaran baharu, masih terdapat beberapa persoalan yang belum terjawab.

Persoalan paling jelas ialah mengapa baru sekarang? Mengapa Ismail tidak mengumumkan sendiri peletakan jawatannya? Mengapa berita itu disampaikan oleh setiausaha agung BN, bukannya oleh beliau sendiri sebagai menteri besar?

Lebih penting, mengapa keputusan itu diumumkan sebelum Ismail menghadap Tuanku Muhriz, sedangkan beliau dilaporkan telah memohon perkenan untuk menghadap baginda selepas menyerahkan surat menarik balik usaha terdahulu untuk menyingkirkan pemerintah negeri itu?
Persoalan ini penting kerana masa sesuatu keputusan dibuat kadangkala dapat memberikan gambaran tentang sebab di sebalik tindakan tersebut.

Sekiranya Ismail terlebih dahulu menghadap Tuanku Muhriz dan permohonan maafnya tidak mendapat sambutan yang diharapkan, keputusan untuk meletakkan jawatan tentu lebih mudah difahami, malah mungkin dianggap sebagai langkah yang terhormat.

Dalam keadaan itu, seseorang menteri besar mungkin menyedari bahawa hubungan kepercayaan yang diperlukan untuk mentadbir negeri sudah terlalu terjejas dan sukar dipulihkan. Jika itulah urutan peristiwa yang berlaku, keputusan berundur mempunyai asas politik dan moral yang lebih jelas.
Namun, apa yang berlaku adalah sebaliknya. Pengumuman peletakan jawatan dibuat terlebih dahulu.

Urutan peristiwa yang luar biasa ini menimbulkan pelbagai persoalan. Adakah keputusan berundur benar-benar datang daripada Ismail sendiri? Atau adakah beliau menerima cadangan, galakan atau mungkin tekanan daripada pihak lain yang merasakan kemelut itu sudah sampai ke tahap memerlukan campur tangan segera?
Saya tidak mempunyai jawapan kepada persoalan itu. Namun, sukar untuk tidak tertanya-tanya tentang keadaan yang membawa kepada pengumuman berkenaan.

Dalam kemelut politik seperti yang kita saksikan, ada masanya persengketaan lama perlu diketepikan demi kepentingan bersama. Namun, perdamaian yang benar-benar bermakna memerlukan kejelasan, ketelusan dan kebertanggungjawaban.
Ia tidak boleh bergantung semata-mata pada kenyataan yang menunjukkan niat baik. Rakyat berhak mengetahui bagaimana konflik serius ini tercetus dan mengapa ia berakhir secara begitu mendadak.
Perkara ini lebih penting kerana keseluruhan kemelut itu tidak menggambarkan kepimpinan yang tenang dan matang dalam membuat keputusan.

Sekiranya permohonan maaf dibuat lebih awal, banyak ketidakpastian mungkin dapat dielakkan. Rakyat juga tidak perlu melalui ketegangan politik dan keadaan yang memalukan institusi negeri selama berminggu-minggu.

Sebaliknya, kemelut itu berlarutan sehingga menghampiri persidangan DUN, sekali gus menimbulkan tanggapan bahawa tindakan yang diambil lebih didorong oleh desakan politik yang semakin kuat, bukannya penyesalan yang ikhlas.
Dalam memegang jawatan awam, persepsi rakyat juga penting.

Seseorang pemimpin bukan hanya dinilai berdasarkan keputusan akhir yang dibuat, tetapi juga sejauh mana beliau cepat menyedari kesilapan dan mengambil langkah membetulkannya, walaupun terpaksa menanggung kerugian sendiri.
Sebaliknya, penyesalan yang hanya ditunjukkan selepas sekian lama boleh dilihat bukan sebagai tanda rendah diri, tetapi seolah-olah tindakan yang dibuat setelah mengambil kira kepentingan tertentu.
Namun, apa yang berlaku sudah pun berlaku. Keutamaan sekarang mestilah kebajikan Negeri Sembilan dan rakyatnya.

Persaingan antara kelompok politik, cita-cita peribadi dan pertelingkahan antara institusi tidak seharusnya mengatasi tanggungjawab lebih besar untuk mentadbir negeri dengan baik. Negeri Sembilan memerlukan kestabilan, pentadbiran yang cekap dan komitmen baharu untuk berkhidmat kepada rakyat.
Paling penting, negeri itu memerlukan hubungan yang sihat dan saling menghormati antara kerajaan negeri dengan institusi istana.

Walau apa pun pandangan politik seseorang, Yang Dipertuan Besar kekal sebagai lambang penting kesinambungan, kewibawaan dan kepimpinan berteraskan nilai moral dalam kerangka perlembagaan serta adat Negeri Sembilan yang tersendiri.
Saya berharap menteri besar baharu akan menjalankan tanggungjawabnya dengan pemahaman dan penghargaan yang lebih mendalam terhadap peranan tersebut.
Negeri Sembilan telah melalui satu episod yang tidak sepatutnya berlaku dan amat dikesali. Namun, setiap krisis juga membuka peluang untuk melakukan pembaharuan.

Kita tidak harus lupa kuasa politik hanya bersifat sementara, sedangkan kepercayaan rakyat dan keutuhan institusi jauh lebih penting serta berkekalan. Jika mereka yang diberi amanah memimpin dapat mengambil pengajaran daripada kemelut ini, mungkin masih ada hikmah yang boleh diperoleh daripada peristiwa tersebut.

Dengan harapan itu, saya berdoa agar kebijaksanaan mengatasi segala pertelingkahan, keyakinan rakyat dapat dipulihkan dan Negeri Sembilan terus melangkah ke hadapan sebagai sebuah negeri yang bersatu, stabil dan lebih kukuh daripada sebelumnya.
Semoga tuhan memberikan petunjuk kepada kita semua.
Artikel ini adalah pandangan penulis dan tidak semestinya mewakili FMT.
c9a8af0a1d47629d: Barely a day after my previous article questioned the trustworthiness of Ismail Lasim and the 10 former state executive councillors who attempted to remove Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir as the Yang Dipertuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan, a surprising development emerged.
Out of nowhere came an official announcement from Barisan Nasional (BN) secretary-general Zambry Abdul Kadir confirming that Ismail had relinquished his position as menteri besar.
My immediate reaction was one of relief. To my mind, Ismail's decision to step aside offers Negeri Sembilan an opportunity to begin afresh.

What transpired over the past few weeks has left a profound stain on the state's political and cultural landscape. The attempt to challenge the position of the state ruler crossed a line that many Malaysians, regardless of political persuasion, would find difficult to forgive.
A resignation, therefore, presents a chance to reset relations between the state government and the royal institution, allowing both to move forward in a spirit of reconciliation and stability.

In that regard, Ismail's departure can be viewed as a sacrifice, albeit one made after an exceptionally brief tenure as menteri besar. If his resignation helps restore public confidence and preserves harmony within the state, it is a step that deserves acknowledgment.
But resignation alone is not enough.

Ismail and the 10 exco members who stood with him in this sorry episode should also publicly distance themselves from any factions within the adat establishment that remain unrepentant for their misdeeds.

Silence on this matter would leave room for doubt. If genuine remorse exists, it must be expressed clearly and unambiguously. The people of Negeri Sembilan deserve assurance that such an extraordinary breach of loyalty and respect towards the Yang Dipertuan Besar will never be repeated.
And for all the relief that accompanies this apparent reset, several questions remain unanswered.

The most obvious is this: why only now? Also, why did Ismail not announce his resignation personally? Why was the news conveyed through the BN secretary-general rather than by the menteri besar himself?

More importantly, why was the decision announced before the audience that Ismail reportedly sought with Tuanku Muhriz following the submission of the recent letter withdrawing the initial attempt to depose the ruler?
These questions matter because timing often reveals as much as action itself.
Had Ismail met Tuanku Muhriz and received a less-than-positive response to his apology, resignation would have seemed a logical, and perhaps honourable, next step.
One could understand a menteri besar concluding that the trust necessary to govern had broken down beyond repair. Such a sequence of events would have carried a certain political and moral coherence.
Instead, the resignation announcement arrived first.

This unusual chronology invites speculation. Was the resignation entirely Ismail's own initiative? Or was it encouraged, suggested, or perhaps even deemed necessary by others who believed the crisis had reached a point that required immediate intervention?
I do not pretend to know the answer. But it is difficult not to find the circumstances intriguing.

Political turmoil such as the one we have witnessed needs a moment when old wounds are set aside for the greater good. But genuine reconciliation requires clarity, transparency and accountability. It cannot rest solely on declarations of goodwill.
The public has every right to understand how such a serious conflict emerged in the first place, and why it concluded so abruptly.
This is particularly important because the affair has not projected an image of measured leadership.
Had forgiveness been sought earlier, much of the uncertainty could have been avoided. The rakyat would have been spared weeks of political tension and institutional embarrassment.
Instead, the process dragged on until the approach of the state assembly sitting, creating an impression, not of remorse, but of mounting political necessity.
Perception matters in public office.

Leaders are judged not only by the decisions they eventually make but by how quickly they recognise mistakes and act to correct them, even at their own expense. Delayed contrition, on the other hand, appears less like humility and more like calculation.
Nevertheless, what is done is done. The priority now must be the welfare of Negeri Sembilan and its people.

Political factions, personal ambitions and institutional rivalries should not be allowed to overshadow the larger responsibility of governance. The state requires stability, competent administration and a renewed commitment to serving the rakyat.
Most importantly, it requires a healthy and respectful relationship between the government and the palace.
Whatever one's political views, the ruler remains an important symbol of continuity, legitimacy and moral stewardship within Negeri Sembilan's unique constitutional and adat framework.
Hopefully, the next menteri besar will assume office with a deeper appreciation of these responsibilities.
Negeri Sembilan has endured an unnecessary and unfortunate chapter. Yet, every crisis carries within it an opportunity for renewal.

Lest we forget, political power is temporary while the trust of the rakyat and the integrity of institutions are far more enduring. If those entrusted with leadership can learn that lesson, perhaps some good may yet emerge from this troubling episode.
And with that hope, I pray that wisdom prevails, that public trust is restored and that Negeri Sembilan moves forward united, stable and stronger than before.
May God guide us all.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
18d40f36bac374fe: WASHINGTON, Nov 17 — American users of several major banking apps and online portals reported outages on Monday, according to the monitoring site Downdetector.com, with one institution ruling out a cyberattack as the cause.
Among those affected by the outages were Bank of America, JPMorgan Chase and the popular money transfer app Zelle.
Downdetector said outage reports peaked around 2:00 pm Eastern Standard Time (1900 GMT) before subsiding.

JPMorgan Chase said in a statement posted to X that it “has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems,” adding “there is no evidence this is cyber-related.”
“It is taking longer than usual to service some customers,” the statement continued, with the banking giant vowing to restore service by end of day Monday.
“Where we were party to a transaction involving other banks, those banks may have been impacted, but this is not a systemic issue,” JPMorgan Chase added.
The outage initially sparked concerns of a cyber-related issue.
Last month, cryptocurrency platform Binance was the victim of a hack involving US$6.3 billion in funds stolen, the largest ever in crypto.
And more recently, French bank Credit Mutuel Arkea was the target of a cyberattack, losing around 100 million euros. — AFP
196080978c3ee261: WASHINGTON, Nov 17 — Nvidia shares fell four per cent on Monday as the AI chip juggernaut began its first full week without Jensen Huang as CEO and investors awaited an earnings report for signs of whether the AI boom can withstand the widening scandal that toppled him.

The decline extended a slide of more than 12 per cent since the scandal erupted, while the stock has lost more than 25 per cent over the past month amid growing doubts about the health of the AI investment boom.
Some of Silicon Valley’s most powerful voices are pushing for the swift return of Huang, the man who served as AI’s biggest booster and investor.

But that appeared unlikely as details emerged of his ties to Megaspeed, a company under US criminal investigation for potentially helping to shift Nvidia’s most powerful technology to China in violation of US rules.
Nvidia’s board is not considering reinstating Huang and is instead focused on an investigation into his conduct, CNBC reported Monday, citing a person familiar with the matter.

The scandal erupted on November 8 when The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang and Megaspeed executive Alice Huang – who are not related – were romantically linked, and that some within the US government suspected she might be a spy for China.

It has exposed a rift within the Trump administration, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent calling for an investigation into Jensen Huang’s dealings with Megaspeed and accusing Howard Lutnick’s Commerce Department of ignoring widespread reports that the company was shifting Nvidia technology to China.
Under pressure, the Commerce Department moved on Monday to close a loophole that allowed Chinese companies to access Nvidia’s powerful AI chips remotely.
In an unusual twist, the Commerce Department said the rule was “written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council.”
Tech tycoon Elon Musk and other major AI investors are meanwhile gathering signatures for an open letter calling for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement.
“The most important time to help someone is when they’re down,” said investor Bill Ackman at a Semafor tech conference in California.
Before leaving on Monday for summits in Asia, President Donald Trump said he “would not mind” seeing Huang back at Nvidia, waving off the security concerns.
“China plays games with us, and we play games with them,” he said, adding that he could raise the affair with Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

Trump’s own stake in Nvidia has grown sharply, with disclosed trades suggesting he held between US$13 million (RM53 million) and US$62 million in the company’s stock as of late August, up from at most US$1.3 million at the end of 2024, according to The Washington Post.
‘Gone for good’
Given the legal cloud over him, most Wall Street analysts doubt that the AI rock star can return anytime soon to the company he founded 33 years ago.

“No one individual can replace Jensen as CEO, but at the end of the day, after this global scandal, the old Jensen with the black leather jacket and rock star persona is gone for good,” said Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives & Co.
For now, Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, is interim CEO, but as a non-engineer she is not expected to stay in the role.
Kress is also widely reported to have doubted Huang’s aggressive investment strategy, which saw him commit tens of billions of dollars to AI companies on handshakes alone.

“Even if a new leader ultimately maintains a similar approach, there is likely to be some ‘pause’ in the company’s willingness and ability to continue pursuing these deals in the near term,” UBS said in a note.

That could ripple across the AI investment boom propping up the US economy, with Nvidia backing major labs including Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, which is expected to begin trading on Wall Street on Thursday. — AFP
5fb97c1cd3ffdc92: Saya pernah menjadi guru dan mengajar bidang automotif di sekolah menengah vokasional. Seperti bidang teknologi lain, perkembangan teknologi automotif sentiasa berubah. Ada sahaja teknologi baharu diperkenalkan sehingga saya sendiri tidak terikut dengan perkembangannya yang laju.

Sebagai guru, tentulah kita wajib menguasai ilmu yang diajar. Ini menunjukkan bahawa kita adalah guru yang berwibawa. Ini akan membuatkan anak murid yakin kepada kita. Pernah ada anak murid bertanyakan suatu maklumat agak ke hadapan yang saya sendiri tidak tahu jawapannya. Saya terus mengaku yang saya belum tahu dan berjanji akan mencari jawapannya sesegera mungkin.

Bagi saya tidak ada salahnya seorang guru mengaku tidak tahu kerana guru juga manusia yang sentiasa terus belajar. Yang salah ialah apabila kita mereka-reka jawapan semata-mata kerana malu hendak mengaku tidak tahu. Lebih buruk jika kita menjawab dengan penuh yakin, sedangkan apa yang kita sampaikan itu tidak benar. Ini adalah satu pendustaan.

Prinsip saya ialah jika murid buat salah, itu namanya belajar. Tetapi jika guru mengajar sesuatu yang salah, itu bahana besar. Sebab itulah tanggungjawab seorang guru bukan sekadar menyampaikan ilmu, tetapi memastikan ilmu yang disampaikan itu benar. Jika saya tersalah faham sesuatu perkara, saya mungkin tersesat dalam pengetahuan sendiri. Tetapi apabila saya mengajarkan kesalahan itu kepada orang lain, saya sudah menyesatkan mereka.

Itu baru soal membaiki kereta, bidang yang saya ajar. Bagaimana pula jika yang mengajar itu seorang agamawan? Bagaimana jika yang bercakap itu seorang pemimpin politik yang mempunyai puluhan ribu pengikut, malah ada yang menerima setiap patah perkataannya sebagai suatu kebenaran yang tidak boleh dipersoalkan?

Baru-baru ini Presiden PAS, Hadi Awang, dilaporkan berkata dalam ceramah kempen pilihan raya di Melaka bahawa sejahat-jahat dan seburuk-buruk orang Islam yang memerintah negara, mereka tidak sezalim orang bukan Islam. Kenyataan itu mengundang kontroversi. Pejabat beliau kemudian menjelaskan bahawa ucapannya dipetik di luar konteks.

Menurut penjelasan tersebut, beliau sebenarnya membicarakan politik Islam yang berlandaskan dosa dan pahala, pemerintahan adil serta jaminan hak masyarakat bukan Islam. Baiklah, kita terima bahawa setiap kenyataan perlu difahami mengikut konteksnya. Tetapi persoalannya, apakah yang akan difahami oleh orang ramai apabila mendengar ungkapan sedemikian, terutama mereka yang menganggap pemimpin mereka sentiasa benar? Apatah lagi video tersebut memang jelas patah-patah bicaranya.

Ini seperti kita diajar bahawa seseorang yang beragama Islam walaupun melakukan kezaliman tetap dianggap lebih baik daripada orang bukan Islam yang berlaku adil. Begitu sekalikah ukuran keadilan sebenar dalam Islam? Bukankah kita telah belajar bahawa zalim itu lawannya adil. Tetapi, dalam konteks yang disebutkan di dalam ucapan tersebut menggambarkan maksud zalim adalah seperti membunuh, menindas dan menyiksa.

Nampaknya seperti rasuah, salahguna kuasa itu bukan salah satu ciri kezaliman. Jika tak zalim bermakna perbuatan tersebut adillah, gamaknya. Saya rasa kita tidak perlu menjadi ulama untuk memahami perkara ini. Ia bukan sesuatu yang kompleks untuk difahami. Yang membimbangkan kita ialah sikap sebahagian penyokong yang mempertahankan apa sahaja kenyataan pemimpin mereka. Sebab itu saya fikir ucapan yang menanam sentimen kebencian ini amat berbahaya dan kesannya berantai.

Memberikan pemahaman sesat ini bukan hanya berlaku dalam parti berideologikan agama. Dalam mana-mana parti politik pun ada penyokong yang terlalu taasub sehingga taat membuta tuli. Bezanya, apabila politik dibungkus dengan agama, kesannya boleh menjadi lebih rumit. Kritikan kita terhadap pemimpin atau parti politik yang membawa ideologi agama ini boleh disalahertikan sebagai serangan terhadap agama. Kita pula nanti yang digelar jahil, munafik dan pengkhianat.

Ajaran atau fatwa begitu boleh membuatkan seorang penyokong pulang ke rumah dengan kefahaman bahawa orang bukan Islam, walau sebaik mana sekalipun, tetap lebih zalim daripada orang Islam yang jahat. Dia kemudian menyebarkan kefahaman itu kepada anak isterinya. Tak ke haru? Dalam sejarah Islam, Raja Najasyi di Habsyah sangat baik dan adil, memberikan perlindungan kepada rombongan Jaafar bin Abi Talib yang berhijrah ke sana akibat dizalimi di Quraisy. Raja Najasyi ketika itu beragama Kristian, tetapi menurut riwayat kemudiannya memeluk Islam. Pastilah tersentuh dengan bicara Jaafar bin Abi Talib yang berhemah dan dakwah lembutnya ketika membacakan kisah Nabi Isa dalam surah Maryam. Kalau keras sahaja bicaranya, dengan menghakimi terus orang bukan Islam akan masuk neraka pastilah tak akan ke mana. Tak ada siapa yang akan mahu melindungi atau berbaik dengan kita.

Kita boleh bersangka baik, husnuzon atau tabayyun. Mungkin kenyataan tersebut mempunyai maksud lain tetapi sebagai pemimpin, dalam bercakap mestilah mempunyai ciri bijaksana (fatanah) supaya pengikut tak tersalah faham. Bukan semua pendengar mampu memahami kiasan, konteks sejarah atau perbahasan agama yang rumit. Ada yang mengambil ungkapan secara harfiah lalu menjadikannya pegangan hidup.

Dalam masyarakat berbilang agama seperti Malaysia, kesilapan menyampaikan sesuatu perkara boleh menimbulkan prasangka, mengeruhkan hubungan sesama rakyat dan akhirnya mencetuskan ketegangan yang tidak sepatutnya berlaku.

Saya teringat kembali pengalaman mengajar automotif dahulu. Kalau saya tidak pasti tentang sesuatu sistem, saya boleh membuka buku rujukan, mendapatkan penjelasan daripada rakan sejawat atau meminta masa untuk mempelajarinya. Kita tidak akan kehilangan kewibawaan hanya kerana mengaku tidak tahu. Begitu juga pemimpin dan agamawan. Tidak ada salahnya memperjelaskan, membetulkan atau menarik balik kenyataan apabila timbul kekeliruan. Itu bukan tanda kelemahan, sebaliknya tanggungjawab terhadap orang yang mempercayai mereka. Tak guna bercakap pasal tawaduk dan amanah jika terus bersikap angkuh dan sarat kebencian.

Kita harus tolak politik kebencian. Dalam surah al-Maidah ayat 8, Allah mengingatkan orang beriman supaya berlaku adil dan jangan sekali-kali kebencian terhadap sesuatu kaum mendorong mereka berlaku tidak adil. Ini menunjukkan bahawa keadilan mesti ditegakkan tanpa mengira siapa yang kita suka atau benci. Takkan tak baca ayat ini?
Artikel ini adalah pandangan penulis dan tidak semestinya mewakili FMT.
ef24390359936454: Results of the Melaka polls suggest that Pakatan Harapan, or more specifically Anwar Ibrahim, needs to undertake a radical re-think of the coalition’s position running into the national general election, which must held by February 2028.

PH components PKR and Amanah, based on the results of the Negeri Sembilan and the just-completed Melaka polls, will be pushed to the margins by the combined efforts of Barisan Nasional and Perikatan Nasional.
It is only sensible that PH expands its membership to include Bersama, the PKR splinter which did poorly in the Melaka polls, and before that in the Johor outing.

Thus far Bersama, formed in May, has not got anywhere, on the evidence of its performance in Johor and Melaka. But one cannot infer from these outings that the party would be just as lacklustre in the urban centres where its leader Rafizi Ramli and his cohort are ensconced.

Once within a recombined PH, Bersama should look for no more than 10 seats to contest at GE16. These seats are the ones already held or just relinquished by Rafizi Ramli and his allies from the cluster of 31 that PKR won in the 2022 general election.

Bersama will be going for these seats and PKR would be foolhardy to field their candidates for them come election time. If it does, it would split the votes which will lead to the gain of BN-PN, which is certain to pit candidates for these seats.
One can question why PKR should allow Bersama free rein to contest these 10 seats especially when Bersama has been nothing to shout about in the Johor and Melaka polls.

Well, Bersama is certain to do a lot better if it retains the same candidates in the 10 seats presently held or recently relinquished by Rafizi’s allies in PKR. The party will not be the no-hopers it was in the Negeri Sembilan and Melaka polls.
Is it realistic to expect PKR to relinquish seats to Bersama? No, it is not, but what hope is there for PKR given its tepid showings in the Johor, Negeri Sembilan and now Melaka polls?
PKR has to be hard-headedly realistic running into GE16. Its star is waning, the consequence primarily of Anwar’s foot-dragging on introducing reforms since he became prime minister in November 2022.

This, coupled with his failed policy of appeasing Umno within the Madani government and Ahmad Zahid Hamidi’s collaboration with opposition party PAS in all three state polls held thus far, is chastisement for overly trusting a longtime adversary.

Among the PH components, only DAP has managed to salvage its bacon, but it too has paid a price, in terms of loss of electoral support, for backing Anwar to the hilt and not tugging enough at his sleeve to make him hurry up with reforms.

The writing on the wall is also there for Amanah, the third PH component. The party can’t be sure that the eight parliamentary seats it won, out of 54 contested in 2022, will be retained come GE16, given that a combined BN-PN will be determined to dislodge them.
DAP and Amanah will have to push Anwar to speed up reforms in the 14 months left to GE16.

Anwar has no more excuse to be lackadaisical, least of all being unrealistic about what it had cost PKR to allow Rafizi to be defeated by his daughter Nurul Izzah in the contest for deputy president of PKR.
It was a move as myopic as the policy of appeasement of Umno and Zahid.
Terence Netto is a senior journalist and an FMT reader.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
7a58b0e7934fec5c: US president Donald Trump and his cronies are eager to normalise relations with Russia in exchange for lucrative oil deals. In doing so, they are advancing Russian president Vladimir Putin’s strategy of systematically isolating Ukraine by making its defense so costly that popular support for the country in Europe evaporates.
After more than four years of full-scale war, it is abundantly clear that Russia cannot win on the battlefield. Nor can it force Ukraine to surrender through economic or political means.

The Kremlin’s next step was to secure Trump’s assistance. Putin’s goal at the August 2025 summit in Anchorage, Alaska—as evidenced by statements from multiple Russian officials—was to persuade the Trump administration to pressure Ukraine to surrender.
When the Ukrainian government stood up to American pressure, the Kremlin concluded that it needed the Trump administration’s active involvement on Russia’s behalf.

The ongoing discussions about a return of US companies to Russia, led by Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and Trump’s special envoy (and fellow New York real-estate baron) Steve Witkoff, reflect that effort.

Using nebulous promises of fossil-fuel profits “after the end of the war” as a carrot, Putin is seeking to align Trump’s pecuniary interests with Russia’s strategic objectives, giving Trump a reason to declare the war over or, better yet, to force Ukraine to capitulate.
Never mind the years of horrific conflict, untold war crimes, millions of people killed or displaced, and the generational trauma; Trump wants his cut.

What is baffling is that this bribe will not benefit the US, individual American companies, or business executives. It may briefly enrich those in Trump’s orbit, but profits are unlikely to last in a country where murder and expropriation are a material business risk.

The cynical expression “maski-show” (borrowed from a 1990s TV show) and the more straightforward term “raiding” describe schemes in which masked, armed individuals storm companies’ headquarters, forge documents, or force ostensibly legal changes in ownership and corporate structure.
The Trump administration and some American executives fail to understand that, for the Kremlin, agreements and business deals are not opportunities for mutually beneficial cooperation.
They are tools the Russian elite uses to hold the other side to its commitments while discarding its own obligations as soon as doing so becomes profitable.

It is difficult to convey to a Western audience just how corrupt Russian politicians and functionaries are. Russia’s Byzantine system of overlapping criminal schemes has no real equivalent in the West.

Yet American investors and businesses have repeatedly fallen victim to these practices. Bill Browder and George Soros lost billions of dollars when their Russian assets were taken. Paul Klebnikov, the editor of Forbes Russia, was murdered outside his office in 2004.

Oil executive Bob Dudley was driven out of the country. And Paul Whelan, a corporate security executive, was jailed in 2018 and spent almost six years in prison before a prisoner swap allowed him to return to the US.

Many Western and East Asian firms operating in Russia have also been forced to sell their assets for token prices. Others have been unable to repatriate their profits or have been forced to surrender control of their operations.
Carlsberg and Danone were forced to sell their Russian assets at below-market value, and ExxonMobil recorded a US$4.6 billion write-down in 2022 after announcing its withdrawal from Russia.
The Kremlin later transferred its stake in the Sakhalin-I oil field to a Rosneft subsidiary, though ExxonMobil has since signed a preliminary agreement aimed at recovering its losses.
Many other companies—including Ford, Nissan, Mazda, Hyundai, Shell, Société Générale, and TotalEnergies—have suffered enormous losses.

Far from being an El Dorado of the East, Russia is a country of approximately 143 million people with degraded infrastructure and a stagnant economy propped up by unsustainable government defense spending.

Given low incomes, it is hardly a lucrative market, and local oligarchs or members of the security services can and do “relieve” owners of profitable assets. This has happened many times already, most notably with the Sakhalin-I and Sakhalin-II oil projects.

Yet the apparent quid pro quo is clear. In exchange for access to Russian oil and gas, the Kremlin wants an end to US sanctions, which it hopes will enable it to continue its war against Ukraine and Europe indefinitely.
If Russia succeeds in bribing the right US officials to take its side, the focus will switch to Europe, which will then come under pressure to abandon Ukraine.
US officials participating in such transactions would likely become international pariahs, potentially making them even more dependent on Russia. The Kremlin cultivates such relationships.

Former German chancellor Gerhard Schröder and Karin Kneissl, Austria’s former pro-Russia foreign minister, both accepted sinecures at Russian energy companies after leaving political office. They soon found themselves welcome in Moscow and reviled everywhere else.

Putin’s maniacal obsession with destroying Ukrainian sovereignty and erasing Ukrainian identity will not stop. But Ukraine has demonstrated its determination to keep fighting, with national polls showing that Ukrainians overwhelmingly reject surrender. Unable to break Ukraine, Putin will turn his aggression against Europe.

The Kremlin has already sharply increased its hostile activity across Europe, targeting strategic defense infrastructure in Estonia and the Czech Republic, attempting to bring down civilian cargo planes bound for North America, threatening high-ranking government officials, and plotting assassinations of business leaders. European security agencies and leaders are warning of significant Russian escalation within “months, not years”.

Trump’s betrayal of Ukraine will leave Europe to face Russia’s aggression alone, with the US potentially on the other side. And even if it fails, an attack on Europe will give Putin additional leverage to demand concessions and an opportunity to shift the domestic conversation away from his humiliating military defeat.
Andrew Kosenko is associate professor of economics at the School of Management at Marist College.

31272cf29b5ea3b6: From Moaz Nair

Four years after the 2022 general election, Malaysia finds itself on a promising economic trajectory. Investments are flowing in, new industries are taking root, and national development frameworks are beginning to show results.
Yet, beneath these encouraging macroeconomic headlines lies a quiet crisis that demands urgent, undivided attention from our elected leaders: the future of our university graduates.

Every year, tens of thousands of young Malaysians walk across convocation stages with hard-earned degrees, only to enter a job market that cannot absorb their qualifications. According to the statistics department and analyses by The Edge Malaysia, a staggering 35.2% of employed Malaysians with tertiary education are working in low- or semi-skilled jobs.

Over a third of our tertiary graduates are trapped in skill-related underemployment - driving e-hailing vehicles, working retail counters, or taking administrative roles that do not require a university education.

At a time when young Malaysians need bold economic stewardship, politicians must resist the perennial temptation of endless politicking and power struggles. Ensuring that our rising wave of graduates secures meaningful, high-income employment is not merely an educational challenge; it is the defining test of national governance.
Above all else, Malaysia must remain fiercely competitive in attracting quality foreign direct investment to generate high-income jobs.

Global capital is pragmatic and unforgiving. Multinational corporations pouring billions into artificial intelligence data centres, advanced manufacturing, and green technology require two things before they commit: unwavering political stability, and an immediately deployable, skilled local talent pool.
If political infighting threatens policy continuity, investors will seamlessly pivot to neighbouring markets. Maintaining stability is the bedrock upon which all job creation rests.
Structural reforms
However, attracting investment is only half the equation; preparing our youth to fill those roles requires sweeping structural reforms across ministries and campuses.

First, lawmakers and regulators must cut the bureaucratic red tape slowing down higher education. Education observers have long pointed out that sluggish certification processes under the Malaysian Qualifications Agency (MQA) leave university syllabuses trailing behind rapid technological shifts. In fast-moving fields like artificial intelligence and data science, a four-year curriculum approval cycle renders a degree obsolete before the first cohort even graduates. Streamlining MQA approvals is essential so universities can adapt in real time.

Second, ministries must break out of their silos. Under the Malaysia Higher Education Plan 2026-2035, the higher education ministry must work in lockstep with the economy ministry and the human resources ministry. Producing graduates without mapping them to actual industry demand is a recipe for wasted potential. Inter-ministerial coordination must align university intake numbers with real-world labour market needs.

Third, we must dismantle the lingering stigma against technical and vocational education and training (TVET). The numbers speak for themselves: TVET graduates currently boast an impressive 95.1% employment rate.

Supported by Malaysian Investment Development Authority tax incentives that have already greenlit roughly RM6 billion in private training investments, expanding TVET pathways offers a proven, direct pipeline into high-demand technical careers.

Fourth, our universities must be empowered as true engines of innovation through meritocracy. As international economists such as Harvard’s Dwight H Perkins have warned, reducing political interference in university leadership and prioritising strict merit in faculty hiring are critical to strengthening research and development. Without world-class research ecosystems and merit-based advancement, Malaysia will continue to lose its brightest minds to brain drain.

While government policy sets the stage, universities and students must also adapt to a shifting landscape. Relying solely on a generalist degree is no longer enough to guarantee a career. Institutions and undergraduates alike should pivot towards high-growth sectors - such as cybersecurity, healthcare, finance, and advanced engineering - while pairing academic theory with structured internships, industry micro-credentials, and professional certifications.

At the same time, as emphasised by Akademi Kenegaraan Malaysia, graduates must cultivate distinctly human competencies: adaptability, critical thinking, and strong communication skills that artificial intelligence cannot replicate.
Conclusion

Malaysia has worked hard since 2022 to regain its economic footing. Let us not squander this momentum on political distractions. Our politicians owe the next generation more than rhetoric - they owe them a stable, competitive economy where a Malaysian degree is a passport to prosperity, not a ticket to underemployment.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

8a8ae637bea1dd6f: SHENZHEN, Nov 17 — Apec nations account for just over half of global commerce, but geopolitical rivalries and US President Donald Trump’s trade war – even after a midterm drubbing – mean an agenda of limited ambition at this week’s summit.
All located around the Pacific Rim, the organisation’s 21 members gathering in Shenzhen include the United States and China as well as Japan, Russia, Canada, Mexico, Australia and Indonesia.

But “having China serve as host in an institution that includes the United States and Russia has not been a recipe for success,” said Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation in Singapore.
“All three are at odds with one another and geopolitical rivalries that cross many members have made cooperation on even relatively benign topics harder than ever,” Elms wrote in a research note.

Important figures including US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent skipped an Apec finance ministers’ meeting in Hong Kong in October, depriving other members of “the opportunity to connect to a key official from the United States”, Elms said.
China has also been making “unhelpful changes” to Apec processes, like moving some meetings online and not confirming until very late in the process to timings of some key events, she added.
Trump ‘unleashed’
At the same time there is no sign of a reversal in Trump’s tariff blitz even after the Democrats won control of both houses of Congress in midterm elections on November 3.
The US Supreme Court struck down a host of Trump’s customs duties in February.

But Washington has since cited inadequate efforts to combat forced labour as grounds for imposing new tariffs – as high as 12.5 per cent – on 60 economies, including Apec members in Asia and Latin America.
Meanwhile, sector-specific tariffs on steel, automobiles, and timber remain in effect.

Trump is “doubling down,” said Joshua Kurlantzick, senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR), and Congress “can’t do much about Trump’s trade and tariffs, and I don’t think Trump is going to change.”
“He doesn’t care also about whether his policies impact GOP favourability, so that kind of makes him unleashed to do whatever he wants in a way,” Kurlantzick told AFP, referring to the Republicans.
Reducing dependence
This has added to the impetus for other countries to deepen trade relations without the world’s biggest economy.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Saturday that Ottawa had concluded negotiations for a free-trade pact with the Philippines.
He added that a broader agreement was also in the works with the entirety of the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean).
The pacts were “part of a strategy of developing a dense web of reliable partners to create more opportunities... and reducing our relative reliance on the United States,” Carney said.
Brazil’s newly re-elected President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, while not an Apec member, sounded a similar note at the Asean gathering in Manila on Sunday.
“Brazil has learned an extraordinary lesson after the US decided to impose tariffs (on other countries),” Lula told reporters.

“Instead of weeping or begging the US government... to have pity on us, we decided to look for other partners for us to sell and for us to buy from,” he said, noting that trade with Indonesia and Vietnam had jumped 15 and 13 per cent, respectively.

The Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) – a free-trade agreement encompassing China, Southeast Asian nations, and other regional partners such as Japan, Australia, and South Korea – has meanwhile set long-term targets for tariff reductions.
However, the agreement’s provisions “suffer from weaker enforcement and dispute settlement mechanisms,” said Nick Marro, principal Asia economist at the Economist Intelligence Unit.

“While the drive to expand and deepen RCEP will stay, the pact will offer middle powers relatively limited shelter in an increasingly fractious geopolitical landscape-especially amid rising US protectionism and the continued global spillover of China’s economic imbalances,” he told AFP. — AFP

043ac0798512173b: Finance ministers from countries around the world meet at COP31 to discuss the costs of energy and climate change. UN Climate Change/Kiara WorthThe 2026 United Nations climate talks are all about real-world impact. That’s evident as I listen to government officials and others from around the world at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. World leaders are seeing their countries suffer from intensifying storms and heat fueled by climate change and from one of the worst global energy crises in history. A U.N. report found that global warming will overshoot 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit), the level countries agreed a decade ago to try to avoid because of the growing risk of dangerous climate change. The Middle East conflict has intensified oil and gas price and supply volatility, pushing economies to the brink as energy and food prices spike and energy security falters. Countries that rely on imported fossil fuels for their energy sources have borne the brunt of the energy crisis. Those doubling down on renewable energy are weathering the crisis better. A worker carries solar panel plates at a market in Lahore on June 12, 2026. Pakistan has seen fast growth in rooftop solar, driven by consumer demand and a government that didn’t impose taxes on cheap Chinese panels when others did. Arif Ali/AFP via Getty Images In Pakistan, for example, the rapid expansion of solar power over the past six years helped the country avoid more than US$12 billion in fossil fuel imports before the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran began in February 2026. One forecast suggests solar could save the country more than $6 billion more by the end of the year. Spain, which relies less on natural gas and more on solar energy for electricity than most European countries, kept electricity prices lower and avoided the worst of the gas-driven spikes seen in more exposed systems such as Italy’s. In formal negotiations and in meetings around the U.N.’s broader Global Climate Action Agenda, countries are working on ways to accelerate the use of clean energy and to provide poorer countries with the resources to adapt to climate change and expand clean energy. I have been following international climate negotiations for years as a former special climate envoy for Germany and senior fellow at the Fletcher School at Tufts University. In 2026, after two years of the Trump administration’s pressure to get countries to abandon efforts to slow climate change, I’m seeing rising concern among leaders about the costs of fossil fuels on economies and people’s lives. The electrification solution A step in transitioning away from fossil fuels is shifting to electrification powered by clean energy. The co-presidents of COP31, from Turkey and Australia, have proposed a global target of 35% of all energy use coming from electricity by 2035 – including for transportation and industry – and they are working to persuade other countries to sign on. Hitting that 35% mark could save fossil-fuel-importing countries $400 billion a year, according to the International Energy Agency. In consumer terms, $100 spent on electricity powers a car up to three times farther than $100 of gasoline, based on global averages. Reaching the goal could slash energy emissions across transportation, buildings and industry by up to 55% by 2035. However, the source of electrification matters. Forecasts from the International Renewable Energy Agency show that at least 78% of the electricity powering the world must come from renewable energy sources to keep global warming under the 1.5 C limit. Electrification delivers for both the climate and energy security if it runs on clean power instead of energy from oil, gas and coal. A map of each country’s largest electricity source shows how many still rely heavily on fossil fuels. Our World In Data Getting the world to that point will require addressing some key barriers: the cost of infrastructure needed to deliver clean energy and the need for policies to encourage the changes. Beyond the formal negotiations, countries are discussing multiple initiatives to provide technical support to one another, as countries develop power grids that can manage the variability of solar and wind power, and financial help to countries that need it. Voters show their frustration with fossil fuels The high financial and environmental costs of fossil fuels have been reshaping global politics. Voters came out in big numbers over the past few months to elect leaders who support clean, affordable energy solutions. The world saw this notably with the reelection of Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and the biggest Democratic congressional victory in the United States in over three decades. Lula, in his first international trip after winning his fourth term, called on the COP31 presidents to carry forward Brazil’s work as host of COP30 on a transition away from fossil fuels. He announced that Brazil will host a future conference on the fossil fuel transition, following the first in Colombia in April 2026 and a second planned in 2027 in the island nation of Tuvalu. Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, whose country hosted the COP30 climate talks in 2025, was celebrated as a leader at the COP31 U.N. climate talks in 2026. UN Climate Change/Kiara Worth Brazil has clearly emerged as a climate superpower in Antalya. With its greatest one-year reduction in deforestation and its leadership in producing three plans, known as road maps, to help the world transition away from fossil fuels, end deforestation and provide the $1.3 trillion in financing needed for developing countries, Brazil has demonstrated it understands the urgency of the climate crisis. We will see whether the co-presidents of COP31 will answer the calls from Lula and U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres to support these road maps becoming formal guidance for all countries. The Americans at COP31 California Gov. Gavin Newsom and a delegation of 18 members of the U.S. House of Representatives also came to COP31 to signal the presence of American leadership on future climate policy. President Donald Trump has pulled the U.S. out of the U.N. Framework Convention on Climate Change, the Paris Agreement and dozens of other international organizations and treaties. The U.S. did not send a formal delegation to the climate talks. California Gov. Gavin Newsom speaks at an event with a coalition of U.S. political leaders. Created in 2021, the ‘America Is All In’ coalition today reflects more ambition than reality. Sean Gallup/Getty Images As former U.S. climate envoy John Kerry said in Antalya, “Americans did vote for clean, affordable energy, and they also voted for clean governance.” The international community will be watching to see whether the newly elected Democratic majority in Congress can help safeguard U.S. climate science after the Trump administration’s extensive funding cuts, and whether it will restore critical funding to international efforts dealing with climate change. What success looks like At COP31, the shift in the real-world politics of energy has dominated several events and the formal negotiations. But the countries that are likely to lose from such a transition are also working diligently to slow this transition. On the opening day, a coalition of oil-producing countries led by Saudi Arabia announced it opposed any mention of Brazil’s road map away from fossil fuels in the official COP31 agreement. For COP31 to be a success, the diplomatic process must demonstrate that it can catch up to the real economy and meet this moment of energy and climate crisis. I believe the summit’s final agreement should accelerate the electrification of infrastructure around the world and, at the same time, drive the transition away from fossil fuels in order to protect global security, economic stability and everyday citizens. Jennifer Morgan does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

9ccf8665576aaeb3: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

On Friday, a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia began circulating on social media, and by Monday it listed some notable signatories, including Elon Musk and several influential Nvidia researchers. But comb through the more than 115,000 names and you’ll notice a significant faction of Huang’s supporters—higher-ups from Hugging Face, a hub for sharing AI models, and venture capital firms Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital—come from a particular slice of the tech world.

These names have a vested interest in the development of open-source AI, models that, unlike ChatGPT or Claude, can be downloaded and run independent of large tech companies. Supporters of such models say that concentrating AI in the hands of a few powerful companies will leave everyone else worse off (a concern that wouldn’t sound out of place among the AI industry’s critics on the left, if so many open-source advocates weren’t also venture capitalists who stand to profit when startups can build on cheaper AI without paying Big Tech).

Huang had become a sort of ringleader for those who defend open source to policymakers against concerns that such models come with no guardrails and cede AI leadership to China, where the most powerful and popular open-source models are created. They now want their most influential voice returned to his post.

But it’s not just Huang’s extramarital affairs that threaten his (and Nvidia’s) credibility as an advocate for open-source AI. New research into China’s startups using Nvidia’s chips, and a new rule from the US Department of Commerce announced Monday, could deal a blow to both the movement’s reputation and its technical progress.

On Thursday, the day Huang resigned, ex-OpenAI researcher Will DePue published findings online suggesting that China’s AI companies had far more access to Nvidia’s advanced Blackwell chips than previously estimated. China is banned from accessing Nvidia’s most cutting-edge chips to help protect America’s AI lead.

It’s unclear how they would have gained access to the chips. DePue claims the results were verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic, but an independent analysis has not confirmed the results. (DePue did not respond to a request for an interview. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.)
The findings do not establish that Nvidia helped Chinese companies obtain the chips, and the broader problem of chip smuggling was already known to extend well beyond Nvidia’s control.

But in suggesting that Nvidia may have profited from the rise of Chinese AI startups, whose models are increasingly being used by American companies instead of domestic alternatives, the findings do leave Huang in an awkward position. He has championed open-source AI as a way to strengthen American technological leadership. “Without open source, startups can’t thrive, university researchers can’t do research, you can’t teach AI, scientists can’t use AI,” he said last December during a talk about helping the US win the AI race against China.

It also makes the idea of reinstating Huang even more of a long shot. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent even said last week that Nvidia should not consider someone from inside the company to replace him. The new findings lower Huang’s chances further.

What happens next? Nvidia announced in September it would acquire Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion. Its support for open source also serves a straightforward financial interest: The more businesses that build their own models instead of forking over money to Anthropic and OpenAI, the more chips Nvidia can sell.

But a new rule from the US Department of Commerce could mean the models popular on Hugging Face will soon stop getting smarter. The rule aims to prevent Chinese companies from training models on Nvidia chips that they can’t own directly, but that they can access remotely in data centers in countries like Malaysia—a workaround that has helped China’s open-source models get so good.

The open-source world rallied around Huang because of his influence on policymakers. That was important, since the rise of China’s open-source models has splintered some in Trump’s orbit. If Huang is out, who is next?

b2955c38ff71d9a1: In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t. No rule had told the agents to do that, and no test had anticipated the behaviors.

For a century, we have built trust in technology on predictability: predefined inputs, predictable outputs, and layers of protection. Consider how a breaker trips at a set current or an aircraft component is tested against known (i.e., predictable) stresses.

AI changes that. Traditional software executes instructions written by humans, whereas AI exercises what might be called synthetic judgment. We use AI because it can interpret situations we did not program and generate responses we did not prescribe. But the more freedom we give AI, the harder it becomes to provide the predictability on which trust has traditionally been built.

We will not make AI trustworthy by predicting what it will do. We will do it by fencing it in with hard limits that are enforced outside its reach. In OpenAI’s case, the safeguards sat inside a system the agents could edit. But a fence the agents can simply move is not a fence.
Where traditional definitions of trust fall short

Recent MIT Technology Review coverage has approached this problem from other directions. One contributor argues that having a human in the loop is an insufficient solution because humans are fundamentally unable to understand AI systems’ intentions and advocates instead for interdisciplinary research and collaboration between academia, government, and the tech industry. And a story on reverse game theory describes using incentives to keep models from deviating from the rules, even when no one understands how they work on the inside.

Both articles acknowledge that we cannot understand or watch every AI decision. Our instruments of trust, including requirements, testing, certification, safety margins, interlocks, and pass/fail criteria, all depend on our ability to bound a system’s behavior. This is the determinism paradox.

With generative and agentic AI, behavior is shaped by training data, architecture, prompts, context, retrieval sources, and the environment. Inputs change, models are updated, tools change, and agents interact. Small variations propagate into outcomes nobody designed. The problem is not randomness; it is that the space of possible behavior is too large to enumerate in advance. Trust must therefore be engineered around boundaries rather than predicted outputs. The goal is not deterministic AI, but bounded, observable, and controllable AI. Trust also cannot be a one-time test. Traditional assurance certifies a product at a point in time, but AI keeps evolving after deployment, and a system that has passed every test can drift outside the conditions that made those tests meaningful. Trust must be continuously earned.

Safety engineering has been accounting for some of this variability for decades. For example, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission determine the likelihood of failures in complex systems, and Systems-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes (STAMP) showed that accidents can emerge from interactions among working components, people, and organizations. But AI raises the stakes, because just a single component can now interpret, infer, and act. The stakes rise further as AI moves from browsers into vehicles, robots, medical systems, industrial controls, and data centers, where a wrong answer can become a life-threatening event.
Building trust that scales

It’s clear that a person rubber-stamping thousands of AI actions an hour is not an acceptable—or scalable—safeguard against risk. But the remedy is not to remove people from the loop; it is to put human judgment where it counts: setting limits in advance and approving the rare actions that have serious consequences while hard constraints handle the rest.

Therefore, trust has to move upstream into architecture. The central questions become: What authority are we willing to give AI, under what conditions, and supported by what evidence? And what happens outside those conditions? That is very different from asking whether a model scored 94% on a benchmark.

The determinism paradox does not mean AI cannot be trusted. It means trust needs a different architecture. Instead of making every output predictable, make the boundaries predictable. An AI medical assistant may be probabilistic in its diagnosis, but deterministic rules govern whether it can change a prescription. An industrial AI may find many ways to optimize a process, while fixed limits keep it within pressure and temperature bounds. An agent may decide how to complete a task, while permissions, transaction limits, and human approvals determine what it is authorized to do.
Let AI be probabilistic inside the box and make the box itself deterministic wherever consequences matter. Leaders can put this into practice by asking five questions:
What authority does AI have? Define not only what it can do but what it is allowed to do, separating interpretation, recommendation, decision, and execution.
Is the function of AI proportional to the consequence? A marketing copilot and AI controlling industrial equipment need different assurance thresholds.

Are we taking the appropriate steps toward autonomy? For example, there needs to be a plan to move from having AI interpret while humans decide, to AI making recommendations, to then taking action with approval, and ultimately to having supervised autonomy, but only as AI can safely work at each step.
Are we testing the system or merely the model? Unexpected interactions emerge among models, data, agents, APIs, and human workflows.
Are we continuously earning trust? Monitor drift, failures, near-misses, and model changes throughout the lifecycle.

The winners in AI will be those who solve the determinism paradox—giving AI enough freedom to create value while engineering boundaries strong enough to make what it does with that freedom trustworthy. Invention earns attention. Trust earns adoption.

9af9c51a7fd2f67a: From Abd Rahim Romle and Ainur Rabiyatul Abd Rahim

A Malaysian applying for a licence, renewing a permit, or seeking government assistance should not have to navigate several websites, remember multiple passwords, or repeatedly submit the same information. Yet for some, accessing public services can still feel more complicated than it should.
We have become good at introducing digital platforms. The more important question is whether these platforms are making life easier for the rakyat.

Malaysia's digital transformation has brought improvements to public administration. Online apps, electronic payments, and digital records have reduced the need for physical visits and made many services more convenient.
These achievements deserve recognition. However, digital progress should not be measured simply by the number of apps launched or systems developed.
A government service is only successful when people can use it easily, reliably, and without unnecessary frustration.

Consider a small business owner applying for an operating licence. The application may be available online, but if the process still requires repeated document submissions, unclear approvals, or visits to different departments, digitalisation has merely changed the location of the bureaucracy.
The same applies to a parent seeking educational assistance, or an elderly person accessing healthcare services.
For these Malaysians, convenience matters more than the technology behind the system.

The 13th Malaysia Plan (2026-2030) places digital transformation and public service efficiency among Malaysia's development priorities. The challenge is ensuring that these ambitions translate into improvements that citizens can experience.

One persistent concern is fragmentation. Different agencies may operate separate systems with different registration requirements, procedures and user interfaces. While each platform may serve an administrative purpose, the combined experience can become confusing.
Citizens should not have to understand the organisational structure of government simply to obtain a service.

A more effective approach would focus on integrating services around people's needs. For example, starting a small business involves several administrative requirements. Instead of expecting entrepreneurs to navigate multiple agencies independently, government systems should provide clearer guidance and better coordination.
Similarly, families applying for assistance should not repeatedly provide information already held by public institutions, subject to appropriate privacy safeguards.

Another challenge is digital inclusion. Not every Malaysian has reliable internet access, the latest smartphone, or sufficient digital literacy to navigate complicated applications. Older citizens, rural communities, and people with disabilities may face additional difficulties.
Digital transformation should, therefore, preserve accessible alternatives while improving online services.

Three priorities deserve attention. First, government agencies should evaluate digital platforms through citizen experience rather than technological output. Processing times, successful applications, accessibility, and complaint resolution should become central performance indicators.

Second, greater emphasis should be placed on interoperability and administrative simplification. Agencies must improve information-sharing and eliminate unnecessary procedures before transferring them online.

Third, public servants should receive continuous training to provide responsive assistance across both digital and physical service channels. Technology cannot compensate for unclear procedures, weak coordination, or poor communication.

Importantly, public feedback must play a stronger role in evaluating service quality. When citizens report difficulties, their experiences should inform system improvements rather than disappear into administrative complaint channels.

Malaysia does not necessarily need another app whenever a service problem emerges. Sometimes, improving an existing platform, simplifying a form, or ensuring that someone answers a telephone call would make a greater difference. The objective should never be digitalisation for its own sake.

Malaysia's ambition to become a competitive digital economy depends partly on building public institutions that are efficient, trustworthy and responsive. A well-designed digital government should save citizens time, reduce costs, and make essential services easier to access.

The rakyat do not judge government efficiency by how many digital platforms exist. They judge it by whether applications are processed promptly, information is clear, and problems are resolved without unnecessary obstacles.
Malaysia's next public sector breakthrough may not require another digital platform. It may simply require making the services we already have work better for everyone.

Abd Rahim Romle is an associate professor and deputy dean at the Ghazali Shafie Graduate School of Government at Universiti Utara Malaysia. Ainur Rabiyatul Abd Rahim is a Master of Teaching English as a Second Language candidate at Universiti Putra Malaysia.

<!--kg-card-end: html--> When writer and musician Samantha Shokin noticed her cover of a public domain Bulgarian folk song had been copyright struck on YouTube, she assumed it would be easy to fix. It wasn’t. And trying to figure out what happened led her to discover an AI content mill that is running 500 slop-filled channels and abusing YouTube’s automated copyright detectors.
“Any human would agree with me that there’s something clearly wrong here that needs to be fixed, but I can’t get in touch with a human being,” Shokin said.
Shokin’s journey is a modern nightmare that highlights the ways AI can be weaponized against human creators, and the ways people fall through the cracks of big tech’s automated systems.

During the pandemic, Shokin recorded a 50 second version of the Bulgarian folk song ‘Bre Petrunko’ and uploaded it to SoundCloud, where it didn’t get much traction. Two years later, she uploaded it to YouTube and watched as her cover grew in popularity, gaining 125,000 views in four years.

Last summer, she noticed an uptick in comments on the video. Unbeknownst to Shokin, her version of “Bre Petruinko” had become popular among DJs and electronic artists and had been sampled in dozens of songs. Someone in the comments pointed her towards one of the more popular tracks. “I look up this video and it’s something that has millions of hits [...] and 30 seconds into this track I hear my own voice and I was utterly shocked. I didn’t know how to react,” she said (the video has more than 4 million views).

“The first thing that comes to mind is, ‘Oh my god, someone stole my voice and didn’t credit me,’” she said. Shokin said she talked to a lot of DJs and figured out how they’d gotten her voice. They’d purchased a pack of samples from a company called Loopmasters that was selling her version of “Bre Petruinko” as part of its “Folk Legends” set.

“I got in touch with the distributor and they were deeply apologetic. They were unaware that this had happened and they immediately tried to make right of the situation and granted me royalties on the sample pack,” Shokin said. “At that point, countless DJs and music producers had been using my voice for their own tracks, unbeknownst to me. At least I’m aware and at least I was making something off of it and I was satisfied with that. I didn’t love the way that it came about, but whatever, they tried to make right of the situation.”

But Shokin’s “Bre Petruinko” saga wasn’t over. Last month, she opened YouTube and noticed her original recording was gone. A company called Media Nov Records had issued a copyright strike against her song, and YouTube had taken it down.She thought it would be easy to get this reversed. It’s a public domain folk song and she had the original recordings and a history with a distributor. “If I just explain it to YouTube, they’ll understand,” she thought.

Media Nov Records advertises itself as a “distribution company” that that partners with artists to release their music on digital platforms. But a lot of its website focuses on rights management and copyright protection. “At Media Nov, we go above and beyond to safeguard your musical creations. Our comprehensive rights management system leverages cutting-edge technology and legal expertise to ensure you receive the royalties you deserve,” it said on its website.

YouTube uses automated systems to work through copyright claims. When someone files a claim against a video, the company tends to automatically approve it. The original uploader can file a “counterclaim,” where they argue that the video should stay up, or that it should not be demonetized.

Shokin filed two counterclaims, but neither worked. “It's unclear to us whether you have a valid reason for filing a counter notification, so we won't be able to honor your request,” YouTube said in its last denial. It told her to contact the copyright holder; in this case, it was a public domain song and so there was no actual “copyright holder,” just Media Nov, which was claiming to hold it.

“I tried emailing them,” she said. “I tried calling them. There doesn’t appear to be a working phone line. I got in touch with [Loopmaster, which was selling her recording]. They tried getting in touch. I’m being ignored by everybody, by YouTube, by this media company that, like, the website seems to be entirely AI-generated, and all I want is to talk to a human about this.”

Media Nov’s site boasted about its use of automated DMCA takedowns, YouTube content ID management, and AI-powered content recognition. “Our advanced AI identifies your music across platforms ensuring accurate tracking and protection,” it said. The company says it has been in existence since 1996, but Archive.org’s Wayback Machine doesn’t show much of a web presence until last year. Its website is basic and barebones.

The company has two addresses on its website. One is an apartment building in Los Angeles on Marina Del Rey. The other is the Black Church in Dublin, Ireland — a cathedral that’s been converted into an office space. The site listed a Los Angeles phone number that was busy every time 404 Media tried to call it.

According to corporate paperwork filed in Ireland and reviewed by 404 Media, Media Nov Records was founded a little more than a year ago. Its listed address is the Black Church in Ireland but both of its shareholders gave addresses in Turkey.

404 Media found four different YouTube pages managed by Media Nov Records. Each contained hundreds of videos — many with AI-generated art assets and music. The songs are sometimes cross posted between the different channels and are mostly looping electronic beats. Think low effort “lofi beats” knock offs. The art assets are footage of sports cars, anime girls, and AI-generated pictures of women. The songs are cross posted on multiple channels and often generate fewer than 100 views. Each also has few YouTube shorts that revolve around “random acts of kindness.” A Douyin (the Chinese version of TikTok) watermark is present in some of these videos.

For example, recent YouTube shorts on its flagship page include a basic beat playing over an AI-generated woman mopping the floor of a store while being berated by her AI-generated boss. Another features an AI-generated woman crying over a well, and a crew of men rescuing her child. One of its other pages looks like this:

Media Nov Records told 404 Media that it operates 500 of these channels and “works with various artists, content creators, and music partners.” The company did not initially return emails or phone calls from Shokin or Loopmaster, but responded to an email from 404 Media.

It said it would look into its copyright claim of Shokin’s track. “We remain willing to review the relevant ownership documentation, original audio files, and supporting evidence to investigate the copyright claim thoroughly. If an error is identified, we are committed to taking appropriate corrective action promptly,” it said.

After 404 Media requested comment, Media Nov Records responded to Shokin and asked her to provide “relevant documentation supporting her ownership of the recording, including original audio files, recording evidence, original publication dates, and any other supporting materials,” which is a wild request considering that it has nothing to do with her recording and does not own the copyright.

The company told 404 Media that Shokin and Loopmaster’s emails had gone to its spam folder. “Regarding ‘Bre Petrunko,’ we would like to clarify that the musical composition and arrangement rights associated with Philip Koutev’s work must be distinguished from the rights in any individual sound recording. Media Nov Records also holds certain rights relating to the relevant musical content,” the company told Shokin in an email reviewed by 404 Media.

“Bre Petrunko” is an old folk song with no known writer. It’s primarily sung and most performances of it do not use instruments. Philip Koutev is a Bulgarian composer who popularized a version of the song in 1963. He died in 1982 and the copyright for that particular version is held by the Smithsonian. There are also many other versions of the song on YouTube, some with millions of views.

“Recording your own cover or performance does not automatically establish ownership of the underlying composition or arrangement. Likewise, rights in the underlying musical work do not automatically establish ownership of your particular recording,” Media Nov said.

“It’s ironic that they’re in the copyright business,” Shokin said. “It’s not the arrangement that’s in question. It’s the voice and performance [...] they clearly have no clue what they’re talking about.”

It's unclear why Media Nov Records brought Koutev into the conversation. 404 Media asked which song or work in its catalog triggered the copyright notice against Shokin but Media Nov Records did not respond.

“That makes it really ridiculous,” Alfred Steiner, an artist and copyright lawyer, told 404 Media. “If it’s her voice and her playing instruments, what could she possibly be infringing if it’s a folk song from the 19th century?”

The situation between Shokin and Media Nov Records sounded odd to Steiner. “I've seen lots of providers where you say ‘I have the rights’ and basically say nothing more than that, and they put it back because they’re taking a risk now. They’re harming her. If they just put it back, they’re at no risk,” he said.

“It sounds, to me, like a small company — despite the fact that they represent or run 500 YouTube channels — that are understaffed and is using a lot of different tools, probably a lot of AI, to identify tracks that are ostensibly owned by its clients and then automatically filing takedown requests,” he said. “They’re probably taking down far more than they have the right to take down.”

Minutes after it sent Shokin an email asking for proof she’d recorded the song, Media Nov Records followed up in an email addressed to both 404 Media and Shokin. “Following our review, Media Nov Records has decided to retract the copyright removal request for Samantha Shokin’s video. We are taking this step because the video has not generated revenue or received views, and we do not consider maintaining the removal request necessary at this stage,” it said. “However, this decision does not constitute a waiver of any rights we may hold. We intend to initiate appropriate legal proceedings regarding the underlying copyright dispute.”
Around 24 hours later, Shokin’s original video was back up. A spokesperson for YouTube confirmed that it reinstated the video after the claimant withdrew their complaint.
“It sounds like they got scared and feel like this is not a battle worth fighting,” Shokin said after seeing the email from Media Nov Records.

“Submitting a takedown request for rights that you don’t have can subject you to liability which includes actual damages and costs and attorney’s fees,” Steiner told 404 Media. “Doing this on a slipshod, shotgun approach is inadvisable from my perspective. Of course, if all of the people you end up offending are small parties and don’t have the resources to respond through the court system, and you are a fly-by-night entity that is hard to pin down and nobody knows who you are [...] it can be difficult to get a remedy.”

Shokin said she felt vindicated but was unhappy that it took a journalist emailing Media Nov Records to get them to listen to her. “They got my emails and they got Loopmaster’s email and they were just ignoring it because they only decided to respond because they got scared that it’ll be bad press,” she said. “It’s just not great all around. The whole system is broken. It feels like a broken system.”
