12604af31481c12b: Butterball Turkey Talk-Line experts take part in cooking and carving classes in 2009. AP Photo/M. Spencer GreenOne of the most quintessential American things is having roasted turkey on the table at a Thanksgiving feast. While that remains the norm, Americans are eating much less of this kind of poultry today than in the past. Annual consumption has fallen by more than 25% over the past three decades, while demand for chicken has soared. I’m a business school professor who has written about the economics of various holidays. I find turkeys fascinating, because even though I live in an urban area, a large group of wild turkeys has taken over my backyard. And I can offer several good explanations for the turkey slump. Receding since the late 1990s Domesticated turkeys, unlike their wild cousins, are a big business. More than US$5 billion worth of the birds were sold in 2025. That’s no chicken feed. However, it’s the latest sign of the industry’s decline. U.S. consumers are drifting away from eating turkey. Back in 1995, the average American consumed 17.7 pounds (8 kilograms) of turkey each year. By 2025, consumption had fallen to just 13.2 pounds (6 kg). While turkey consumption started to recede in the late 1990s, it began accelerating around 2008, when the Great Recession was underway. Occasionally, turkey production ticks upward a little, as happened in 2026 as demand for niche products like turkey jerky rose, but the long-term picture is one of steady decline. It’s not like Americans are eating less poultry overall. Chicken consumption has steadily grown during this turkey slump, rising about 50% from 69 pounds (31 kg) in 1995 to 104 pounds (47 kg) in 2025. In other words, we’re eating almost eight times more chicken than turkey. Well, at least the 95% of Americans who aren’t vegetarian or vegan are. More costly at every step in the supply chain Government agencies, researchers and some pundits have identified two possible explanations for why Americans are eating less turkey. First: pocketbook concerns. Turkey often costs more than chicken, except when it goes on sale just before Thanksgiving. Over the past 25 years, wholesale turkey prices per pound averaged about 10% higher than chicken, according to U.S. Department of Agriculture data. That price, which is what big retailers typically pay, affects what you owe at checkout. For example, just before the 2026 Thanksgiving sales began, a Bell & Evans fresh whole turkey was going for $4.99 a pound, while a Bell & Evans fresh whole chicken cost $3.49 a pound at my local supermarket. That’s $1.50 a pound difference, which is significant in an economy where many people feel economically pinched. Nationally, you will see similar price differences, with fresh turkey being more expensive than fresh chicken. So, why is turkey pricier than chicken? Both turkeys and chickens are fed a diet of corn and soybeans. However, turkeys consume a higher percentage of soybeans. And soybeans currently cost about twice as much as corn. The latest data shows turkey feed costs are up almost 80%, without accounting for inflation, since 2000, while chicken feed costs have climbed only 60%. Too big for more families The second reason has to do with the size of today’s families. The typical Bell & Evans whole chicken my grocery store sells weighs approximately 4 pounds, while its fresh turkeys tend to range between 10 and 12 pounds. Big birds are handy if you have a lot of mouths to feed, but American families have shrunk over time. Today the average household includes only 2.5 people. The extra half-person does not represent children who are picky eaters or people who don’t like eating meat. It just means the typical family has between two and three people. That means cooking a 10-pound turkey results in 4 pounds of food per person, which is far more than almost anyone who is not a competitive food eater can consume. Cooking a 4-pound chicken, however, results in a more manageable 1.2 pounds of poultry per eater after getting rid of the bones, which make up about a quarter of a chicken. In simple terms, buying a whole chicken often results in one or two meals per person. Cooking a whole turkey often yields enough meat to produce meals for an entire week. Raymond Baker carves a turkey in 1948 while his wife and 16 kids surround him. Getty Images There are two more factors to consider. First, a 10-pound turkey costs a lot more than a 4-pound chicken. A 10-pound fresh bird at $4.99 a pound sets you back almost $50, while a $3.49-per-pound chicken that weighs 4 pounds costs under $14. Last, bigger birds take longer to roast. Cooking a 10-pound turkey in an oven takes about three hours, while a 4-pound chicken takes about two. That extra hour is a big burden in an increasingly time-pressed society. In case you were wondering, the world record for eating a turkey is held by Joey Chestnut. He gobbled down 9.35 pounds of turkey off the bone in 10 minutes in 2014. Please do not try that at home. What about wild turkeys? If you need to save money on turkey this holiday season, you should consider buying a frozen one. They are much cheaper. But can you save even more by going turkey hunting? Given all the large wild turkeys roosting in my backyard, I looked into what it would take. I live in Massachusetts, where hunting wild turkeys before Thanksgiving is legal. For much of the fall, hunters are allowed to use only bows and arrows. Beyond needing to be a proficient archer, they also have to purchase a sporting license, a turkey permit and an archery stamp for $95 each year. Having learned about that, I’m sticking to buying my turkeys in the supermarket. Jay L. You can stream and download our full conversation, including any podcast extras, on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube, and Bloomberg. All of our earlier podcasts on your favorite pod hosts can be found here.
Masters in Business: Salim Ramji, CEO of Vanguard Interview transcript · Bloomberg Radio
[00:00:02] Bloomberg Audio Studios, podcasts, radio, news.

[00:00:07] BARRY RITHOLTZ: This week on the podcast, yet another fascinating conversation. I sit down with Vanguard’s CEO, Salim Ramji. Previously he was at BlackRock, helping to oversee iShares and indexing. He’s got a fascinating background, and really is one of the people in the wealth management industry who is so uniquely situated to see all of these different things that are going on.

What a great perch to observe the future of wealth management. I thought this conversation was fascinating, and I think you will also. With no further ado, my conversation with Vanguard’s Salim Ramji. Salim, welcome to Bloomberg.
[00:00:58] SALIM RAMJI: Well, thanks, Barry. It’s great to be back. I think we did this about half a dozen years ago, right?
[00:01:02] BARRY RITHOLTZ: In the middle of peak COVID. It was a frightening time.
[00:01:07] SALIM RAMJI: It’s nice to be in a studio.
[00:01:09] BARRY RITHOLTZ: Yes. I want to talk about your career and what led you to Vanguard. But I have to start by asking about your academic background.
Bachelor’s in economics and politics from the University of Toronto, and then a master’s in law at Cambridge. And I’m assuming a master’s at Cambridge is like a JD here, is that right?
[00:01:19] SALIM RAMJI: Yeah, kind of.
[00:01:33] BARRY RITHOLTZ: Was the original career plan becoming an attorney?

[00:01:37] SALIM RAMJI: Neither of my parents finished high school. My dad used to run a grocery store that I worked in as a kid. And from my parents’ point of view, they just wanted me to go to college. I don’t think there was any great original plan other than I thought going to college would be a good thing. I was drawn to the law, and ultimately my first job was at a law firm in London, in part because there were so many exciting and interesting things happening in the world of law and business in the early nineties in Europe at the time.

And so that, for me, was a compelling piece. But I wasn’t one of these kids who, from the age of 10, wanted to be a lawyer. It was more—it felt like a really interesting time, with markets liberalizing and lots of new markets opening up all over the world.

[00:02:41] BARRY RITHOLTZ: I’m curious how your upbringing affected how you look at money. You mentioned you worked in your dad’s grocery store; both your parents were immigrants working and living in British Columbia. How did that affect your relationship with money and work?

[00:02:56] SALIM RAMJI: It probably—some of these things you don’t really truly understand until years later. But we didn’t always have a lot of financial security growing up. And I’m at a company that cares very deeply about people’s financial security, and you can sometimes abstract that away in terms of what it means.

But at least for me, I know what having it is, and I know what the absence of it is. Obviously, having some financial security is far better. And I think it really drove home for me the real importance, at a very personal level, of what financial security means in somebody’s life or somebody’s family, and the importance of it to so many other things: the general happiness of the house, the levels of stress in the house, the freedom to be able to do things once you’ve attained it. And so financial security is something that I know deeply, because I know its absence too.
And so I think it makes it meaningful for me. Even if you asked the 20-year-old version of me, I wouldn’t have thought of it in that way.

[00:04:12] BARRY RITHOLTZ: I think a lot of people don’t realize the first checkbox—lack of financial stress—is a huge weight off people’s minds. So if you could solve for that, everything after that feels like gravy.
[00:04:23] SALIM RAMJI: Yeah. No, I absolutely agree.
[00:04:26] BARRY RITHOLTZ: So you’re working in London at Clifford Chance, and you also spent some time in Hong Kong? Was that doing legal work, or was that—
[00:04:33] SALIM RAMJI: I did. It was doing legal work.
[00:04:34] BARRY RITHOLTZ: And then how do you transition from that to McKinsey? What led to that?

[00:04:39] SALIM RAMJI: I enjoyed the business part of being a lawyer. I’d worked in financial markets, in M&A, and I was always interested in what happened after the deal closed, in the business aspects. And McKinsey offered me the chance to still be in a professional services firm, which I liked, still serve clients, which I liked, but also to get a little deeper on the business of things. And I had a wonderful career there for a dozen or so years, really learning about financial institutions and advising a whole range of financial institutions in New York and beyond.

[00:05:23] BARRY RITHOLTZ: So I’m fascinated, ’cause attorneys and consultants advise people running businesses, and then you made the transition to actually running a business at BlackRock. And when you were at McKinsey, you were running their asset and wealth management practice, so it wasn’t a radical jump to go to BlackRock, but how different is it offering advice versus actually, where the rubber meets the road, actually running the shop?

[00:05:50] SALIM RAMJI: It’s really different. And I’d worked with them as a client for a number of years before joining them. It’s a very different aspect when you’re owning the outcomes, when you’re having to lead broader groups of people.

And when you’re having to sweat every single detail, every single moment of every single day. And it was a great learning experience for me, ’cause I joined them in my early forties, and it’s a chance to really learn a whole new set of skills. Even though you know the industry, and you think you know a thing or two about the firm, you really don’t until you’re deep into it.
And for me it was a great source of renewal, revitalization, a whole series of things that, even to this day, I’m very grateful for.

[00:06:47] BARRY RITHOLTZ: And I think—if my research is correct—you started in 2014 at BlackRock as head of corporate strategy, which is probably the most advice-oriented position within BlackRock. You’re advising the board, you’re advising management: hey, this is our strategic outlook, here’s how we should proceed.

From there you end up running US Wealth Advisory and eventually taking over iShares and index investing in 2019, which I want to say was about $3 trillion, more or less. I don’t know if it started there or finished there, but about that. That’s some real money. Now you’re actually running a business, as opposed to offering advice, at BlackRock. Tell us what it was like taking over such a massive part of the firm.
[00:07:40] SALIM RAMJI: You’re talking about—
[00:07:42] BARRY RITHOLTZ: iShares. iShares and index investing.

Now, as AI agents begin to move into the workflows that run the business, that model is starting to look inadequate. Organizations moving from isolated pilots toward AI agents and autonomous workflows are confronting a deeper challenge: rethinking how data, business processes, governance, and people fit together, turning AI from a collection of tools into part of the enterprise operating model.

For Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, that shift begins with treating AI as an enterprise platform rather than a collection of disconnected projects. “AI is absolutely dependent on the data foundation,” he says, arguing that companies need a connected, semantically rich layer that reflects their business before they can reliably deploy AI across processes. The stakes also change as AI moves into mission-critical workflows. For some everyday applications, “80% might be good enough,” he says, but in areas such as supply chains or financial close, that level of accuracy is “a very terrible result.”

That foundation also determines which AI applications are worth pursuing. Satinder Pal Singh, associate VP North America for SAP BAIP and SAP AI Strategy at Infosys, frames AI agents as “digital coworkers” and recommends evaluating potential use cases through three lenses: impact, feasibility, and scalability. Companies should identify where an agent can move meaningful business metrics, determine whether their data and talent can support the use case, and then establish whether successful applications can be replicated. “A pilot that can’t scale is just an experiment,” he says.

Scaling also brings governance into sharper focus. Clear policies, access controls, monitoring, and oversight are necessary to ensure agents remain trustworthy and aligned with business requirements. “The absence of governance doesn’t speed up AI adoption,” Singh says. “It creates a risk backlog” that can ultimately force a more disruptive stop and audit.

Those considerations will become more important as AI agents take on more responsibilities as digital coworkers. Both executives see a future in which agentic systems coordinate work across applications, while customer-specific knowledge graphs and governed data become critical enterprise assets. For Singh, the longer-term opportunity is a shift from AI as a productivity tool to “AI as a decision-making partner,” helping leaders understand what is happening, anticipate what comes next, and determine how to respond.

Megan Tatum: From MIT Technology Review, I’m Megan Tatum, and this is Business Lab, the show that helps business leaders make sense of new technologies coming out of the lab and into the marketplace.

Now, the development and democratization of AI tools has the potential to reconfigure how enterprises operate. It requires a complete reconfiguration of what’s inside and how it’s used.
Two words for you: conscious configuration.
My guests today are Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, and Satinder Pal Singh, Associate VP for North America, SAP Business AI Platform and SAP AI Strategy.

Thorsten: Yeah. Megan, as you mentioned, AI is on the agenda of every client conversation today, but many customers are really struggling how to convert that interest into an operationalized model and to unlock the value of AI across the enterprise. And the reason is that too many programs start as isolated POCs on different AI technologies and in an inconsistent fragmented data foundation.

For example, BCG has launched a report, which shows that 74% of the organizations are stuck in pilot mode with no plan to scale. The path forward is really to treat AI not just as a project, but more holistically, as an enterprise platform, one that really consistently connects an unified data layer with the process context of the applications, and then embed AI capabilities governed across the entire life cycle. Megan: Yeah, really, to provide that support. And, Satinder, would you agree, why is it that we’re seeing enterprises get a touch of almost AI paralysis here? What’s the mindset shift that needs to happen and, perhaps, why is this something organizations need to be thinking about now, as well?

Very critical in an enterprise context. You need to set clear policies, access controls. You need to have monitoring ability, capabilities, to really make sure that what then the AI agenda capabilities or agents are executing is fully aligned, is trustworthy, and scalable.

Megan: Right. Which is quite a lot of things for organizations to be thinking about. Satinder, how do SAP and Infosys work with organizations to streamline some of these processes, perhaps and make unlocking AI’s capability a little bit easier?

Satinder: Megan, I think at the onset, I want to acknowledge that, at Infosys, we are uniquely positioned for our relationship with SAP, because we are a customer to SAP, as well as one of their key global suppliers. And the way SAP and Infosys work together is designed around the architecture Thorsten described, that defines a coherent partnership.

SAP brings the platform foundation, business data cloud for the semantically-rich enterprise, generative AI hub for governed LLMXs, and agent hub for the lifecycle governance, enterprise grade from day one. Infosys brings implementation depth, industry context, and use case accelerators. Through Infosys Topaz, we have built over 50 pre-configured AI use cases on Business AI Platform, production-ready configurations deployable without building from scratch. We co-develop use cases within SAP’s industry AI engagement with clear customer-specific FTE metrics. That shared accountability for results is different from a typical implementation engagement.

What I would emphasize is change management damage. Technology is increasingly deployable, and Thorsten also spoke about it earlier. What’s hard is helping an organization internalize that their agents are digital coworkers, not automations. That mindset shift is 70% of the implementation challenge that platform cannot solve alone, and Infosys and SAP run joint adoption programs addressing both the dimensions in parallel.

Megan: Fantastic. Some great real-world examples there, as well. Thorsten, can you tell us a little bit more about SAP’s Business AI Platform, or BAIP, in particular? How does that work and what sets it apart from other platforms?

Thorsten: Yeah, so SAP Business AI Platform, if you will, is the foundation for our SAP autonomous enterprise framework, which really consists of a unified user interface and is enabled as an agentic orchestration layer, which we call Joule. And you have the autonomous read with all the applications, and then you have the Business AI Platform, which powers the other capabilities, and is closely connected, and is basically organized around three core pillars.

The first one is, really, what we call build. What it means is you provide the respective intent-based development tools, so that customer, or partners like Infosys, can really create and development agents, applications and workflows using best-in-class tools and model to extend SAP’s own assistant, or customizing those, or really building own agents as needed.

Complimenting what Satinder said, it’s really critical for us that we have a thriving ecosystem, who is innovative, and is building innovations, and is complementing our own SAP agentic portfolio. We are focusing on specific areas on the domains, from a line of business industry perspective, where we deliver assistance as part of our organization, but to really then customize them from a last mile execution from really complimenting areas which we don’t cover and really driving the innovation towards the customer, our ecosystem is the multiplier force and Infosys is really playing a leading role here with us, together.

Second is, and we talked about this, is what we call the contextualize and reason pillar, which is literally as a foundation data, we address with SAP Data Cloud and comprehensive data strategy, where we establish an end-to-end data fabric across partner provider platforms, like Databricks, Snowflakes, where we promote and zero copy access to data. For the customer, this is very important. So, we allow, basically, promote to customers if you have made investments in any of those platforms, reserve those investments and just leverage BDC to connect without moving data around your, for example, Databricks, Snowflake environment to BDC.

3411c497853951d7: From Ahmad Zaharuddin Sani Ahmad Sabri
There is something more dangerous in politics than losing an election: winning one without understanding why.
The Melaka state election should be a wake-up call for both Pakatan Harapan (PH) and the Barisan Nasional-Perikatan Nasional (BN-PN) alliance.
BN-PN may celebrate its overwhelming victory, while PH may console itself with retaining a loyal support base. But beneath the celebrations and disappointments lies an uncomfortable reality.

PH has yet to demonstrate that it can significantly expand its appeal among Malay voters. BN-PN, meanwhile, has yet to prove that Malay political consolidation can translate into broader national acceptance.
Let the numbers speak.
In 2021, PH secured 114,457 votes, representing nearly 35.8% of the popular vote. In 2026, its tally increased to 143,273, but its vote share declined to 29.3%.
PH gained almost 29,000 votes, yet lost 6.5 percentage points of electoral support.
That is not an insignificant distinction.
PH is not necessarily losing its existing voters. It is losing the race to win over new ones.
More embarrassingly, all four seats won by PH went to DAP. PKR and Amanah failed to secure even a single constituency.

This raises an uncomfortable question: how can a coalition led by a Malay prime minister, supported by Malay ministers and commanding federal power, struggle so badly to translate that leadership into electoral success in Malay-majority constituencies?
PKR must ask whether its reformist identity still inspires confidence beyond its traditional supporters.
Amanah must explain why its supposedly progressive Islamic alternative has struggled to establish meaningful electoral traction.
A political party cannot survive indefinitely by reminding voters of what it once fought for. Eventually, voters want to know what it has delivered.
Reformasi cannot remain a historical slogan. It must become a measurable improvement in people's lives.
DAP should not celebrate too comfortably either.
Preliminary turnout estimates suggest that nearly 78% of Malay voters participated, compared with 59% of Chinese voters and 58% of Indian voters.
Although Chinese support for PH among those who voted appears relatively resilient, the weaker participation should worry DAP.
Chinese voters are not PH's permanent electoral fixed deposit.
They have expectations concerning education, economic opportunities, institutional reform and fair governance.
Fear of PAS may motivate some voters. But fear is not a substitute for trust, and disappointment can be expressed through silence at the ballot box.
Now consider BN-PN.
In 2021, BN and PN collectively received 200,472 votes while contesting separately. In 2026, their combined tally reached 308,668.
That represents an impressive 54% increase in absolute votes.
However, their combined popular vote share moved only marginally, from nearly 62.7% to 63.1%.
The alliance achieved a landslide in seats without achieving a comparable breakthrough in its combined share of the electorate.
This is not to diminish its victory. It is to distinguish electoral consolidation from a genuine expansion of political appeal.
And here lies BN-PN's greatest contradiction.

If its political identity increasingly revolves around Malay nationalism and religious conservatism, how does it intend to persuade Chinese, Indian, Sabah and Sarawak voters that their interests will be equally protected?
MCA and MIC may have won constituencies, but isolated victories do not automatically demonstrate a nationwide recovery of non-Malay confidence.
If Umno's ambition is merely to become more Malay than PAS, what exactly is MCA's future role? A political partner or a decorative guest at victory celebrations?
Defending Malay interests should never require making other communities feel politically expendable.
Malaysia's future cannot be secured by making one community believe that another community's progress represents its own defeat.
So what should PH do?
First, abandon the assumption that government performance automatically produces electoral loyalty.
I would propose an independent, constituency-level voter confidence audit, particularly among rural Malays, younger voters and the lower-middle-income population.
Ask those who rejected PH one simple question: what would convince you to reconsider?
Then publish measurable commitments on wages, housing, employment and living costs, with progress assessed every six months.

Second, PH must rebuild its political language. Ordinary Malaysians do not wake up thinking about coalition arithmetic. They wake up worrying about groceries, school expenses, wages and their children's future.
Third, stop treating criticism as hostility. Sometimes the harshest critics are identifying problems that loyal supporters refuse to acknowledge.
BN-PN should undertake an equally uncomfortable exercise: test its policies and political messaging among voters who do not share its ethnic or religious identity.

If the alliance cannot convince a substantial number of non-Malays that they have a secure future under its leadership, it risks becoming a powerful regional force with a national credibility problem.
The elections in Johor, Negeri Sembilan and Melaka offer valuable lessons, but they are not a reliable national forecast.
Umno should remember what happened after its victories in Melaka in 2021 and Johor in 2022.
Confidence turned into pressure for an early general election. Yet GE15 delivered BN its worst parliamentary performance up to that point.
Winning several states does not mean the keys to Putrajaya are already in your pocket.
Malaysia's electoral landscape is shaped by different demographics, local personalities, regional identities and economic expectations.
There is another reality politicians rarely admit openly: patronage, financial assistance and personal obligations remain influential in electoral politics.
Malaysians understand the saying, "orang berbudi kita berbahasa" ... kindness deserves appreciation.
But gratitude should never become political indebtedness.
A RM100 handout may ease household expenses today. A poor government can impose economic costs on an entire generation.

Ultimately, PH must learn to attract new voters rather than merely retain old supporters. BN-PN must learn to build confidence across communities rather than simply consolidate Malay political strength.
Neither side can claim to have solved Malaysia's political future.
An election determines who governs for five years. But the consequences of choosing the wrong leaders may be inherited for five generations.
Perhaps that is the greatest tragedy of Malaysian politics — our politicians are obsessed with counting the seats needed to capture power.
The people should be counting the price their children may eventually pay for it.
Ahmad Zaharuddin Sani Ahmad Sabri is an analyst with Global Asia Consulting.

a7623fa46c90cf7a: Officials claim the measure ‘protects society,’ but civil society organizations see a threat to freedom of expression
Originally published on Global Voices
Post-election protests in Maputo, Mozambique, in 2025. Photo by Wilson Thole. Used with permission.

Civil society organizations in Mozambique, such as the Center for Democracy and Human Rights (CDD), submitted a document to the Ombudsman contesting the constitutionality of Decree No. 48/2025, issued in December 2025, which establishes control mechanisms and potential blocks on access to telecommunications networks in the country.<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->

According to the portal Moz24h, journalists and experts are concerned that the measure could threaten rights such as freedom of expression, access to information, and communication, particularly in contexts of social mobilization or political tension. The challenge arises in an environment still heated from the conflicts following the 2024 elections.

Activists and civil society actors argue that the decree could enable restrictions on access to the internet and digital platforms — tools that have become increasingly central to the circulation of information, the organization of protests, and civic participation. The approved text allows the state to suspend telecommunications services for up to 48 hours without needing a court order, reports Deutsche Welle.

Also, according to civil society organizations, the decree grants broad powers to authorities to intervene in telecommunications networks on grounds of national security or the maintenance of public order.<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->

By appealing to the Ombudsman, the organizations are requesting an analysis of whether the decree is compatible with the Constitution of the Republic of Mozambique, as well as Mozambique’s international commitments regarding human rights and freedom of expression.

In March 2026, the Minister of Communications and Digital Transformation, Américo Muchanga, denied that the measure restricted rights. He defended it as a way to protect society in critical moments, strengthening the state’s capacity to manage crises and protect critical telecommunications infrastructure.
Experts diverge in their reading
In discussions with Global Voices, various experts presented different interpretations of its potential impacts.

One researcher, who asked not to be identified for security reasons, recalls that several democracies around the world have legal mechanisms allowing temporary restrictions on communications. For the researcher, political contexts where social demonstrations are frequently interpreted as threats to stability can make the application of this type of legislation particularly sensitive. He notes:

O que foi feito neste decreto é tentativa de legalizar toda e qualquer ação que o governo possa ter em uma situação de protesto social. Na França existe, no Brasil existe, nos Estados Unidos existem. Em qualquer parte em que exista alguma democracia, que chamamos a dita democracia consolidada, existem dispositivos estatais, governamentais, que limitam o acesso às comunicações, quando se entende que eles violam o direito de outras pessoas ou imposições em causa do próprio Estado. Não é o decreto o problema. O problema é como pode ser aplicado. O nosso problema é que não há tolerância. Tudo aquilo que parece ser protesto é visto como tentativa de subversão, tentativa de colocar em causa a ordem. É um problema histórico de governança e questão central na interpretação também do próprio decreto.

What was done in this decree is an attempt to legalize any and all actions the government might take in a situation of social protest. It exists in France, it exists in Brazil, and it exists in the United States. Anywhere there is some form of democracy, what we call so-called consolidated democracies, there are state, governmental mechanisms that limit access to communications when it is understood that they violate the rights of other people or impose demands against the state itself. The decree is not the problem. The problem is how it can be applied. Our problem is that there is no tolerance. Everything that looks like a protest is seen as an attempt at subversion, an attempt to jeopardize order. It is a historical problem of governance and a central issue in the interpretation of the decree itself.

Meanwhile, activist and journalist Nadio Taimo emphasizes that the decree comes at a time when Mozambique’s digital civic spaces face growing pressure. According to him, internet access has become fundamental for the circulation of information and the exercise of freedom of expression. Taimo observes that many media outlets migrated to digital platforms because of the high costs of traditional printing, making the online environment an important space for news dissemination, public debate, and social mobilization. In this context, potential blocks on internet access could significantly limit access to information.

Já temos uma expansão, uma onda crescente de jornais eletrônicos. Já não imprimimos jornais, devido aos custos. Migramos para a era digital, logo, há aqui um bloqueio de acesso à informação, e até o próprio espaço de opinião, de promoção da liberdade de expressão, pode ser limitado. Os órgãos de comunicação social são todos, a maior parte deles, do governo, e controlados, e nos é fechado o espaço cívico, o espaço físico, nas ruas, quando nos proíbem de realizar marchas.

We already have an expansion: a growing wave of electronic newspapers. We no longer print newspapers due to costs. We migrated to the digital era; therefore, there is a block on access to information here, and even the very space for opinion, for promoting freedom of expression, can be limited. The media outlets are all — most of them — government-owned and controlled, and our civic space, the physical space in the streets, is closed to us when they prohibit us from holding marches.
The activist further adds that the decree could formalize practices that, according to civil society organizations, have already occurred during moments of political tension:
Este documento é apenas uma formalização de uma intenção política de bloqueio da internet, que já vinha sendo aplicada, só que não havia uma formalização legal.
This document is merely a formalization of a political intention to block the internet, which was already being applied, only without a legal framework.
Precedent cases: Protests and control

The debate over telecommunications control in Mozambique is also linked to previous episodes of social mobilization. In February 2008 and September 2010, mass protests in the cities of Maputo and Matola were triggered by the rising cost of living, particularly the prices of transport and essential goods. During those demonstrations, mobile phones and text messages were widely used to mobilize and coordinate actions. In response, the government at the time promoted stricter communications regulation measures, including mandatory SIM card registration for all users.

New protests broke out again in November 2012 as young people protested the fare hikes for urban semi-collective transport, locally known as chapa-100. Swift intervention by police forces in areas with the highest concentration of protesters prevented the demonstrations from spreading.

These episodes occurred during defining moments of social demand by Mozambican youth in the post-independence period (1975), reflecting frustrations over economic inequalities, unemployment, and the rising cost of living amid economic liberalization. In this scenario, urban culture also played an important role in expressing social discontent. Artists like the rapper Azagaia became influential voices among young people, with social critique songs widely broadcast during demonstrations and across digital platforms.
A regional trend of internet shutdowns

The debate in Mozambique is not an isolated situation. International digital monitoring organizations have documented numerous cases of internet shutdowns in African countries in recent years, often linked to electoral processes, popular protests, or internal conflicts. In Angola and Guinea-Bissau, for instance, blocking or restricting internet access has been utilized by governments during periods of political instability.<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->

Human rights organizations and digital freedom advocacy groups argue that shutdowns limit access to information, hinder the work of journalists, and restrict civic participation, while digital governance experts warn that such measures can have significant impacts not only on public debate, but also on the livelihoods of the civilian population.

Despite the ratification of the aforementioned decree in Mozambique, its practical application has not yet been documented, making it difficult to assess its potential effects in practice. Concurrently, the Constitutional Council has not yet ruled on civil society organizations’ position regarding the decree’s potential unconstitutionality, contributing to a landscape of legal and institutional uncertainty.

428730d65d2647f0: On November 14, Asia fired up its wind machines and pyrotechnics for the inaugural Eurovision Song Contest Asia, aka Eurovision Asia. Eleven countries competed – from Bangladesh and Bhutan to Vietnam and host country Thailand. Notably absent this first year were most of the continent’s most populous nations: China, India, Japan, Pakistan and Indonesia. The format was familiar: three-minute songs performed with no more than six people permitted on stage. But there was a distinct regional inflection in the staging, costuming and language choices. Regional flavour Many of the artists wove in elements of traditional sound and traditional dress, and artists expressed gratitude to the audience with the traditional Thai gesture wai (hands together). While the original Eurovision is hosted in a combination of English and French, Eurovision Asia was delivered in English only. But most artists performed either in their own language (36%) or a combination of that language with English (54%). Only South Korea’s song was performed entirely in English. By comparison, Eurovision 2026 featured 43% of songs entirely in English, 38% in languages other than English, and 19% multilingual. Musically, it was a diverse offering. The delicate lotus leaves of Vietnam’s Tóc Tiên and her back-up dancers broke into a high-energy opening number, Em Tiên. Malaysia’s Aina Abdul finished the show with a pitch-perfect power ballad, Bluest Sky. In between, audiences were treated to Cambodian and Bhutanese ballads, Bengali a capella, South Korean K-pop and, perhaps most surprisingly, Nepali rock. Girls to the front But it was the Philippines’ Carmelle – the youngest contestant, at 19 – who won the night with Sobra-Sobra. The focus of the empowering pop song in English and Tagalog was about Filipino women’s right to be who they want to be. “It’s about how unapologetic, independent and strong Filipinas are. It describes me – not just me, but of course all the Filipinas,” Carmelle told The Guardian. Carmelle received 211 points, winning both the jury and the public vote, encompassing viewers from 183 countries and territories. With her victory, the Philippines has won the right to host Eurovision Asia in 2027. In the meantime, Carmelle will also perform at the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest in Bulgaria. Carmelle rehearsing Sobra-Sobra at the Eurovision Song Contest Asia. Eurovision Song Contest Asia Spectacle and snags Eurovision is known for its spectacle, and Eurovision Asia delivered, albeit on a more modest budget. Stage production made the most of stunning visual projections, smoke and flares. Eurovision is also known for its non-political stance, with political or ideological messages prohibited. But it has been more forgiving toward humanitarian statements. And at Eurovision Asia, Nepal’s Pratik Himal Rai used the end of his set to call for support for his country as it recovers from the August flood disaster. The show was not without its hitches. Laos’ representative, Thinla, couldn’t hear her music due to an issue with her earpiece, so footage of her technical rehearsal was shown at the end of the performances to ensure fair judgement of her act. Thai artists Mang x Daou experienced wardrobe malfunctions during their ballad Aroma, though this didn’t affect their chances in the voting – Thailand came in second place, with 169 points. Why not Asiavision? If Europe has Eurovision, why can’t Asia have Asiavision? For one, the name “Asiavision” is already taken: it’s the broadcasting network of the Asia-Pacific Broadcasting Union (ABU), which has its own song contests and festivals. But mostly, it’s about branding. Although the name Eurovision has become synonymous with the song contest, it actually refers to the European Broadcasting Union’s (EBU) pan-European telecommunications network. The Eurovision Song Contest was created in 1956 to promote the network and attract audiences across borders. (No, it was not created to unite a war-torn Europe.) The purpose of Eurovision Asia is specifically to expand the Eurovision brand and format into the region. This is a project the EBU has been attempting for more than two decades. It plans to continue the expansion of the brand through other continental editions. MANG x DAOU rehearsing for Thailand at Eurovision Song Contest Asia in Bangkok. Ralph Larmann/Eurovision The future of Eurovision Asia Staging the inaugural competition is one thing, but securing the longevity of the franchise in Asia is another matter. Buy-in from economic powerhouses Japan, China and India may be the key to its success. Negotiations were underway with China and Japan to participate this year, and organisers are optimistic that they and several others will join in 2027. The broad geographical scope of “Asia” also has the potential to draw in participants from the Middle East. But broader participation presents its own challenges. The original Eurovision is heavily associated with LGBTQIA+ acceptance and pride, which may not be well-received by certain broadcasters and their audiences within Asia. We saw this play out in the inaugural Eurovision Asia contest: Malaysian broadcaster TV3 cut drag performer Vice Ganda, the Phillipines’ jury spokesperson, from its broadcast. There was also speculation about whether Islamophobia played a role in Malaysia’s Aina Abdul’s results; despite being a favourite to win going into the contest, she finished in fourth place. Soft power and pop Like the OG Eurovision, Eurovision Asia offers great potential for soft power politics. It also has the potential to be a powerful global platform for Asian pop. The inaugural competition was a diverse showcase for the unique voices and cultures of its participants, beyond the dominant trends of J- and K-pop. Hopefully we will get a chance to see more in Manila next year. It is the first time the event is being hosted here, reflecting the growing recognition of Malaysia's considerable potential to have a more important role in the regional cruise tourism industry.

The event, Seatrade Cruise Asia 2026, brings together more than 18 international cruise line brands, including some of the biggest names such as Royal Caribbean International, StarDream Cruises, Norwegian Cruise Line, MSC Cruises, Azamara, Disney Cruise Line and Princess Cruises.

Senior executives and industry representatives from Europe, the US and Asia will participate in discussions on the future of cruising in this region, including new itineraries, emerging destinations, home-porting opportunities, port infrastructure and the growing demand for cruise holidays among Asian travellers.

Indeed, the event is being organised across several Malaysian destinations, with Kuala Lumpur hosting the main conference, followed by activities in Penang and Langkawi. This provides an opportunity to showcase not just our ports but also the country's wider tourism attractions.
Malaysia's opportunity

For many years, Singapore has established itself as the principal cruise home port in Southeast Asia. Its strategic location, international airport connectivity, modern cruise terminals and well-developed tourism infrastructure have made it a natural starting point for many international cruise operators.
From Singapore, cruise itineraries frequently extend along the Straits of Malacca, with calls at Melaka, Port Klang, Penang and Langkawi before continuing towards Phuket in Thailand.

Another attractive itinerary, depending on the season and weather conditions, covers the eastern side of the peninsula, with destinations such as Tioman, Redang and neighbouring destinations including Koh Samui in Thailand. Further itineraries can extend towards Cambodia and Vietnam, which includes Sihanoukville, Ho Chi Minh City and Da Nang.

All these routes offer considerable opportunities for Malaysia. We have the geographical advantage of being located along some of the busiest and most established maritime tourism corridors in Southeast Asia.
We also have a diverse range of destinations, from historical cities and cultural attractions to islands, beaches, rainforests and natural landscapes.

However, geographical location alone does not guarantee success. Cruise operators are commercial businesses. They look at passenger demand, port accessibility, terminal facilities, operating costs, immigration procedures, shore excursions and the overall attractiveness of destinations before deciding where to deploy their vessels.
Growing Asian market
The timing is particularly important because the Asian cruise market is developing rapidly.

According to figures released by the Singapore Tourism Board, Southeast Asia recorded approximately 3.9 million cruise passenger visits in 2024. Singapore accounted for 48% of these visits, while Malaysia captured approximately 22%.
Together, the two countries accounted for around 70% of the growing regional market. These figures also demonstrate that Malaysia is already an important cruise destination.

However, it has also been suggested that there is considerable room to grow, particularly if we can attract more international cruise operators and encourage more Malaysians to experience cruise holidays.

The potential domestic market should not be underestimated either. Malaysia has a sizeable middle-income population, an expanding travelling public and a growing number of families looking for alternative holiday experiences.

Cruise holidays could become increasingly attractive, particularly for families who prefer an all-inclusive holiday package with accommodation, meals, entertainment and multiple destinations incorporated into one journey.
There is also an opportunity to develop more regional cruise packages catering specifically to Malaysian, Indonesian, Thai and other Southeast Asian travellers.
This is a growing market that cruise operators are looking to explore and I think Malaysia is ready for it.

5a2587b6eab93678: Sabtu lalu, Menteri Besar Negeri Sembilan, Ismail Lasim, mengesahkan beliau telah menarik balik surat yang dihantar kepada Penyimpan Mohor Besar Raja-raja berhubung 'penyingkiran' Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir sebagai Yang Dipertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan.
Surat itu juga difahamkan mengesahkan sokongan sebulat suara bekas 10 anggota Majlis Mesyuarat Kerajaan Negeri terhadap Tuanku Muhriz.

Ini membawa kita kepada soalan satu juta ringgit: Bolehkah kita meletakkan kepercayaan kepada Umno Negeri Sembilan? Adakah kata-kata mereka benar-benar ikhlas? Atau adakah ini satu lagi helah untuk cuba menjatuhkan pemerintah negeri?
Teguran terbuka Tuanku Muhriz terhadap Ismail baru-baru ini secara tidak langsung menggambarkan Ismail sebagai seorang yang tidak boleh dipercayai.
Terdapat empat sebab mengapa saya masih sangsi terhadap tindakan Ismail.

1. Kenapa baru sekarang Ismail menarik balik surat itu? Teori saya ialah beliau memerlukan perkenan untuk mengadakan sidang DUN. Walaupun dari segi teori menteri besar boleh mentadbir sesebuah negeri tanpa anggota Majlis Mesyuarat Kerajaan Negeri, sidang DUN diperlukan untuk meluluskan belanjawan dan rang undang-undang.
Perkara ini menimbulkan persoalan: adakah Ismail benar-benar insaf atas tindakannya? Atau beliau hanya terdesak?
2. Tindakan Ismail ketika kontroversi itu

Tindakan Ismail menggambarkan dengan jelas mengenai beliau. Sebelum ini, Ismail berkata beliau dipaksa menandatangani dokumen untuk menurunkan Tuanku Muhriz, namun kemudian menyokong kenyataan Majlis Mesyuarat Kerajaan Negeri yang mengumumkan pemerintah negeri itu telah diturunkan.

Pada 2 Ogos, Ismail mengangkat sumpah sebagai menteri besar di hadapan Tuanku Muhriz dan melafazkan ikrar taat setia kepada baginda. Sehari selepas itu, Ismail menandatangani pengisytiharan untuk menurunkan pemerintah negeri itu.
Ada pepatah yang berbunyi, 'sekali terkena, dua kali beringat'. Namun, dalam keadaan ini, kita sepatutnya empat kali beringat.
3. Isu Undang Luak yang masih belum selesai
Masih terdapat isu membabitkan Undang Luak, termasuk beberapa orang yang telah diturunkan, serta individu yang dilantik oleh mereka sebagai Yang Dipertuan Besar yang baharu.

Kumpulan ini masih rancak dengan aktiviti mereka, dilihat tidak menunjukkan sebarang kekesalan atas tindakan mereka apabila secara terbuka mencabar notis warta Dewan Keadilan dan Undang (DKU) yang mengesahkan penyingkiran dua Undang dan seorang pemimpin adat.
Dikatakan kumpulan ini mempunyai hubungan rapat dengan Adun Umno Negeri Sembilan. Perlu diingat, tiada seorang pun Adun Umno tampil secara terbuka menolak kumpulan tersebut.
Jadi, bagaimana kita sebagai rakyat boleh menaruh kepercayaan terhadap tindakan Ismail menarik balik surat itu sedangkan Umno dipercayai masih mempunyai kaitan dengan kumpulan berkenaan?

4. Adakah Ismail memberikan jaminan melalui perisytiharan bertulis yang ditandatangani bahawa beliau dan kumpulan anggota Umnonya tidak akan sekali-kali lagi berpakat dengan pihak lain untuk menjatuhkan Tuanku Muhriz? Jika Ismail benar-benar insaf, beliau sepatutnya menunjukkan lebih untuk membuktikannya.

Kini, kemenangan besar Umno dalam PRN Melaka akan memberikan parti itu sedikit kelebihan untuk berbangga susulan kontroversi isu tahanan rumah bekas perdana menteri Najib Razak serta kewangan Felda dan Lembaga Tabung Haji, yang tidak menjejaskan sokongan terhadap parti itu.
Umno yang kembali bangkit berkemungkinan lebih berani untuk melakukan satu lagi tindakan serupa di Negeri Sembilan, memandangkan percubaan pertama mereka tidak berjalan seperti yang dirancang.
Tak banyak sebab untuk saya mempercayai Ismail dan Umno Negeri Sembilan ini benar-benar insaf dengan kesalahan mereka.
Artikel ini adalah pandangan penulis dan tidak semestinya mewakili FMT.
a8becbed55c716fd: On Saturday, Negeri Sembilan menteri besar Ismail Lasim confirmed he had withdrawn a letter sent to the Keeper of the Rulers’ Seal concerning the “removal” of Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir as the Yang Dipertuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan.
The letter was also understood to affirm the unanimous support of the 10 sacked executive council members for Tuanku Muhriz.

This brings us to the million-ringgit question: can we trust Negeri Sembilan Umno? Is there any sincerity in what they say? Or is this yet another sleight of hand in an attempt to topple the state ruler?
Tuanku Muhriz's recent public rebuke of Ismail does not paint the latter as someone trustworthy.
There are four reasons why I remain wary of Ismail’s actions.

1. Why is Ismail retracting the letter only now? My theory is that he needs the ruler’s consent to convene the state assembly. While one could, on paper, administer a state without executive councillors, a state assembly sitting is needed to pass budgets and proposed laws.
Which raises this question: is Ismail really remorseful for his actions? Or is he acting out of desperation?
2. Ismail’s actions amid the controversy

They speak volumes about the man himself. He previously said he was coerced into signing a document deposing Tuanku Muhriz, only to later endorse a state executive council statement announcing the ruler’s purported removal.
On Aug 2, Ismail took his oath of office as menteri besar and pledged allegiance to Tuanku Muhriz before signing a proclamation the following day to remove the ruler.
There is a saying, “once bitten, twice shy”. In this instance though, we should be shy four times over.
3. There is still the matter of the other undangs (traditional territorial chieftains), some of whom have been removed, and the matter of the person whom they appointed as the state’s new ruler.

This faction, which is still alive and kicking, has apparently shown no remorse for its actions by openly challenging a Dewan Keadilan dan Undang Negeri Sembilan gazette notice formalising the removal of two chieftains and a customary leader.
It is said that this faction is close to Umno assemblymen in Negeri Sembilan. Mind you, none of the Umno assemblymen have come out to publicly distance themselves from this faction.
So how can we, the people, have any faith in Ismail’s retraction of a letter when Umno is presumably still linked to the said faction?

4. Has Ismail provided assurance via a written and signed declaration that he and his band of Umno men will never again conspire with others to overthrow Tuanku Muhriz? If Ismail were truly repentant, he would have gone the extra mile to show it.

Now, Umno’s decisive win at the Melaka polls will give the party some bragging rights following the controversies over former prime minister Najib Razak’s house arrest and the finances of Felda or Tabung Haji, which did not dent support for the party.
A resurgent Umno is likely to be emboldened to pull off another stunt in Negeri Sembilan, seeing as how the first one didn’t pan out exactly as they planned.
Ismail Lasim and Negeri Sembilan Umno give me very little reason to trust this mea culpa.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
13c955d113761972: It began, as most modern Malaysian sagas do, not with a bang, but with a grumble. A mamak shop, that near-sacred 24-hour temple of roti canai and teh tarik, had the audacity to close its doors on Deepavali day.

The reason? To allow its staff, many of whom are Hindus, to celebrate the Festival of Lights. A simple, humane and frankly logical decision. And yet, within hours, it had ignited a firestorm on social media, transforming a shop’s holiday schedule into a national debate on race, religion and the soul of our nation.
This can only happen in Malaysia. “Mamak tutup? On Deepavali? How can a Muslim-run restaurant close for a Hindu-based celebration?” So began the stream of religious insults and slurs.

For most people, the mamak shop is more than a restaurant; it is a cultural institution, a neutral ground where everyone can sit side-by-side at 3am, arguing over football or who should be the prime minister.

But the debate triggered by the post made out the closure to be almost a betrayal of the social contract. The real fireworks began when the keyboard warriors logged on and the debate fractured along predictable, yet deeply depressing, lines.

On one side, some who described the closure as an act of placing Deepavali celebrations over Islam, an analogy that is mind-boggling. On the other side, those who celebrated the closure as a victory for inclusivity, while simultaneously weaponising it against the owners. A simple act of employee appreciation became a truncheon in the never-ending racial culture war.

The comments sections devolved into a cesspool of racial slurs and religious mockery. The practices of each community – from fasting to praying to celebrating – were dissected, mocked and used as ammunition.

This is the Malaysian paradox. We are a nation that prides itself on our diversity, our muhibbah spirit and our ability to live together. We celebrate each other's festivals with open houses and open hearts. But the moment a minor racial or religious issue is raised, the harmony ruptures and the nation's ugly, tribalistic underbelly is exposed for all to see.

The debate exposed a deep-seated insecurity, the fear of being marginalised, anxiety over the “other” and the constant, exhausting need to assert one's own identity in a multi-racial landscape. The mamak shop became a proxy for a much larger, unresolved national conversation about what it means to be Malaysian.

The fact that we lose our minds over such a small matter is precisely the problem. We have become experts at finding offence, at drawing battle lines over the most trivial of issues. A shop closure becomes a religious war. A wrong word becomes a racial slur. A difference in opinion becomes a declaration of enmity.
We are so quick to insult each other, yet so slow to extend the basic courtesy of understanding.

The next time you see a shop closed for a holiday that isn't “yours”, take a breath. Instead of reaching for your phone to type a scathing comment, maybe reach for a packet of murukku from a Hindu neighbour.
The mamak shop will reopen, but the damage done by our own intolerance, the scars we inflict on our national psyche with every hateful comment, are far harder to heal.
Only in Malaysia can a day of light be turned into a war of darkness. Sadly, that is the most Malaysian thing of all.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
afff4032dd146415: Israel’s laws are built to entrench ethnic domination, and international courts are under attack for noticing
Originally published on Global Voices
Roadblocks at the entrance to Shuhada Street in Hebron, Palestine. Photo by Travel 2 Palestine on Flickr (CC BY 2.0).

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank are subject to Israeli civil law. Palestinians who suffer their violence and occupation are subject to Israeli military law. The two face two different legal systems.

Palestinian, Israeli and international rights groups, and UN findings, have long argued this is not a malfunction of Israeli justice but its design, and that the international system meant to check, and failed to do so, is being taken apart.
Two legal systems, one occupation
For years, Israeli military data has shown conviction rates for Palestinians in Israeli military courts to be anything between 99.74 and 96 percent.

A May 2025 report by Adalah, the legal center for Palestinian citizens of Israel, documents how Israel moved settlement governance in Area C under civilian authority while Palestinians remain under military rule. Adalah calls the arrangement a system of apartheid and de facto annexation.

Inside Israel, the Knesset keeps adding to the structure. Adalah’s Discriminatory Laws Database listed over 65 laws that discriminate against Palestinian citizens of Israel or residents of the occupied territory in 2017. Its November 2025 report reviews more than 30 further laws passed between October 7, 2023 and July 27, 2025, which Adalah says rest on the principle of Jewish ethno-national supremacy that the 2018 Nation-State Law enshrined.

In March 2026, the Knesset passed a death penalty law with 62 votes. Adalah and four other Israeli rights groups argue its wording excludes Israeli Jewish perpetrators of similar offenses, so that in practice it applies only to Palestinians. They have petitioned the Supreme Court to annul it.
Impunity as procedure

The Israeli group Yesh Din has tracked police investigations into settler violence against Palestinians since 2005. Of the files it monitored through 2025, 93.6 percent ended without an indictment, and only about 3 percent ended in a full or partial conviction. Most closures cited an unidentified suspect or insufficient evidence, which Yesh Din attributes to police failures. In roughly half of the nearly 30 mass settler attacks it documented between 2023 and late 2025, soldiers or police were present.

Soldiers face similar odds. In March 2026, the military’s top lawyer dropped charges against five reservists accused of severe sexual and physical abuse against a Palestinian detainee at the Sde Teiman detention camp. Yesh Din said only two indictments existed over soldiers’ conduct in the Gaza war.
Courts have not interrupted the pattern. In March 2025, Israel’s Supreme Court unanimously rejected a petition by five Israeli rights groups seeking unimpeded humanitarian aid into Gaza.
The UN Commission of Inquiry concluded in September 2025 that Israel committed genocide in Gaza, joining findings by Amnesty International and B’Tselem.

In October 2026, the commission added that Israel committed crimes against humanity in the West Bank, including extermination, and that military operations since January 2025 caused the largest displacement there since 1967.
Sanctioning the world courts

In July 2024, the International Court of Justice ruled that Israel’s presence in the occupied territory is unlawful and must end as rapidly as possible. It also found that Israel’s legislation and measures breach Article 3 of the International Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Racial Discrimination (ICERD), which prohibits racial segregation and apartheid. In September 2025, UN experts criticized the failure to act on the General Assembly resolution that followed the ruling.

Meanwhile, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former defense minister Yoav Gallant in November 2024. In December 2025, its Appeals Chamber rejected an Israeli challenge and left the warrants in force.

The reaction to the warrants, like that to the UN findings regarding apartheid, genocide and crimes against humanity perpetrated by Israel, has contributed to the failure of international law in delivering justice.

By August 2026, nine of the court’s 18 judges and both deputy prosecutors were sanctioned by the US. On October 9, 2026, the US sanctioned the ICC itself, citing its jurisdiction over US nationals abroad, after earlier sanctions on three Palestinian human rights groups and UN special rapporteur Francesca Albanese. Human Rights Watch and three other groups have sued in US federal court, and say the aim of the sanctions is to shield US and Israeli officials from prosecution.
A system, not an anomaly

None of this is an aberration of the post-October 7 period, a rogue government or a failure to apply the rules. Adalah traces these laws to Israel’s constitutional and political culture, built on Jewish ethno-national supremacy, and notes that, unlike apartheid South Africa or Jim Crow in the US, “most of the laws cited in the report use neutral legal language.”

The UN Commission of Inquiry reaches the same conclusion from another direction. It traces the root causes back to 1947–1948 and says the aim of seizing maximum land while minimizing the Palestinian population stems from Israel’s colonizing policies.

That is how settler colonial states have always worked. Law does not sit outside the project. It is the project’s instrument. Military rule in the West Bank rests on emergency regulations the British Mandate wrote in 1945 to subdue the local population. Declaring “State land” has been, in Adalah’s words, the primary legal mechanism for taking Palestinian land since the late 1970s. Each layer converts dispossession into a legal procedure: a permit denied, a file closed, a petition dismissed, a statute passed.

Seen this way, the evidence describes one logic working across three levels. Statutes define who holds rights. Police, prosecutors and courts decide whom those rights protect. And the Israeli state has moved to shield itself from outside scrutiny, backed by a US government that now sanctions the institutions that try to apply international law.
A state built to secure one people’s dominance over another people’s land will produce exactly this legal order.
Written by Walid El Houri
4e3b3836efc8ff88: From Hisham Aziz

The corporate anxieties following the tabling of Budget 2027 prompt a critical question: when did Malaysia’s apex industry associations transform from champions of free-market resilience into professional victims of helplessness?
The press releases and policy papers issued by the Federation of Malaysian Manufacturers (FMM) suffer from structural issues that expose their lack of analytical weight and credibility.

FMM’s press statements exhibit the distinct characteristics of automated text generation — relying heavily on template-driven headers, passive phrasing, and generic buzzword aggregation like “supply chain resilience” and “digital transformation” in place of plant-level operational data. This reliance on high-level abstraction obscures true empirical rigor.

Rather than presenting detailed microeconomic data, unit-cost offsets, or lead-time data, FMM’s advocacy frequently uses sweeping language backed by disproportionately small survey sample sizes to demand massive policy concessions like credit lines, grant facilities, and tax deferments.
To the public and policymakers, organisations like FMM present themselves as fragile, over-burdened entities teetering on the edge of ruin due to basic regulatory adjustments.

Yet, a glance at public policy performance reveals an entirely different reality. These bodies represent the primary beneficiaries of decades of state largesse — enjoying extensive energy subsidies, infrastructure support, and generous tax incentives.

Under Budget 2027, this patronage continues unabated with fresh financing facilities from Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) alongside a transitional exemption from the RM2,000 minimum wage threshold for micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs).
Despite this comprehensive safety net, the lobbying apparatus remains ever unquenchable.

In October 2026, FMM publicly expressed deep disappointment, lamenting a “lack of support” for the manufacturing sector simply because the government did not grant their requested RM1.5 billion extra support package. The danger lies not just in this sense of entitlement, but in the dubious, lightweight methodologies used to justify it.

Consider the statistical acrobatics deployed to influence national economic policy. In June 2026, FMM issued sweeping, alarmist warnings about global supply chain shocks — specifically the impact of the Strait of Hormuz conflict on domestic oil prices and SME survival.
The data to back these massive macroeconomic warnings? A survey pool of exactly 196 companies (FMM Geopolitical Impact Survey, June 2026).
To suggest that a survey pool smaller than a single mid-size factory floor can accurately reflect the structural vulnerabilities of Malaysia’s entire SME sector is absurd.
Yet, it is precisely on the back of these minuscule data sets that case studies are built to demand more credit lines, heavier grants, and broad credit deferments from the taxpayer.

This audacity reaches its peak when looking at their tax advocacy. In their September 2026 Business Conditions Survey (1H2026) briefing, FMM aggressively pushed for a return to the Goods and Services Tax (GST) but demanded it be implemented at a rock-bottom introductory rate of 3.0% — down from the historic 6% floor.
According to FMM’s own polling, while 68% of respondents demanded a rate below 5%, a full 41% explicitly called for a 3% rate.

How peak industrial representatives can genuinely look at Malaysia’s expanding national expenditure and rising infrastructure commitments and suggest halving consumption tax revenues is a great wonder.
They demand that public tax collection be gutted for their operational convenience, while simultaneously expecting the public purse to keep funding their multi-billion-ringgit economic safety nets.
FMM’s platform runs completely counter to the Madani government’s explicit agenda to transition Malaysia away from its unhealthy dependency on low-cost, low-skilled migrant labour.
By fighting tooth and nail against statutory wage floors and basic family protections, FMM is actively working to keep Malaysian wages artificially suppressed.
This short-sighted resistance eliminates the exact economic pressure businesses need to innovate.

If labour is kept artificially cheap through state exemptions and structural suppression, manufacturing firms will feel zero urgency to invest in research and development (R&D), upgrade their technology, or pursue genuine, automation-led productivity growth.
It is not possible to build an Industry 4.0 economy on an automated AI-generated script that begs to preserve an Industry 2.0 labour pool.
This irony peaks when looking at how FMM constructs its internal narratives.
In that same 1H2026 Survey, FMM dedicated an entire section to aggressively policing government administration, using curated survey questions to put HRD Corp in a distinctly negative light.

FMM explicitly complained that HRD Corp’s revised e-TRiS grant conditions actively “hindered training and planning” for 44% of businesses, highlighting that rigid bureaucratic rules — like the mandatory 14-day advance approval window — made it nearly impossible to provide urgent training.

FMM will meticulously poll its members to complain about public sector administrative flexibility, and they will rightfully demand accountability following HRD Corp’s financial mismanagement scandals.

Yet, they weaponize these administrative hurdles as a convenient shield to demand that training funds remain entirely under corporate autonomy. We see this exact transactional morality in their response to parental benefits.

While FMM aggressively fought the statutory 98-day maternity leave mandate as an unbearable operational cost when forced to pay for it, they happily celebrate the newly proposed Budget 2027 post-maternity allowance simply because the state is funding it through the Employment Insurance System (EIS).

They expect national tax revenues to be minimised and public funding maximised whenever it protects their corporate ledger but completely reject socioeconomic flexibility when asked to internally finance a liveable wage or grant a recovering mother an extra month of leave.
The government must stop treating these large corporate blocks as fragile patients in need of permanent economic life support.
True economic restructuring requires rigorous data, authentic feedback, and shared sacrifice. Not fake narratives and political manipulation.
Policymakers should look past the AI-generated statements and reports based on questionable methodologies and unreliable sample sizes and look closely at the empirical reality.

Malaysia’s industrial sector is well-capitalised and heavily subsidised. It is time they scaled up through innovation, automation, and R&D, rather than lobbying their way out of basic social contracts.
Malaysia’s manufacturing cannot be on permanent life-support to pander to a small group of people, nor held ransom by people using trade associations for their political agenda.
Hisham Aziz is an FMT reader.

8a6b39297448afa6: From Sadiq Asyraf

When Umno president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi left the hall at the Melaka International Trade Centre on Saturday night, he was not sent off with a victory song. Barisan Nasional supporters chanted one word, over and over: "Bubar!" Dissolve.

Umno still sits in the unity coalition government, and its president is one of the two deputy prime ministers. But since September, BN has said it will leave the government the moment Parliament is dissolved.

Spontaneous or not, the chant fits Umno's position all year, which might be called minimum loyalty: do exactly what the coalition agreement requires and nothing more. That lets Umno push the government towards the edge without pulling it down itself.
Minimum loyalty

Umno information chief Azalina Othman Said set out the limits the day before polling. On her reading, the agreement obliges Umno to back the prime minister only on confidence votes, supply bills and procedural motions touching the government's legitimacy. Beyond that, Umno is free to disagree.

That reading covers Umno's conduct this year: going solo in Johor, partnering Perikatan Nasional in Negeri Sembilan and Melaka, and defending the conditional pardon of former prime minister Najib Razak against DAP's objections. All of it sits within the letter of the agreement.
Umno supplies just enough votes to keep the government standing while campaigning against its partners in the states. The unity government now rests more on seat arithmetic than on trust.

Azalina answered DAP's call for Umno ministers to resign with four options: mediate, stay calm, end the agreement, or review the clause on Islam, the Malays and the Rulers at the risk of unpredictable consequences.

With no termination clause in the agreement, Azalina presented dissolution as the logical political outcome. But ending a coalition agreement does not, by itself, constitutionally require Parliament to be dissolved. The next move, she told DAP, was theirs.
Read together, the options allow Umno to shift to Pakatan Harapan much of the immediate political cost of a rupture.

On Tuesday, Zahid said he would rather see Parliament dissolved than the Cabinet reshuffled. On Thursday, after DAP's challenge, he said BN still backed Anwar Ibrahim federally. On Saturday, his victory press conference spoke of a hattrick and, according to media reports, not of dissolution. About 40 minutes later, his supporters at the MITC entrance said it for him.

Unless the leadership distances itself from the chant, it is one message sent through two channels. Agenda-setting theory explains why the second channel matters: the media may not decide what audiences think, but they shape what audiences think about. Supporters filmed and shared the "Bubar!" clips themselves.

The likely effect is to shift attention from BN's victory in a state contest to the stability of the federal government. The question of the week becomes when Parliament will be dissolved, and it is the prime minister, rather than Umno, who is pressed to answer it.

PH plays the same game. Two nights before polling, Anwar quipped that some government critics sat beside him in Cabinet, then said he was not targeting Zahid. The same night, defending DAP, he asked whether it was DAP that had been responsible for the problems at Tabung Haji, Felda and 1MDB, a pointed reference to administrations led by his own federal partner.
After the results, he offered congratulations and cooperation. Both partners campaign against each other, then make up on paper.
The dissolution trap

Melaka gave the dissolution push its evidence. According to official results, BN won 21 seats, PN three and PH four, all of them urban DAP seats. BN matched its 2021 tally, and the combined BN and PN vote share barely moved, at about 63%.

The difference is that BN and PN no longer split their votes by contesting against one another. PH's share fell from 35.7 to 29.3%. Its candidates in Ayer Limau and Serkam lost their deposits with less than 12% of the vote.
That shifts bargaining power: PH has struggled to demonstrate electoral strength in Malay-majority constituencies, while Umno remains the government's principal Malay political partner.

The strategy has limits. PN won three of its five allotted seats, including Bukit Katil from PH. Outside government, Umno would face the same PN partners for Malay-majority seats at GE16 without the advantages of office.

Minimum loyalty pays best while Umno is inside the government. That creates a strong incentive for Umno to let PH initiate any rupture, so that it can present itself as the party that honoured the agreement until the end.

For Anwar, every exit has a price. Dissolving now means facing BN and PN together at PH's weakest point, after setbacks in Sabah, Johor, Negeri Sembilan and Melaka. Holding on lets Umno enjoy power in Putrajaya while building the story of a government clinging to office.

Some DAP supporters want Umno ministers sacked. Whether the government could survive without BN's MPs depends on parliamentary arithmetic that has shifted this year. But the case for keeping Umno is political as much as numerical: it is the government's principal Malay political partner. Melaka suggests that value is under strain, and sacking Umno would simply set it free.
Whatever Anwar decides, minimum loyalty gives Umno a ready story. Sacked, it leaves as the betrayed partner. If Parliament is dissolved, it is merely keeping its promise to the king.

The unity government may yet be reshaped or run its full term. But if the partnership does break, the contest that matters will be over who controls the story of the separation. On Saturday night, Umno's supporters showed they intend to write the first draft.
Sadiq Asyraf is a political communication and media warfare analyst.
